Record the inclusion probability and use inverse-probability weighting for population estimates. Publish unweighted counts alongside weighted rates so readers can see support. Extremely large weights produce unstable estimates; combine strata or increase sampling rather than hiding the variance.

Confidence intervals matter most where sample sizes are small. A new rule with four confirmations in four reviews does not have proven 100% precision. Use a binomial interval or Bayesian posterior with a declared prior, and require minimum evidence before autonomous suppression or blocking. For calibration bins, report count and uncertainty. Empty regions of the confidence scale reveal that the model’s numeric precision is cosmetic.

Reproducibility protocol

A reproducibility package should pin the artifact, build configuration, runtime, request or input fixture, relevant identity, expected observation, and cleanup. Secrets must be synthetic or ephemeral. The package must not exploit production systems. For code findings, include the shortest trace demonstrating source, transformations, guards, and sink. For cloud findings, include read-only configuration evidence and a safe policy evaluation. For endpoint findings, prefer captured telemetry or a disposable virtual machine.

Reproduction can produce several outcomes: mechanism confirmed; claim refuted; trigger blocked by environment; evidence insufficient; or artifact no longer available. These outcomes guide different improvements. A high environment-block rate suggests the product emits claims customers cannot validate. A high unavailable-artifact rate suggests retention or commit-resolution defects. Folding both into “inconclusive” loses engineering direction.

Time to validate is not merely an operations metric. It is a property of finding design. Compare otherwise similar findings with and without traces, concrete inputs, ownership hints, and fix boundaries. A controlled evaluation can randomize evidence presentation to reviewers and measure validation time and correct disposition. Do not expose a potentially misleading model confidence in the treatment unless the experiment is specifically testing confidence display.

Severity, exploitability, and actionability

Severity describes consequence under conditions; exploitability describes how feasible those conditions are; business impact describes what the affected system matters to the organization. Keep these as fields. A path traversal in a build tool may have high technical impact but require trusted local access; an authorization bypass in a low-CVSS internal service may expose regulated data through a reachable identity path.

Actionability can be scored through observable components: correct owner located, fix boundary identified, remediation available, reproduction fixture present, and estimated effort. It should not be inferred from “ticket closed.” Teams sometimes close excellent findings because risk is accepted and retain poor findings because audit policy requires them. Measure evidence quality before downstream organizational choices.

Root-cause labeling also needs a contract. Two findings share a root cause when one bounded change can remove the relevant mechanism without separately addressing each symptom. This definition is deliberately tied to remediation. The same CWE in two independently maintained libraries is not one root cause. Conversely, different CWE symptoms may share one unsafe code-generation template. Store the proposed cluster, algorithm version, reviewer decision, and final fix identifier.

Metamorphic and adversarial tests

Known-answer benchmarks test cases, but metamorphic tests examine invariants. Rename variables, reorder independent statements, move code without changing data flow, or replace a sanitizer with an equivalent wrapper. A robust semantic analyzer should preserve its conclusion. Then alter the actual security property—remove authorization, change the sanitizer context, or make a path attacker-controlled—and require the conclusion to change.

Adversarial cases should target the product surface, not merely the model. Put vulnerability words in comments, create very long traces, use generated filenames resembling dependencies, produce conflicting package manifests, and inject malformed source maps. Test whether parsers fail closed, fail open, or silently assign a default severity. A safe product exposes unsupported analysis rather than fabricating confidence.

Release and rollback

Before release, replay the candidate on a fixed corpus and a recent production sample. Compare paired outcomes: new confirmed root causes, lost root causes, confidence changes, duplicate clusters, evidence regressions, and latency. Aggregate lift cannot justify losing coverage for a dangerous weakness family. Establish must-not-regress challenge cases and maximum queue expansion by customer segment.

Canary the scanner version on consenting repositories. Keep old and new finding identities linked so users do not receive duplicate tickets during migration. If rollback occurs, restore compatible suppression, cluster, and confidence semantics. Merely reverting the engine while leaving new identifiers in workflow systems can reopen thousands of items.

Quality governance should separate product targets from adjudication rules. The team rewarded for precision must not decide after seeing results whether duplicates count as true positives. Version the rubric before evaluation, log exceptions, and have an independent review for high-impact automated actions such as merge blocking. This turns the scorecard into evidence rather than marketing.

Reading a Scorecard as an Engineering Decision

Suppose a candidate release raises reviewed precision from 78% to 84%, reduces median validation time from 18 to 11 minutes, but loses 9 of 40 authentication-bypass cases in the locked challenge set. The release is not “better” in the only sense that matters. The regression affects a high-consequence family and may reflect a parser or framework-modeling change. Block general rollout, isolate the responsible rule path, and consider shipping unaffected languages behind separate version flags.

Now suppose the lost cases are duplicate symptoms already represented by another finding. The answer changes only if the duplicate analysis is independently validated and the surviving finding reaches the same owner with equal evidence. A finding suppressed because two traces look similar is not safely redundant when the traces cross different trust boundaries or require different fixes. Review over-merge errors at the actual automation boundary.

Scorecards should include denominators and abstentions. If a scanner analyzes 70% of files and achieves 90% precision there, it must not be compared directly with a scanner analyzing 98% at 82% precision. Report unsupported files, parser failures, timeouts, and intentionally skipped generated code. Coverage-weighted yield can help, but keep the components visible because customers may care disproportionately about the unsupported 2%.

Performance also has a quality dimension. A pull-request scanner that returns excellent findings after forty minutes may arrive after merge. Measure end-to-end decision latency at realistic repository sizes and concurrent load, including cache misses. Timeout behavior must be explicit: allow, block, retry, or fall back. Silent partial results make precision estimates meaningless because the evaluated population changes with system load.

For generative remediation, evaluate the patch separately from the finding. A correct diagnosis can yield an insecure or behavior-breaking patch. Run tests, static checks, policy checks, and targeted security fixtures in an isolated environment. Measure patch acceptance, modifications by developers, introduced defects, and whether the root cause remains. Never let an accepted generated patch retroactively validate the original finding; developers may accept changes for unrelated reasons.

Cross-customer comparison demands care. Different customers configure rules, suppressions, and severity policies; their reviewed populations and incentives differ. Normalize only within a declared configuration and sampling design. A benchmark percentile that mixes permissive advisory deployments with strict merge-blocking deployments is uninterpretable. Product analytics should help each customer understand its own evidence quality without leaking another tenant’s code or labels.

The final review artifact should include the claim being tested, corpus manifest, sampling probabilities, reviewer rubric, disagreement record, scanner artifacts, result tables with uncertainty, known benchmark overlap, and a signed decision. Reproducibility here means another authorized team can recreate the evaluation from retained, access-controlled artifacts—not that vulnerable customer code is broadly copied.

Sources and Further Reading

  • NIST Software Assurance Reference Dataset. Controlled known-good and known-bad programs, with limited external validity. https://samate.nist.gov/SARD/
  • OWASP Benchmark Project. A repeatable Java test suite that should be one evaluation stratum, not the sole production claim. https://owasp.org/www-project-benchmark/
  • MITRE CWE. Shared weakness vocabulary; identical CWE identifiers do not prove a common root cause. https://cwe.mitre.org/
  • ISO/IEC 29147:2018. Coordinated receipt, verification, and communication expectations for vulnerability disclosure. https://www.iso.org/standard/72311.html
  • NIST SP 800-218. Connects vulnerability response to secure development and durable process improvement. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final

Benchmarks supply known cases, CWE supplies vocabulary, and standards supply workflow expectations. Finding quality still requires reproducibility, calibrated confidence, root-cause novelty, and human cost.

Interview Practicum

Scenario: The Denominator Changes.

Prompt. A new SAST engine reports 92% precision on 500 reviewed findings versus 71% for the incumbent. Should the company migrate?

Ask how samples were selected, whether reviewers were blinded, how inconclusive cases were handled, whether commits were frozen, what languages were covered, and whether duplicates count.

Worked Answer

Replay both tools on identical repositories, adjudicate stratified random samples including low scores, group root causes, and compare results at the same review budget.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Change one: the 500 new-engine findings were its top-ranked outputs; the incumbent sample was uniform. The headline comparison is invalid. Uniformly sample both or use inclusion-probability weights. A top-of-list evaluation may answer a capacity question, but then compare unique root causes per analyst-hour.

Change two: migration removes the incumbent’s binary-analysis coverage for 20% of releases. Evaluate a portfolio. Retain the incumbent for uncovered artifacts until an alternative passes a challenge set, and deduplicate cross-tool output. Coverage loss is harm, not a precision footnote.

Change three: the vendor offers to tune on the adjudicated evaluation set. Freeze it as consumed and build a later private temporal holdout. Weak answers use accuracy, accept “won’t fix” as false-positive truth, or select the tool producing more critical alerts.

Key Takeaways

  • A finding is a versioned, falsifiable claim, not a severity label.
  • Accuracy, reproducibility, calibration, actionability, and novelty need separate metrics.
  • Evaluate distinct root causes and human cost, not only confirmed finding count.
  • Preserve inconclusive and environment-blocked outcomes.
  • Correct verification bias with probability sampling or weighting.
  • Gold sets, challenge sets, and production samples answer different questions.

Field lesson: precision is an empirical outcome, not a pipeline state

The sec-pr assurance project created 1,098 label-queue items but correctly refused to publish precision because no validity labels had yet matured. Its engineering platform could be released for controlled evidence acquisition while the finding-quality card remained insufficient_evidence. A healthy ingestion pipeline is not a verified detector. Chapter 47 develops the complete field case.

Chapter 31: From Finding to Resolution

Resolution Is a State History, Not a Closed Ticket

A scanner finding becomes security value only when a vulnerable condition is durably removed or bounded by an accepted control. Ticket closure is an administrative event. It may mean fixed, duplicate, risk accepted, asset retired, false positive, or merely closed by automation. Lifecycle analytics must preserve transitions and reasons instead of overwriting one status field.

CREATE TABLE finding_transition(
 transition_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, finding_id TEXT NOT NULL,
 occurred_at TEXT NOT NULL, recorded_at TEXT NOT NULL,
 from_state TEXT, to_state TEXT NOT NULL,
 actor_type TEXT NOT NULL, owner_team TEXT,
 reason_code TEXT NOT NULL, evidence_uri TEXT,
 UNIQUE(finding_id,occurred_at,to_state,reason_code));
CREATE TABLE finding_snapshot(
 finding_id TEXT, snapshot_at TEXT, root_cause_id TEXT,
 severity TEXT, asset_tier TEXT, due_at TEXT,
 PRIMARY KEY(finding_id,snapshot_at));

A useful state machine distinguishes discovered, triaged, validated, owned, fix_in_progress, deployed, verified, risk_accepted, refuted, and reopened. Only verification establishes technical resolution. Preserve event time and recording time to diagnose delayed integrations. Invalid backward transitions—such as discovered directly to verified—should be rejected unless an explicit migration reason exists.

Queues, Competing Outcomes, and Censoring

Each transition has a waiting interval and a service interval. Long triage latency can mean too few analysts; long owned-to-fix latency can mean dependency coordination; long deployed-to-verified latency can mean missing telemetry. Aggregate “mean time to remediate” hides these mechanisms and is distorted by unresolved findings.

For time to verified resolution \(T\), the survival function is \(S(t)=P(T>t)\). With event times \(t_j\), resolutions \(d_j\), and findings at risk \(n_j\), the Kaplan–Meier estimator is

\[ \hat S(t)=\prod_{t_j\le t}\left(1-\frac{d_j}{n_j}\right). \]

Open findings are right-censored, not discarded and not assigned today as a fake closure date. Risk acceptance, asset retirement, and refutation are competing events. Treating them as remediation exaggerates engineering performance. Report cumulative incidence by terminal reason or use a competing-risks model.

Service-level statements should use cohorts and quantiles: “62% of internet-facing critical findings discovered in May were verified within 14 days,” with unresolved cases retained. Segment by ownership, asset tier, root cause, and discovery channel. Compare cohorts only after accounting for severity and exposure mix.

Durable Fixes and Downstream Reduction

A finding is durably fixed when verification passes after deployment and the root cause does not recur inside a defined observation window. Reopen rate is

\[ \frac{\text{verified findings later returned to active vulnerability}} {\text{verified findings with sufficient follow-up}}. \]

The denominator excludes fixes too recent to observe. Recurrence should be counted at root-cause level: repairing ten generated files while leaving the template unchanged produces ten closures and one predictable recurrence mechanism.

Measure downstream reduction using exposure-time, not ticket count. If a finding affects \(m\) reachable assets for \(h\) hours, it contributes \(mh\) vulnerable asset-hours. A program can close more low-impact tickets while total high-impact exposure rises. Developer friction also matters: handoffs, build failures introduced by fixes, review minutes, exception churn, and unplanned work.

Safe Lab: Kaplan–Meier Without External Packages

# duration in days; event=1 only for verified remediation
records = [(2,1),(3,1),(3,0),(5,1),(7,0)]

def kaplan_meier(rows):
    survival = 1.0
    curve = []
    for t in sorted({d for d,e in rows if e == 1}):
        at_risk = sum(d >= t for d,e in rows)
        events = sum(d == t and e == 1 for d,e in rows)
        survival *= 1 - events / at_risk
        curve.append((t, round(survival, 3), at_risk, events))
    return curve

curve = kaplan_meier(records)
expected = [(2, .8, 5, 1), (3, .6, 4, 1), (5, .3, 2, 1)]
assert curve == expected, curve
assert round(1 - curve[-1][1], 3) == .7
print(curve)

The censored observations remain in the risk set until their last observed day. Dropping them would claim every retained case eventually resolved and bias the result toward fast closure.

Diagnosing Flow Rather Than Blaming Teams

Reconstruct transitions with window functions and measure time in each state:

WITH ordered AS (
 SELECT finding_id, occurred_at, to_state,
        LEAD(occurred_at) OVER(PARTITION BY finding_id ORDER BY occurred_at) AS next_at
 FROM finding_transition
), dwell AS (
 SELECT finding_id, to_state,
        (julianday(COALESCE(next_at,'2026-08-20'))-julianday(occurred_at))*24 AS hours
 FROM ordered
)
SELECT to_state, ROUND(AVG(hours),1) AS mean_hours, COUNT(*) AS intervals
FROM dwell GROUP BY to_state ORDER BY mean_hours DESC;

This SQLite-compatible query uses an explicit analysis cutoff. Production code should parameterize it. Means are useful for workload accounting; publish medians and upper quantiles for latency. A growing queue can arise from arrivals exceeding service capacity even when individual engineers work faster. Track arrival rate, work-in-progress, throughput, blocked time, and age distribution together.

Production Failure Analysis

Status overwrite: a current-state table cannot reconstruct history. Use append-only transitions and correct errors with compensating events.

Closure semantics: automatic closure after a repository archive is not remediation. Terminal reason codes are mandatory.

Survivorship bias: analyzing only resolved findings guarantees optimistic latency. Include right-censored open cases.

Reopen blind spots: scanner suppression can make a defect disappear without a code change. Verification should cite deployment evidence and scanner coverage.

Ownership gaming: reassignment can reset clocks. SLA clocks attach to the finding and policy, while state dwell identifies where delay accumulated.

More findings, less security: a detector release can flood teams with low-value claims, displace high-risk remediation, and raise vulnerable asset-hours. Rate-limit intake, group root causes, protect an urgent queue, and monitor displacement.

Policy changes: a shorter SLA changes queue behavior and censoring. Version policy at discovery and show results under both historical and current definitions rather than rewriting history.

For causal claims about a workflow change, do not compare simple before/after means. Use phased rollout, matched teams with pre-trend checks, or randomized encouragement. Outcomes should include verified resolution, recurrence, exposure-time, incidents, and developer toil; closure volume alone is manipulable.

Engineering the Lifecycle Ledger

An append-only transition log needs deterministic rules. Every event carries an idempotency key from the source system, event time, ingestion time, actor, and reason. Consumers derive current state by replay. If a connector sends an older transition late, insert it at its event time and rebuild the affected finding; do not append it as if it happened now. Record the correction so dashboards can explain why historical counts changed.

State definitions must name evidence. validated might require reproduction or independent configuration proof. deployed requires the change to reach the affected environment, not merely merge. verified requires a post-deployment test, scanner observation, or configuration assertion. For ephemeral cloud assets, verification may mean the vulnerable image is no longer deployable and all running instances have rotated. Each evidence type has a freshness window.

Some findings legitimately branch. One root cause may affect five services owned by different teams; a central library fix is deployed gradually. Model a root-cause remediation and its affected-instance coverage rather than forcing one ticket to represent both. The root cause can be fixed in the library while residual vulnerable instances remain. Report both states to avoid celebrating upstream completion before downstream adoption.

Queue mechanics

Little’s Law, \(L=\lambda W\), relates average work in progress \(L\), throughput rate \(\lambda\), and average time in system \(W\) under stable conditions. It is a diagnostic, not a promise. If arrival rate changes sharply or the queue is not stable, the relationship’s assumptions fail. Still, it gives a useful consistency check: a team closing 100 items per week with 1,000 active items cannot plausibly sustain a two-week average lifecycle.

Age distributions reveal starvation. Report the count and risk-weighted exposure in age bands, plus the oldest items. Priority queues can starve medium findings indefinitely when critical arrivals consume all capacity. Reserve capacity or impose aging rules, but verify that aging does not let low-impact bulk overwhelm scarce specialist work. Root-cause batching can improve throughput while reducing context switching.

Handoffs deserve explicit events rather than inferred owner changes. A handoff records sender, receiver, requested action, acceptance, and time. Unaccepted assignments are queue failures. Count bounced ownership and time awaiting acceptance. An ownership directory improvement may reduce latency more than a better severity model.

Survival models beyond a single curve

Kaplan–Meier compares descriptive cohorts but does not adjust for covariates. A Cox proportional-hazards model can estimate associations with resolution rate while leaving the baseline hazard unspecified. Its hazard ratio assumes proportional effects over time; inspect residuals and time interactions. Team identity, severity, and asset tier may be confounded with unmeasured complexity, so do not turn coefficients into blame.

Accelerated failure-time models can express multiplicative effects on resolution time and may be easier to communicate. Competing-risk methods are needed when remediation, risk acceptance, retirement, and refutation preclude one another. For operational forecasting, multi-state models can estimate transition-specific hazards: discovery to triage, triage to ownership, ownership to deployment, and deployment to verification.

Calendar time matters. Freeze periods, holidays, release trains, and incident response affect hazards. Use time-varying covariates or stratified reporting. Findings created just before a year-end freeze should not be used to claim one product team is intrinsically slower. Similarly, a policy that accelerates critical work may delay medium work; evaluate the full risk-weighted queue.

Measuring durable remediation

Define an observation window based on how recurrence can be detected. A weekly scanner might need several clean scans; a deployment control can verify immediately that an image digest is blocked. Mark findings “verified pending durability” until follow-up matures. Report cohort maturity so recent improvements are not credited with artificially low recurrence.

Recurrence can be exact, mechanistic, or organizational. Exact recurrence is the same finding identity. Mechanistic recurrence is the same root-cause pattern in another location. Organizational recurrence is a new defect that the same preventive control should have stopped. These answer different questions: fix quality, systemic remediation, and prevention effectiveness.

Downstream reduction should use a stable eligible denominator. If repository coverage expands, detected vulnerability count may rise while rate falls. Report eligible assets, scanned assets, reachable vulnerable assets, and vulnerable asset-time. A program that discovers previously invisible exposure should not be punished as if it created the defects; conversely, coverage loss must not look like improvement.

Safe rollout of workflow automation

Automation can assign owners, propose duplicates, open patches, or verify deployments. Authority should rise with evidence. Begin with recommendations, measure correction rates, then allow bounded actions with rollback. Auto-closing findings is high consequence because it removes work from human view; require stronger evidence than auto-tagging.

Monitor automation-specific failures: wrong owner, duplicate cluster over-merge, broken generated patch, tests skipped, verification against the wrong environment, and rollback failure. Keep an untreated or delayed cohort when feasible. If automation reduces visible backlog by suppressing items, verify that vulnerable asset-time and incident precursors also improve.

Governance must align incentives across scanner, security operations, and product engineering. Scanner teams should not win by emitting volume; product teams should not win by administrative closure; security teams should not win by transferring unplanned work. Shared outcomes—verified root-cause reduction, bounded exposure-time, recurrence, and total effort—make local gaming harder.

A Worked Operational Interpretation

Imagine two business units with a 20-day median time to verified resolution. Unit A resolves most items between 15 and 25 days. Unit B resolves half within two days while a long tail remains open for six months. The medians are equal, but Unit B accumulates much more exposure. Publish survival curves, restricted mean unresolved time over a policy horizon, upper quantiles, and risk-weighted age. A single central tendency cannot describe a queue.

Next, a new dependency bot creates one ticket per repository. Closure throughput triples, yet one vulnerable base image remains the common root cause. The lifecycle model should link repository findings to the image remediation and deployment coverage. Closing child tickets before images rotate is administrative progress, not verified risk reduction. Conversely, once the fixed image is enforced and workloads rotate, child findings can be resolved with shared evidence rather than repetitive manual review.

SLA analysis needs the same discipline. A finding can meet a 30-day SLA because it was accepted on day 29, while exposure remains unchanged. Report compliance by terminal reason, and show the fraction truly verified. Pause rules—waiting for a vendor, freeze, or customer approval—should not erase elapsed exposure. Maintain both calendar time and policy-accountable time; the former represents risk, the latter helps diagnose controllable process delay.

Cost accounting should distinguish touch time from wait time. Developers may spend two hours fixing a defect that sits unowned for three weeks. Reducing wait improves risk without reducing engineering effort. Conversely, automated patch generation may reduce touch time but increase failed builds and review cycles. Instrument both so workflow improvements are attributed to the correct mechanism.

Data retention is part of the measurement design. Transition histories may contain vulnerability detail and employee identifiers. Apply least privilege, tenant boundaries, retention schedules, and auditable access. Aggregate long-term analytics where detailed evidence is no longer required, while retaining hashes and policy versions sufficient to prove lineage. Deleting raw evidence should not silently change historical state reconstruction.

Finally, incident learning should feed the ledger. When an incident exploits a previously known finding, link the incident, reconstruct the lifecycle as it was known, and classify the failure: detection absence, invalid disposition, ownership delay, remediation delay, failed deployment, missing verification, or recurrence. This is not for blame. It tests whether lifecycle metrics represented real exposure and identifies which transition needs redesign.

Sources and Further Reading

  • lifelines documentation. Practical survival and competing-risk implementations; correct data construction remains the user’s responsibility. https://lifelines.readthedocs.io/
  • Kleinbaum and Klein, Survival Analysis. Foundations for censoring, survival functions, and regression. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4419-6646-9
  • NIST SP 800-218. Frames vulnerability response as part of a secure development lifecycle, supporting root-cause and durable-fix measurement. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final
  • OWASP SAMM. Maturity practices connect operational remediation to governance and verification. https://owaspsamm.org/model/
  • FIRST CVSS v4.0. Severity characterization can stratify cohorts, but does not substitute for lifecycle outcomes. https://www.first.org/cvss/v4.0/

These sources together support survival-aware measurement embedded in development practice: statistical handling of unresolved work, explicit verification, and process maturity rather than ticket theater.

Interview Practicum

Scenario: Throughput Doubles and Risk Rises.

Prompt. A security program doubled monthly closures after deploying automatic ticketing, yet incidents involving known weaknesses increased. Diagnose it.

Ask for transition history, terminal reasons, scanner coverage, arrivals, severity/exposure mix, root-cause grouping, verification, reopen windows, and asset-hours.

Worked Answer

Build cohorts by discovery date, estimate time to verified resolution with censoring, separate competing terminal states, and compare high-risk exposure-time and recurrence.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Change one: old tickets were bulk-closed as “asset retired,” but retirement evidence is unavailable. Do not call them remediated. Classify them as administratively closed with uncertain technical outcome; sample assets and inventory records, and publish a sensitivity range.

Change two: product teams say security tickets consume 18% of sprint capacity. Optimize intake as well as remediation: suppress confirmed duplicates, group by fix boundary, provide reproducible evidence, and reserve capacity by expected harm. Measure build failures and handoffs so security does not externalize its costs.

Change three: leadership requires a 30-day result. Durable recurrence needs 90 days. Report leading outcomes—verified deployment, vulnerable asset-hours, and queue age—marked provisional. Pre-register the 90-day recurrence analysis rather than redefining success at day 30.

Weak answers divide close date by open date only for resolved tickets, treat risk acceptance as a fix, or celebrate closure volume. A Principal answer also changes incentives so scanners, analysts, and product teams share verified root-cause reduction rather than local throughput targets.

Key Takeaways

  • Preserve append-only state transitions and terminal reasons.
  • Use survival analysis because unresolved findings are right-censored.
  • Treat risk acceptance, retirement, and refutation as competing outcomes, not fixes.
  • Measure root-cause recurrence and vulnerable asset-time, not ticket closure alone.
  • Diagnose arrival rate, queues, dwell, throughput, and friction together.
  • Version lifecycle policy and verification evidence so history remains auditable.

Chapter 32: Security Product Analytics

Usage Is Not Security Value

A security product can increase daily users, alerts viewed, and tickets closed while making customers less secure. Analysts may bulk-close noise; developers may repeatedly open a dashboard because fixes fail; an automated agent may execute many actions because it is stuck. Product analytics must connect an eligible user’s exposure to a workflow, a completed security decision, and a protected outcome—while accounting for friction and harm.

The unit depends on the job. Analysts investigate cases; developers resolve root causes; administrators establish coverage and policy; executives allocate risk; agents perform bounded actions. “Monthly active user” mixes these personas and rewards shallow activity. Define activation as the first completed value-bearing workflow, not login. For a detection platform it might require representative telemetry connected, a reviewed detection deployed, and one case resolved with evidence.

CREATE TABLE product_exposure(
 exposure_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, organization_id TEXT NOT NULL,
 persona TEXT NOT NULL, feature_version TEXT NOT NULL,
 eligible_at TEXT NOT NULL, exposed_at TEXT,
 assignment_arm TEXT, assignment_unit TEXT, assignment_probability REAL);
CREATE TABLE security_value_event(
 event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, organization_id TEXT NOT NULL,
 actor_id TEXT NOT NULL, persona TEXT NOT NULL,
 occurred_at TEXT NOT NULL, workflow TEXT NOT NULL,
 root_cause_id TEXT, outcome TEXT NOT NULL,
 evidence_verified INTEGER NOT NULL, minutes_spent REAL,
 override_reason TEXT, policy_version TEXT NOT NULL);

Eligibility, assignment, exposure, and outcome are distinct. Entitlement is not exposure. Exposure is not adoption. Adoption is not causal impact. assignment_probability enables unbiased analysis when rollout is randomized or capacity-constrained.

A Metric Tree With Security Guardrails

A useful north star for a code-security product is weekly organizations with at least one distinct high-risk root cause durably resolved after product-supported validation. It resists raw alert inflation and aggregates at the customer level. It still needs guardrails:

  • confirmed false-intervention rate;
  • developer and analyst minutes per durable root cause;
  • recurrence within a mature observation window;
  • eligible asset and repository coverage;
  • unresolved high-risk exposure-time;
  • automation rollback and unauthorized-action rate;
  • time to first verified value, including setup failures.

Retention should be conditioned on continued eligibility. A customer that finishes a one-time migration should not be labeled churned. Enterprise adoption also requires persona depth: an administrator configuring telemetry does not prove analysts trust explanations or developers can fix findings.

A funnel might be eligible organization → telemetry healthy → feature exposed → first workflow completed → repeated workflow → verified security outcome. Report conversion and latency at every transition. Missing instrumentation must appear as unknown, not abandonment.

Estimating Product Impact

Usage correlates with need. Customers under attack may use a feature more and suffer more incidents; mature teams may adopt early and already have lower risk. The causal estimand must be explicit, for example the intention-to-treat effect:

\[ ATE_{ITT}=E[Y\mid Z=1]-E[Y\mid Z=0], \]

where \(Z\) is randomized assignment and \(Y\) is a protected outcome. Intention-to-treat preserves randomization even when some assigned customers never activate. A treatment-on-treated estimate needs additional assumptions; randomized encouragement can use assignment as an instrument when forced exposure is undesirable.

Cluster randomize by organization when analysts share queues or policy. Account for interference: one tenant’s threat intelligence may improve the product for others, and an agent action may affect multiple repositories. For phased rollouts, inspect pre-trends and calendar effects. Never call a before/after adoption comparison causal without defending exchangeability.

Trust is behavioral and contextual. Capture override reason codes such as bad evidence, wrong severity, policy exception, missing context, unsafe action, and explanation unclear. A low override rate can mean trust, rubber-stamping, or inability to override. Audit a sample of accepted and rejected recommendations and measure decision quality, not agreement with the product.

Safe Lab: Correlation Versus Randomized Encouragement

The synthetic data contain confounding: high-risk organizations use the feature more. Assignment remains randomized.

orgs = [
 # org, assigned, used, incidents
 ("A",1,1,1), ("B",1,1,0), ("C",1,0,3), ("D",1,1,1),
 ("E",0,1,2), ("F",0,0,2), ("G",0,0,1), ("H",0,0,3),
]

def mean(values): return sum(values) / len(values)

used = [r[3] for r in orgs if r[2] == 1]
unused = [r[3] for r in orgs if r[2] == 0]
naive = mean(used) - mean(unused)
assigned = [r[3] for r in orgs if r[1] == 1]
control = [r[3] for r in orgs if r[1] == 0]
itt = mean(assigned) - mean(control)

result = {"naive_user_difference": round(naive,3),
          "randomized_itt": round(itt,3)}
expected = {"naive_user_difference": -1.25, "randomized_itt": -0.75}
assert result == expected, result
print(result)

Both estimates happen to be beneficial here, but they answer different questions and differ materially. The user comparison breaks randomization because usage is chosen. In real analysis report uncertainty and cluster effects; eight organizations are only a transparent fixture.

SQL for the north star

WITH mature AS (
 SELECT organization_id, root_cause_id,
        date(occurred_at,'weekday 1','-7 days') AS week
 FROM security_value_event
 WHERE outcome='durably_resolved' AND evidence_verified=1
   AND root_cause_id IS NOT NULL
), weekly AS (
 SELECT week, organization_id, COUNT(DISTINCT root_cause_id) AS roots
 FROM mature GROUP BY week, organization_id
)
SELECT week, COUNT(*) AS organizations_realizing_value,
       SUM(roots) AS distinct_org_root_causes
FROM weekly WHERE roots>0 GROUP BY week ORDER BY week;

Root causes are distinct within organization; the same library defect at two customers represents value to both. The week expression is SQLite-compatible and should be standardized in the semantic layer.

Product Failure Analysis

Metric gaming: alerts viewed rises when noise rises. Pair value events with false intervention, effort, recurrence, and exposure-time guardrails.

Instrumentation-induced selection: events appear only after successful setup, erasing failed onboarding. Begin the funnel at eligibility and preserve missing/failed states.

Identity errors: shared SOC accounts and service principals distort user retention. Model organization, persona, human actor, and agent separately.

Outcome delay: incident reduction may take months. Use pre-registered leading indicators, label them provisional, and revisit mature outcomes.

Interference: shared detections, global models, and cross-repository agent actions violate independent-unit assumptions. Randomize at the highest interacting cluster or estimate spillovers explicitly.

Novelty effects: usage spikes after launch. Measure repeated workflow completion and cohort retention after the novelty window.

Agent activity inflation: an agent can generate actions without value. Require bounded authority, action provenance, human override, rollback success, and outcome verification. Token count and tool calls are cost metrics, not security outcomes.

Survivorship: churned or breached customers disappear from telemetry. Join billing, support, and security outcome sources under a governed organization identifier and retain censoring reasons.

Rollout should progress from instrumentation validation to shadow measurement, randomized or phased exposure, and bounded expansion. Stop conditions should cover unauthorized actions, false interventions, customer effort, telemetry loss, and worsening protected outcomes. Rollback must restore compatible workflow and policy, not only a UI flag.

Building the Product Measurement System

Start with a semantic specification, not a dashboard. For every metric define eligibility, unit, event-time rule, late-arrival policy, identity resolution, deduplication, observation window, exclusions, and owner. Version the specification with product releases. A feature rename must not split history; a workflow redesign may require a deliberate metric version because “completion” has changed meaning.

Identity resolution is particularly difficult in enterprise security. One human may use several accounts, a managed service provider may act across tenants, and an agent may operate under a service principal. Preserve raw actor identifiers and map them to governed person, persona, organization, and automation entities with validity intervals. Never merge tenants because email domains match. Tenant isolation applies to analytics tables as well as product storage.

Event collection should represent state-changing facts rather than UI clicks whenever possible. investigation_verified is stronger than button_clicked, provided its evidence contract is stable. Keep raw interaction events for usability diagnosis but build value events from server-side workflow records. Include failures: attempted integrations, rejected agent actions, rollback attempts, and workflows abandoned after an error.

Time to value and retention

Time to value starts at a customer-relevant eligibility point—contract activation, completed prerequisite, or explicit trial start—and ends at a verified value event. Starting only after successful setup erases onboarding pain. Use survival curves because some organizations have not yet activated. Treat contract cancellation and trial expiry explicitly rather than dropping them.

Retention should follow the natural cadence of the job. A quarterly compliance workflow does not require weekly activity. Define retained value as repeated successful work when the need recurs, conditioned on continued eligibility. For automation, “no human sessions” may coexist with excellent retained value if policies remain healthy and verified outcomes continue.

Enterprise rollups need weighting choices. Organization-weighted metrics answer how many customers realize value; asset-weighted metrics answer how much protected surface does; revenue-weighted metrics answer commercial concentration. Publish them separately. A revenue-weighted north star can hide poor outcomes for smaller customers, while an unweighted average can understate systemic exposure in a few large tenants.

Experiment design under security constraints

Randomize the smallest unit that does not create contamination. If analysts share recommendations, randomize the queue or organization rather than individual alerts. If one repository’s fix updates a common library, repository-level assignment interferes. Document the interference graph and select clusters accordingly.

Before launch, specify the primary estimand, guardrails, minimum detectable effect, duration, and stopping rules. Sequential monitoring without correction inflates false positives. Security stop rules for harm can be asymmetric: stop immediately for unauthorized containment even if the primary outcome is inconclusive. Benefit stopping should be more conservative when outcomes are delayed.

Randomized encouragement is useful when customers choose adoption. Assignment might provide guided onboarding, an in-product prompt, or priority access; the feature remains optional. Intention-to-treat estimates the effect of encouragement. Using assignment as an instrument for adoption requires relevance, exclusion, and monotonicity assumptions that should be defended, not merely named.

When randomization is unavailable, phased rollout can support difference-in-differences if treated and comparison cohorts had credible parallel trends and no simultaneous differential change. Plot event-time effects and pre-period coefficients. Matching cannot repair unmeasured confounding. Regression discontinuity may be possible when eligibility follows a threshold, but manipulation around the threshold and limited external validity need attention.

Trust, explanations, and overrides

Trust should be calibrated reliance: users accept correct recommendations and reject incorrect ones. Measure acceptance conditional on audited correctness, not raw acceptance. Explanation quality can be tested by randomizing evidence formats and measuring correct decisions, time, and confidence. Longer explanations may feel transparent while obscuring the decisive fact.

Override taxonomies should permit multiple reasons and free text, then be reviewed for drift. “Policy exception” may conceal an incorrect recommendation if it becomes the easiest button. Forced reason codes can also add friction, so sample lightweight follow-up rather than burdening every action. Analyze whether particular teams cannot override because of role permissions.

For agents, record proposal, authorization, tools invoked, parameters, result, verification, and rollback as separate events. An agent that proposes the right action but calls the wrong tenant is unsafe. Outcome analytics must join the action trace to a policy decision and protected asset without exposing sensitive prompts or secrets broadly.

Economic value without fictional precision

Translate outcomes into ranges. Analyst time saved can use loaded labor cost; avoided incident loss is much more uncertain. Report assumptions and sensitivity rather than a single inflated return-on-investment number. Separate realized savings, capacity redeployed, and modeled risk reduction. Ten hours “saved” are not cash savings if staffing and workload do not change, but they may be valuable capacity.

Customer value also includes option value: faster evidence during an incident, auditable control state, or safer automation. These may be measured through response time, audit effort, and bounded action coverage. Do not invent dollar values where operational measures are more defensible.

The product review should show a metric tree, causal evidence grade, segment distributions, reliability state, and unresolved uncertainties. Decisions then become explicit: expand, hold, redesign, or retire. A feature with high engagement but no outcome evidence may remain in discovery; a low-engagement automation with verified value may deserve expansion.

Measurement itself needs reliability objectives. Track event acceptance, schema rejection, end-to-end freshness, identity-match coverage, experiment-assignment integrity, and late outcome arrival. If assignment logs are incomplete, stop causal reporting rather than substituting observed use. If value events lag, label the current period provisional. A trustworthy product organization is willing to show an empty metric instead of manufacturing continuity from incompatible data.

Privacy review should minimize collection to the decision. Full source code, prompts, or investigation text rarely belongs in broad analytics. Prefer derived reason codes, bounded counts, and access-controlled evidence links. Define retention and deletion propagation before launch, especially when agents can capture secrets in traces.

Segment review is mandatory before declaring success. Tenant size, industry, geography, deployment model, and maturity can concentrate both benefit and harm. An average improvement does not authorize expansion when a regulated or low-maturity segment experiences unsafe interventions.

Sources and Further Reading

  • Rodden, Hutchinson, and Fu, HEART. A useful user-experience lens, but security outcome and harm guardrails remain domain-specific. https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/
  • Kohavi, Tang, and Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Foundations for assignment, exposure, guardrails, novelty, and experiment validity. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108653985
  • Google SRE Workbook, Implementing SLOs. Service reliability is necessary context for interpreting product funnels and safe degradation. https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. Provides outcome-oriented security functions against which product workflows can be mapped. https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework
  • NIST SP 800-55 Volume 1. Emphasizes measures tied to information-security objectives rather than activity counts. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/55/v1/final

The synthesis is deliberate: HEART helps diagnose experience, experimentation literature supports causal claims, SRE constrains reliable delivery, and NIST anchors measurement to security outcomes. No framework licenses replacing protected outcomes with clicks.

Interview Practicum

Scenario: Engagement Falls After the Product Improves.

Prompt. An AI SOC assistant reduced weekly active analysts by 25%. The product leader wants to roll back. Decide what to do.

Ask whether eligible organizations changed, which personas declined, how exposure is logged, what workflows completed, whether incidents and decision quality matured, and whether the assistant now automates work.

Worked Answer

Compare cohorts on verified cases, analyst minutes, false interventions, overrides, unresolved exposure, and incidents. Lower activity may be the intended outcome.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Change one: case-resolution time fell 40%, but analysts override 18% of containment recommendations. Stratify overrides by reason and consequence. Unsafe-action overrides may trigger a stop even when speed improves; policy exceptions may indicate configuration work. Audit accepted recommendations too, because non-override is not correctness.

Change two: only large customers received the feature, chosen by customer-success managers. Do not use untreated small customers as controls. Seek a randomized encouragement among eligible large customers or a phased rollout with credible pre-trends and matching. State that causal certainty is limited until assignment improves.

Change three: the agent begins auto-containment next quarter. The metric system must add authorization scope, attempted and executed actions, rollback success, business disruption, and human escalation. Randomization may be unethical for high-risk autonomous actions; use shadow decisions, simulation, red-team challenges, and bounded canaries before outcome experiments.

Weak answers maximize MAU, infer impact from correlation, or A/B test autonomous containment without a harm model. A Principal answer changes the north star so leadership benefits when customers need fewer interactions to achieve a verified outcome.

Key Takeaways

  • Separate eligibility, assignment, exposure, adoption, workflow completion, and protected outcome.
  • Define activation around first verified value, not login.
  • Pair a security-value north star with friction, coverage, recurrence, and harm guardrails.
  • Use randomization or defensible quasi-experiments; feature users are a selected population.
  • Model personas, organizations, humans, and agents explicitly.
  • Reduced usage can indicate improvement when the product removes work safely.

Chapter 33: Ranking, Triage, and Decision Support

The Queue Is the Product

A vulnerability ranker does not protect anything. Protection occurs when a finite group of analysts investigates the right findings soon enough, sends actionable cases to owners, and avoids spending its week on plausible-looking noise. The output is not a probability; it is a queue whose arrival rate, service time, deadlines, and error costs interact.

Suppose five analysts each have six effective investigation hours per day. A scanner produces 240 findings daily, requiring between ten minutes and two hours each. Sorting by severity cannot make 30 analyst-hours absorb 80 hours of arriving work. The system must decide what enters service, waits, is grouped, or is explicitly deferred. A silent tail is not abstention; it is unrecorded risk acceptance.

Chapter 30 separated finding quality from severity, and Chapter 31 treated remediation as a stateful workflow. Here the decision unit is a finding at a decision time. Its value depends on harm that timely review can avert, probability that it is real, time required to resolve uncertainty, and the deadline after which review loses value.

Capacity-Constrained Architecture

flowchart TB
 A[Scanner and researcher findings] --> B{Duplicate and identity resolver}
 B --> C[Point-in-time feature snapshot]
 C --> D[Probability calibration]
 D --> E[Expected avoidable-loss estimate]
 E --> F{Queue admission optimizer}
 F -->|assign| G1[Cloud analyst lane]
 F -->|assign| G2[Application analyst lane]
 F -->|abstain| H[Evidence request lane]
 F -->|defer| I[Risk-owned backlog]
 G1 --> J[Disposition and service time]
 G2 --> J
 J --> K[Policy replay and audit sampling]
 K --> C

Deduplication comes first because ten manifestations of one root cause must not occupy ten slots. The snapshot contains only admission-time evidence. Calibration converts raw scores into empirical probabilities within relevant cohorts. The optimizer accounts for effort and deadlines. Specialist lanes acknowledge that five analysts are not five interchangeable servers.

Every outcome must be named. assigned consumes capacity. evidence_request has an owner and expiry. deferred records who accepted delay and when it will be reconsidered. suppressed_duplicate points to its canonical case. These states expose displaced work.

Mathematics of Attention

For finding \(i\), define calibrated validity \(p_i\), impact \(L_i\), preventable fraction \(q_i(t)\) when service starts at \(t\), review effort \(s_i\), and friction cost \(c_i\). Expected net value is

\[ v_i(t)=p_iL_iq_i(t)-c_i. \]

One urgency curve is \(q_i(t)=e^{-\lambda_i t}\); contractual deadlines may instead require a step. With capacity \(C\), admission resembles a knapsack:

\[ \max_{x_i\in\{0,1\}}\sum_i x_iv_i(0) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_i x_is_i\le C. \]

Sorting by probability is wrong when a moderately likely privilege escalation dominates an almost-certain informational issue. Sorting by value density \(v_i/s_i\) is a transparent baseline, but can starve large valuable cases. Reserve capacity for high-impact long cases and random below-threshold audits.

For analyst \(j\), let \(a_{ij}\) indicate skill compatibility and \(C_j\) capacity. Assignment variables satisfy \(\sum_i s_{ij}x_{ij}\le C_j\), \(\sum_jx_{ij}\le1\), and \(x_{ij}\le a_{ij}\). This exposes specialist shortages instead of burying them in scores.

Calibration, abstention, and learning

Ranking metrics do not show whether the first case merits interruption. Reliability diagrams and Brier score test whether 0.8 means roughly eight valid findings in ten. Calibrate on later time periods and segment by scanner, asset, and evidence regime; a global calibration map can hide overconfidence in a new detector.

Abstain when required evidence is absent, inputs fall outside supported conditions, or estimates are too uncertain. An abstention should request a specific artifact—reachable-route evidence, package version, or exploit precondition—not merely announce low confidence. Evidence-acquisition cost belongs in the decision.

Triage determines which labels become observable. Review a probability sample below the cutoff. Given inclusion probability \(\pi_i\), use weights \(1/\pi_i\) when estimating prevalence or recall. Otherwise the system congratulates itself for precision while blind regions accumulate.

Measure confirmed avoidable loss per analyst-hour, deadline-weighted recall, wait time by impact, backlog age, duplicate effort, and calibration. Precision at \(k\) is meaningful only when \(k\) equals service capacity. Replay candidate and incumbent policies over identical arrivals and service times.

Executable Lab: A Two-Lane Shift

This standard-library simulation creates synthetic cases and compares severity ordering with capacity-aware value density. It uses no network, credentials, files, or subprocesses.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from random import Random

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Finding:
    fid: str
    domain: str
    severity: int
    probability: float
    loss: int
    minutes: int
    sla: int

def workload(seed=7):
    rng = Random(seed)
    rows = []
    for n in range(30):
        rows.append(Finding(
            f"F{n:02}", ("app", "cloud")[n % 2], rng.randint(2, 10),
            round(rng.uniform(.18, .96), 2),
            rng.choice((5, 10, 25, 60, 120)),
            rng.choice((15, 30, 45, 60, 90)),
            rng.choice((120, 240, 480))))
    return rows

def value(f, start):
    return f.probability * f.loss * (1.0 if start <= f.sla else .35)

def simulate(items, policy):
    free = {"app": 0, "cloud": 0}  # one specialist per lane
    key = ((lambda f: (-f.severity, f.fid)) if policy == "severity" else
           (lambda f: (-(f.probability * f.loss / f.minutes), f.fid)))
    captured = late = reviewed = 0
    for f in sorted(items, key=key):
        start = free[f.domain]
        if start + f.minutes > 480:
            continue
        captured += value(f, start)
        late += start > f.sla
        reviewed += 1
        free[f.domain] += f.minutes
    return reviewed, captured, late, sum(free.values())

items = workload()
for name in ("severity", "capacity"):
    n, v, late, minutes = simulate(items, name)
    print(f"{name:8} reviewed={n:2} value={v:6.1f} "
          f"late={late:2} minutes={minutes:3}")

Expected output:

severity reviewed=27 value= 595.4 late= 9 minutes=915
capacity reviewed=28 value= 844.5 late= 7 minutes=885

The capacity policy wins through objective alignment, not sophistication. Add online arrivals, duplicate clusters, evidence requests, or reserved audit capacity. In an online implementation priorities must age as deadlines approach; a static priority-heap key becomes stale.

Operational Failure Analysis

Fast-case starvation

Value density can fill a shift with small wins and postpone a two-hour catastrophic case. Track maximum wait by risk band and reserve large-case capacity. An aging term prevents permanent starvation, but should not allow old low-value work to bury urgent arrivals.

Service times change with workflow

Historical duration reflects case difficulty and the old evidence interface. After evidence packets improve, old estimates become biased. Log active work separately from calendar duration, version the evidence bundle, and monitor residuals by case type. Do not turn these data into punitive individual rankings; analysts will game them.

Labels encode attention

“Confirmed” is mostly observed for reviewed cases; “closed benign” may mean time expired. Keep disposition, truth, and remediation separate. Random audits and researcher-confirmed challenge cases provide evidence outside the selected region.

Fundamental overload

If mean arriving work exceeds service capacity—\(\lambda E[S]\ge m\) for \(m\) equivalent analysts—no queue policy is stable. Use deduplication, admission control, automation, staffing, or threshold changes. A model cannot repeal conservation of work.

Adversarial flooding

An attacker or broken integration can generate superficially urgent findings and displace genuine work. Apply source budgets, correlated-finding collapse, provenance checks, and diversity constraints. Alert on concentration of assigned capacity by source and root cause.

Automation bias

Analysts need evidence-linked reason codes. Overrides should capture a structured reason without harming a private performance score. Otherwise disagreement disappears and the ranker loses its most valuable correction channel.

Decision records and review cadence

For every policy release, preserve the training interval, calibration interval, replay interval, feature definitions, cost table, capacity assumptions, solver version, tie-breaking rule, reserved-capacity rules, and approving risk owner. The record should include rejected alternatives and sensitivity analysis. If modest changes to loss estimates reverse most assignments, the policy is fragile and should expose that uncertainty to operators.

Review cadence follows change, not the calendar alone. Re-evaluate after scanner releases, staffing changes, major incidents, new contractual SLAs, or material shifts in service time. A monthly governance meeting can inspect backlog composition and override themes, while automated monitors run continuously. Never retrain directly from recent dispositions without checking whether the old policy created the sample.

The user interface is part of the queue algorithm. Show the evidence that drives priority, the deadline, expected effort range, duplicate cluster, and why the case is in this analyst’s lane. Permit analysts to request reassignment or flag corrupted evidence. Hide speculative monetary precision when impact is ordinal; false exactness damages trust.

Finally, distinguish remediation priority from investigation priority. A case may be cheap to validate but expensive to fix, or hard to validate but trivial to mitigate. The triage queue ends with a disposition and evidence package; remediation enters the lifecycle described in Chapter 31 with different owners, capacities, and deadlines. Combining both into one score obscures where work is actually constrained.

Source Synthesis

Combining investigation and remediation also corrupts measurement: remediation latency includes engineering ownership, release windows, and business acceptance that the ranker cannot control. Report handoff quality and downstream outcomes, but optimize the triage decision against consequences it can influence. This boundary keeps accountability fair and makes experiments interpretable. A later causal analysis may estimate whether faster validation changes remediation, but that claim requires its own design rather than an assumed chain of credit.

From Offline Scores to a Queue Policy

Productionization begins with a replay table, not a model endpoint. One row represents a case becoming eligible, with arrival time, evidence version, canonical root-cause identifier, skill requirement, estimated work, deadline, eventual disposition, and observed service intervals. Reconstruct the queue after every arrival and completion. This reveals whether apparent lift depends on future workload, labels, or true case duration.

Service-time prediction deserves its own loss function. Underestimating a long case crowds out deadlines; overestimating it leaves valuable capacity idle. Quantile estimates are often more useful than a mean. A scheduler can reserve the 75th-percentile duration for feasibility while estimating utilization from the median. Evaluate errors separately for cases that timeout, transfer, or wait on another team.

Policies need deterministic tie-breaking. If equal scores resolve by database return order, replay is unreliable. Use deadline, value density, arrival time, then stable case identifier. Record why an item moved: probability revision, impact revision, aging, capacity change, or override.

Analysts as information gatherers

Review is not a binary label factory. Analysts request artifacts, reproduce behavior, and discover clusters. A two-stage policy can spend five minutes resolving cheap uncertainty before committing to a full investigation. Expected value of information for evidence (e) is

[ EVI(e)=E[max_a U(amid e)]-max_a E[U(a)]-Cost(e). ]

This separates uncertain but cheaply resolvable cases from cases with no available evidence. The first belongs in a probe lane; the second may require abstention. Capture which artifact changed the decision so product teams can improve finding packets.

Fairness and tenant obligations

A globally efficient queue can starve small tenants because large customers generate more high-scoring cases, or starve legacy environments whose evidence is incomplete. Define whether guarantees are contractual, risk-based, or both. Constraints may set maximum wait per tenant, minimum review share for critical infrastructure, or separate capacity pools. Publish their displaced expected value so governance makes a conscious trade.

Check calibration and service across relevant groups, but avoid simplistic parity when exposure and contracts differ. Ask whether similarly consequential cases receive comparable treatment and whether evidence gaps systematically deny review. Improve instrumentation before correcting scores for missing evidence.

Rollout and incident response

Shadow mode must simulate assignment timing, not generate a second ordering at day end. During canary rollout, cap the capacity controlled by the candidate and retain a manual freeze. Trigger incidents on critical SLA misses, source concentration, calibration collapse, or backlog growth beyond recoverable capacity. Rollback restores the old admission policy without discarding already displaced cases.

After an incident, replay arrivals under both policies and identify the first divergent decision. Distinguish model error from optimizer error, stale evidence, capacity loss, or operator override. Correcting the wrong layer creates recurring failure; the queue decision log is as important as the trained artifact.

Learning-to-rank work supplies ordering objectives, but security triage adds asymmetric loss and finite service. Queueing and optimization supply admission and assignment constraints. Calibration research explains why order is insufficient for thresholds; selective classification supplies risk–coverage reasoning. CVSS describes severity, not an enterprise’s queue objective. NIST measurement guidance requires the resulting service to be assessed against operational outcomes. Their combined lesson is to evaluate model, optimizer, and workflow as one decision system.

Sources and Further Reading

  • NIST, Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/CSWP/NIST.CSWP.29.pdf
  • NIST SP 800-55 Volume 1: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-55v1.pdf
  • Burges et al., Learning to Rank using Gradient Descent: https://icml.cc/2015/wp-content/uploads/2015/06/icml_ranking.pdf
  • Guo et al., On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/guo17a/guo17a.pdf
  • Geifman and El-Yaniv, Selective Classification: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.08500
  • FIRST, CVSS v4.0 Specification: https://www.first.org/cvss/v4-0/specification-document

Interview Practicum

You inherit triage for a cloud-security product. Five analysts receive 1,200 weekly findings; only 300 can be reviewed within SLA. Leadership requests “the top 300.” After your initial design, constraints change: one analyst alone can investigate identity cases, 40 percent are duplicates, labels exist only above the old threshold, and a strategic contract requires every critical finding to receive a human touch in four hours.

Explain the decision unit, objective, allocation algorithm, calibration, exploration, rollout, and the metric you will refuse to optimize.

Worked Answer

I would not promise a universal top 300. First canonicalize duplicate manifestations into root-cause cases while retaining affected assets and contractual obligations. Each row is a canonical case at admission. Estimate calibrated validity, impact, preventable fraction, service time by skill, and deadline. Maximize expected avoidable loss subject to skill capacities, the four-hour critical-touch constraint, and a reserved audit budget.

The identity specialist is an explicit bottleneck. Critical cases receive a quick validation touch even when evidence is weak; contractual service is not proof they deserve full investigation. Duplicate clusters share investigation but fan out remediation ownership.

Old labels are policy-selected, so run stratified random review below the cutoff and weight by selection probability. Calibrate temporally within scanner and asset cohorts. Replay both policies on identical arrivals. Launch through shadow mode and a canary. Require positive lower-bound improvement in avoidable loss per hour, fewer critical SLA misses, bounded backlog age, and no material segment regression. Refuse to optimize closure count because it rewards easy dismissals and hides displaced work.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

The identity specialist takes leave tomorrow. What changes?

Expose infeasibility immediately. Route critical cases to a prequalified backup, pause low-value identity admission, and show the risk owner which deadlines cannot be met. Never silently assign unqualified staff.

A scanner doubles volume after an update. Is that model drift?

It is operational drift even if features did not shift. Quarantine the version behind a source budget, compare duplication and yield, and prevent it from consuming the queue during validation.

Analysts repeatedly override the ranker. What do you do?

Sample overrides and separate missing evidence, wrong cost assumptions, and wrong predictions. Correct the relevant layer. High-quality disagreement is system evidence.

When should ML ranking be abandoned?

When an auditable rule policy achieves equivalent queue utility, outcomes cannot support calibration, or contractual constraints determine nearly every action.

Key Takeaways

  • A ranker is useful only relative to arrivals, skills, service times, deadlines, and capacity.
  • Optimize expected avoidable loss, not severity or probability alone.
  • Make abstention, deferral, duplication, and displaced work explicit.
  • Evaluate at service capacity and audit below the cutoff.
  • Queue overload is a capacity fact, not a modeling defect.
  • Human overrides are evidence, not disobedience.

Chapter 34: Foundations of Agentic AI Security

Authority, Not Intelligence, Defines the Blast Radius

An enterprise coding agent reads repositories, searches tickets, runs tests, proposes patches, and sometimes deploys. Its language model is only one component. Security depends on which principal the system represents, which objects it can observe, which actions it can cause, and which evidence can influence those actions. A mediocre model with production credentials is more dangerous than an exceptional model confined to a disposable workspace.

Traditional application diagrams emphasize data flow. Agent threat models need authority flow. A retrieved issue can contain instructions; a generated plan can select a tool; a tool broker can mint a credential; a deployment service can change production. The important question is not merely “can untrusted text reach the model?” It is “can that text cross a consequence boundary without an independent authorization decision?”

A Typed Authority Graph

Model the system as \(G=(V,E)\). Every vertex has a type: Principal, Agent, Model, Data, Tool, Credential, Environment, or Policy. Every directed edge has a relation such as READS, INFLUENCES, INVOKES, AUTHORIZES, MINTS, WRITES, or DELEGATES. Edge attributes include scope, tenant, expiry, conditions, and provenance.

This is not cosmetic typing. A data-flow path issue -> model -> deployment may be expected. An authority path containing untrusted Data INFLUENCES Agent, Agent INVOKES Tool, and Tool WRITES production Environment is a candidate confused-deputy path unless an authorization edge from an accountable principal constrains the write.

flowchart LR
 subgraph Untrusted[Untrusted evidence plane]
   I[Issue text: Data]
   R[Repository content: Data]
 end
 subgraph Reasoning[Reasoning plane]
   A[Coding agent: Agent]
   M[Language model: Model]
   W[Ephemeral workspace: Environment]
 end
 subgraph Authority[Authority plane]
   P[Engineer: Principal]
   B[Tool broker: Policy]
   C[Scoped token: Credential]
 end
 subgraph Consequence[Consequence plane]
   T[Deploy API: Tool]
   E[Production: Environment]
 end
 I -->|INFLUENCES| A
 R -->|READS| A
 A -->|QUERIES| M
 A -->|WRITES| W
 P -->|AUTHORIZES change digest| B
 B -->|MINTS short lease| C
 C -->|SCOPES| T
 A -->|INVOKES| T
 T -->|WRITES| E

The diagram deliberately separates reasoning from authority. The model never receives a reusable production secret. The broker evaluates an immutable action proposal: repository, commit digest, environment, operation, expiry, and approver. Approval of “deploy something later” is too broad; approval must bind to what will occur.

Assets, Boundaries, and Abuse Cases

Protect more than source code. Assets include signing identities, CI provenance, private dependencies, customer data in test fixtures, system prompts, tool schemas, long-term memory, audit evidence, approval channels, and the integrity of generated changes. Availability matters too: an agent can create costly build loops or exhaust API quotas without exfiltrating anything.

Trust boundaries occur at retrieval, model providers, plugin/tool servers, workspaces, credential brokers, approval interfaces, memory stores, and agent-to-agent messages. Treat retrieved content as data even when it looks like policy. A repository file named AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md may legitimately guide local behavior, but it cannot grant deployment rights. Only the authority plane can do that.

Threats fall into interacting families:

  1. Indirect prompt injection. An issue, README, test output, web page, or dependency description tells the agent to ignore policy, reveal context, or invoke a tool.
  2. Excessive agency. A legitimate objective is paired with permissions broader than required—write access to every repository, wildcard cloud roles, or an unbounded shell.
  3. Confused delegation. A parent agent gives a subagent a task but fails to attenuate credentials or communicate prohibitions. The child becomes a laundering step for authority.
  4. Memory poisoning. Untrusted claims become durable preferences or facts and influence later tasks after their origin is forgotten.
  5. Tool semantic mismatch. A tool called preview_change performs writes, parameters have surprising defaults, or the agent misunderstands an idempotency boundary.
  6. Supply-chain substitution. Models, MCP/tool servers, packages, container images, or retrieved indexes change without compatible attestation.
  7. Approval capture. The interface hides the true diff, batches unrelated actions, or conditions humans to approve repetitive prompts.

Risk for an abuse path can be prioritized as

\[ R(path)=P(activation)\times P(policy\ bypass\mid activation) \times Impact(authority)\times Persistence. \]

Do not pretend these factors are precisely known. Use ordinal ranges and test the paths. The graph is valuable because it identifies where to cut reachability: remove an edge, attenuate its scope, insert a policy decision, or change the target to a sandbox.

Design Rules for Coding Agents

Capabilities should be task-scoped, object-scoped, action-scoped, tenant-scoped, and time-bounded. Mint them just in time. A read token should not imply write; repository write should not imply merge; merge should not imply deployment. Separate the identity that proposes a change from the identity that approves it.

Run generated code only in disposable environments with no ambient credentials, constrained network egress, resource quotas, and immutable base images. “Sandboxed” is a claim requiring escape testing and a documented host boundary, not a checkbox.

Canonicalize tool requests before policy evaluation. Validate types, resolve symbolic references, make defaults explicit, and hash the normalized proposal. Bind approval to that digest. Re-evaluate policy at execution because repository state, approver role, or environment freeze may have changed.

Memory needs provenance, scope, expiry, and deletion. Separate user-authored preferences, observed facts, model hypotheses, and security policy. A model-generated note cannot overwrite policy. Cross-tenant memory is forbidden unless a separately governed aggregation explicitly permits it.

Executable Lab: Detect Dangerous Authority Paths

The lab builds a typed graph and rejects paths where untrusted data can influence a production write without an intervening authorization node. It is intentionally small enough to audit and uses only synthetic objects.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from collections import defaultdict, deque

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Node:
    name: str
    kind: str
    trusted: bool = True

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Edge:
    src: str
    rel: str
    dst: str

nodes = {
    n.name: n for n in [
        Node("issue", "Data", False), Node("agent", "Agent"),
        Node("shell", "Tool"), Node("broker", "Policy"),
        Node("approval", "Principal"), Node("deploy", "Tool"),
        Node("prod", "Environment")]
}

def unsafe_paths(edges):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    for edge in edges:
        graph[edge.src].append(edge)
    queue = deque([("issue", ["issue"], False)])
    bad = []
    while queue:
        here, path, authorized = queue.popleft()
        for edge in graph[here]:
            now_auth = authorized or edge.rel == "AUTHORIZES"
            new_path = path + [f"-{edge.rel}->", edge.dst]
            if edge.rel == "WRITES" and edge.dst == "prod" and not now_auth:
                bad.append(" ".join(new_path))
            elif edge.dst not in path and len(path) < 12:
                queue.append((edge.dst, new_path, now_auth))
    return bad

unsafe = [Edge("issue", "INFLUENCES", "agent"),
          Edge("agent", "INVOKES", "deploy"),
          Edge("deploy", "WRITES", "prod")]
safe = [Edge("issue", "INFLUENCES", "agent"),
        Edge("agent", "PROPOSES", "broker"),
        Edge("approval", "AUTHORIZES", "broker"),
        Edge("broker", "AUTHORIZES", "deploy"),
        Edge("deploy", "WRITES", "prod")]

for name, edges in (("unsafe", unsafe), ("safe", safe)):
    bad = unsafe_paths(edges)
    print(f"{name}: dangerous_paths={len(bad)}")
    if bad:
        print(" ", bad[0])

Expected output:

unsafe: dangerous_paths=1
  issue -INFLUENCES-> agent -INVOKES-> deploy -WRITES-> prod
safe: dangerous_paths=0

The program is a design linter, not a proof of safety. Its authorization state is path-local; a production version must verify that approval actually binds to the proposed action, that the principal is eligible, and that no alternate write edge exists. Useful extensions check credential expiry, delegation attenuation, tenant equality, and forbidden Data -> AUTHORIZES relationships.

Operational Failure Analysis

Ambient credentials defeat the graph. If the workspace inherits a cloud token, the documented broker is fiction. Scan process environments and metadata endpoints from inside the sandbox; deny credential-bearing mounts by default.

Approval becomes ritual. Hundreds of low-context prompts teach operators to click. Aggregate only actions sharing a consequence boundary, show semantic diffs and destination, and require fresh confirmation for scope expansion. Measure approval reversals and time-to-review, not approval rate.

Tool descriptions drift. Policy may approve yesterday’s semantics. Pin tool versions, verify manifests, test side effects, and record the exact schema digest used for each call.

Delegation amplifies authority. A parent may have permissions that a research subagent does not need. Derive a child capability as an intersection of parent scope and task scope; never copy the parent token.

Egress turns read access into disclosure. A read-only agent can still leak secrets through HTTP, DNS, package names, logs, or pull-request text. Apply destination allowlists, content controls, secret scanning, and rate limits while recognizing none is perfect.

Rollback is incomplete. Reverting a commit does not revoke a leaked credential or remove published artifacts. Incident playbooks must cover credential rotation, package yanking, audit preservation, memory cleanup, and downstream notification.

Residual risk decisions

Not every dangerous path can be removed without eliminating the product. Document residual paths with preconditions, maximum authority, detective controls, recovery steps, and an accountable owner. “The model is unlikely to do that” is not ownership. A valid acceptance states why preventive control is disproportionate and when the decision expires.
