If it allowed the call and a generic proxy happened to intervene, the agent boundary failed.

I would preserve the fixture, releases, action digests, receipts, and sandbox image; search by observation digest; revoke unnecessary network grants; and add this family to adaptive replay. Deleted raw prompts limit semantic reconstruction but should not prevent reconstructing origin, proposal, decision, and effect. If they do, the schema is inadequate.

I would allow continued S0/S1 only if there was no out-of-scope effect and telemetry is complete. I would hold broad S2 expansion until the team proves draft PRs cannot carry secrets or attacker-controlled links, reruns the family against the candidate, and computes a stratum-specific risk bound. A small canary may proceed with network-deny defaults, scanning, human review, and stops.

The Principal move is to split ownership: platform owns a broker defect, model engineering owns instruction adoption, product owns friction, and security owns risk acceptance. I would document the counterfactual without the proxy and the incremental effect enabled by S2. The answer is a reversible capability-specific rollout, not a vote on whether the model is trustworthy.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

What if it was one failure in a million tasks? Use exposures to the malicious pattern as the denominator, report the stratum rate and uncertainty, then weight by production prevalence without hiding severity.

How do you estimate false refusals? Sample by reason code and task stratum, replay with independent test oracles, and combine adjudication with abandonment and manual-completion evidence. Random audits correct policy-selected labels.

Store prompts longer? Not automatically. Test encrypted incident sampling against privacy cost. Durable provenance, decisions, and effects are mandatory; full prompt retention is not.

What forces shutdown? An executed prohibited effect, cross-tenant access, an adapter accepting an unmatched action, agent-disabled audit, or loss of containment without reliable reconstruction.

Key Takeaways

  • Govern a coding agent by executable authority, not its system prompt.
  • Typed capabilities and sandboxed adapters turn model failures into containable proposals.
  • Connect untrusted observations to decisions and effects while minimizing content retention.
  • Evaluate adaptive attack paths, production exposure, uncertainty, and benign utility separately.
  • Rollout memos must name action classes, population, stops, evidence gaps, and owners.

Chapter 46: Case Study: Identity Compromise Detection

Identity compromise is not a row-classification problem. An account can be legitimate at 09:00, have its refresh token stolen at 09:12, and be used simultaneously by its owner and attacker at 09:20. The evidence is distributed across authentication, device, session, privilege, application, and recovery systems. The intervention changes what becomes observable: a challenge stops some attacks, annoys some users, and selectively produces labels. A useful system must therefore model time, relationships, uncertainty, action capacity, and causal friction together.

This capstone designs Helios, an enterprise compromise system for workforce identities. Its unit of decision is not “the user” but an identity episode: a bounded interval in which related credentials, sessions, devices, resources, and actions may share control. Helios may permit, silently monitor, require step-up authentication, revoke a session, or route an episode to an investigator. It does not automatically disable an employee from one anomalous event.

Temporal identity graph

The graph has typed nodes and interval-valued edges:

  • Person, Account, Credential, Session, Device, Network, Application, Resource, and Case nodes;
  • OWNS, AUTHENTICATED_WITH, ISSUED, OBSERVED_ON, ACCESSED, ASSUMED_ROLE, and REVIEWED_AS edges;
  • valid_from, valid_to, observed_at, source, and confidence on every edge.

Event time and ingestion time are distinct. A mobile device can upload an authentication event late; a directory correction can change the historical owner mapping. Point-in-time features use only graph state known at decision time. Otherwise the model “learns” from a later analyst verdict or asset enrichment.

flowchart LR
 A[Auth/device/app events] --> N[Normalize and resolve entities]
 N --> G[(Bitemporal identity graph)]
 G --> E[Episode builder]
 E --> F[Point-in-time feature service]
 F --> B[Rules and behavioral baselines]
 F --> M[Calibrated supervised model]
 B --> C[Risk composer]
 M --> C
 C --> P[Capacity-aware intervention policy]
 P --> X[Allow / step-up / revoke / investigate]
 X --> O[Outcome and friction ledger]
 O --> G
 O --> Q[Evaluation and causal analysis]

An episode begins with a credential issuance or authentication and links later events while continuity evidence remains plausible. It closes after inactivity, explicit revocation, or a maximum horizon. Concurrent sessions remain separate but share account and credential ancestors. This permits a “good owner plus bad token” representation rather than forcing one label onto the account.

Concrete schemas

identity_event(
 event_id, event_time, ingest_time, source, event_type,
 account_id, session_id NULL, credential_id_hash NULL,
 device_id_hash NULL, network_prefix, app_id, resource_id NULL,
 auth_method, result, source_confidence, raw_ref
)

episode_feature(
 episode_id, as_of_time, feature_version,
 geo_velocity_kmh, new_device_score, peer_app_rarity,
 session_overlap_s, token_age_s, failed_auth_30m,
 privilege_delta, resource_novelty, graph_fanout_10m,
 sensor_missing_mask
)

decision(
 decision_id, episode_id, decision_time, model_version,
 raw_score, calibrated_risk, risk_band, action,
 policy_version, capacity_state, explanation_codes
)

outcome(
 episode_id, outcome_time, signal_type, value,
 label_strength, reviewer_id_hash NULL, available_after,
 intervention_observed, friction_seconds NULL
)

The missingness mask is a feature and a health signal. “No device evidence” differs from “known unmanaged device.” Entity-resolution confidence propagates into risk rather than disappearing after a deterministic join.

Labels that admit uncertainty

Confirmed compromise is rare and delayed. Helios combines sources without pretending they are equivalent:

EvidenceLabel treatment
user reports “not me,” forensic token theft, attacker infrastructure matchhigh-confidence positive
analyst-confirmed benign travel or approved automationhigh-confidence negative for that episode
successful phishing-resistant step-upweak negative; attacker may have abandoned
password reset, help-desk recovery, bulk session revokeweak positive
no case openedunlabeled, not negative

Let latent compromise be \(Y\), labeling functions be \(L_j\in\{-1,0,1\}\), and their conditional accuracies be learned from overlap and a small adjudicated set. A generative weak-label model estimates

\[ q_i=P(Y_i=1\mid L_{i1},\ldots,L_{im}), \]

while accounting for correlated functions such as “password reset” and “help-desk recovery.” These soft targets can train a discriminative model, but evaluation uses time-separated, independently reviewed episodes. Cases sampled only above the old threshold are corrected with randomized below-threshold audits and inverse-probability weighting.

Reviewers see evidence available at decision time plus separately marked later evidence. They assign compromised, benign, indeterminate, or mixed-control, record confidence, and identify the controlled credential or session. Double review is concentrated where disagreement changes policy, not spread uniformly.

Three model layers and calibration

Helios deliberately keeps three layers. Deterministic rules catch high-specificity facts such as an impossible refresh-token binding or use after revocation. Behavioral baselines compare an episode with the identity's own history and an appropriate peer group. A supervised gradient model combines stable graph and sequence features. The composer records which layer contributed; a model outage therefore degrades to rules instead of failing open.

A useful sequence statistic is the decayed surprise of event \(e_t\):

\[ S_t=\sum_{k<t}\exp[-(t-t_k)/\tau],[-\log P(e_t\mid context_{t_k})]. \]

Graph fanout and privilege escalation then distinguish an unusual login from an episode that rapidly touches many sensitive resources.

Raw scores are calibrated on a later time block using isotonic regression or Platt scaling, stratified when major populations have different base rates. Reliability diagrams, Brier score, and expected calibration error accompany precision-recall results. Calibration is monitored by model release, authentication method, region, workforce type, and sensor availability. An apparently calibrated aggregate can hide severe contractor overestimation and administrator underestimation.

From risk to intervention

An intervention is selected by expected loss, capacity, and constraints:

\[ a^*(x)=\arg\min_a\{p(x)L_{miss}(a)+(1-p(x))L_{friction}(a)+L_{ops}(a)\}. \]

Actions have different attack interruption and user costs. Silent monitoring is cheap but weak. A phishing-resistant step-up is stronger and measurable. Session revocation may destroy unsaved work. Account disablement can block emergency operations and requires corroboration.

The policy is monotone in calibrated risk but context-sensitive. At equal risk, a privileged admin accessing a production control plane may receive a stronger action than an employee reading a public wiki. Capacity is explicit: if investigators can handle 60 episodes per day, ranking is by expected avoidable loss, not raw anomaly. Helios abstains when key sensors are missing or entity resolution is ambiguous and routes the episode to a safer action.

Guardrails prohibit use of protected personal attributes, cap repeated challenges, provide accessible recovery, and prevent an attacker from weaponizing the detector to lock out a victim. Explanation codes state evidence such as new_hardware_key + token_reuse_after_revocation; they do not expose a recipe precise enough to aid evasion.

Safe SQL lab: build temporal episodes

The following SQLite lab creates a tiny event stream and calculates episode-level signals. It uses synthetic data and no credentials.

CREATE TABLE events(
  event_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  account TEXT, session TEXT, event_time TEXT,
  event_type TEXT, device TEXT, country TEXT,
  privilege_delta INTEGER, resource TEXT
);

INSERT INTO events VALUES
(1,'alice','s1','2026-04-03 09:00:00','login','laptop-A','US',0,'mail'),
(2,'alice','s1','2026-04-03 09:04:00','access','laptop-A','US',0,'docs'),
(3,'alice','s2','2026-04-03 09:07:00','login','unknown-X','NL',0,'mail'),
(4,'alice','s2','2026-04-03 09:08:00','assume_role','unknown-X','NL',1,'cloud-admin'),
(5,'alice','s2','2026-04-03 09:09:00','access','unknown-X','NL',0,'payroll'),
(6,'bob','s3','2026-04-03 10:00:00','login','laptop-B','US',0,'mail');

WITH session_rollup AS (
 SELECT account, session, MIN(event_time) AS start_time,
        COUNT(DISTINCT resource) AS resources,
        MAX(privilege_delta) AS privilege_jump,
        COUNT(DISTINCT device) AS devices,
        MIN(country) AS country
 FROM events GROUP BY account, session
), overlap AS (
 SELECT a.account, a.session,
        EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM session_rollup b
          WHERE b.account=a.account AND b.session<>a.session
          AND ABS(strftime('%s',b.start_time)-strftime('%s',a.start_time)) < 900)
          AS concurrent_session
 FROM session_rollup a
)
SELECT s.account, s.session, s.resources, s.privilege_jump,
       o.concurrent_session,
       20*s.privilege_jump + 15*o.concurrent_session + 5*(s.resources-1) AS risk_points
FROM session_rollup s JOIN overlap o USING(account,session)
ORDER BY risk_points DESC, account, session;

Expected output:

alice|s2|3|1|1|45
alice|s1|2|0|1|20
bob|s3|1|0|0|0

This is an explainable feature calculation, not a production detector. It reveals an important modeling issue: Alice's legitimate session receives overlap points because the graph contains a suspicious sibling. A production composer should allocate evidence to the likely controlled session while retaining a shared episode link. Run the lab with sqlite3, or through Python's standard-library sqlite3 module when the CLI is unavailable.

Causal evaluation of step-up friction

Observed challenge success is not the causal effect of step-up. High-risk episodes receive the treatment, so naive treated-versus-untreated comparisons are confounded. Define two primary estimands for eligible episodes:

\[ ATE_{attack}=E[Y(1)-Y(0)], \qquad ATE_{friction}=E[F(1)-F(0)], \]

where \(Y\) is compromise completion and \(F\) is user time lost. Because withholding a control from extreme-risk cases is unethical, randomize only within an equipoise band between two acceptable policies—for example immediate phishing-resistant step-up versus step-up at the first sensitive action. Always-treat high-risk cases and never-treat low-risk cases remain observational.

Instrument assignment before outcome, analyze intent-to-treat, and use cluster-robust errors when a user can contribute repeated episodes. Outcomes include confirmed downstream compromise, session revocation, sensitive action completion, challenge success, recovery invocation, abandonment, time to resume work, repeated challenges, and support contacts. Estimate heterogeneous effects for admins, mobile users, accessibility cohorts, and device health, with privacy review.

When randomization is impossible, emulate a target trial using the policy threshold. Regression discontinuity near a stable calibrated-risk cutoff can estimate a local effect if actors cannot precisely manipulate the score and no other action changes at the cutoff. Interrupted policies, detector changes, and label delay must be modeled. Report sensitivity to unmeasured confounding rather than calling a propensity-weighted association causal by default.

Operations and failure drills

Offline replay without temporal leakage

Identity data makes leakage unusually easy. “Device later marked compromised,” a case opened after the decision, or a corrected owner mapping can yield spectacular offline results while being unavailable online. Helios materializes every row with an as_of_time and joins only records whose knowledge time precedes it. Labels have a separate available_after timestamp. Feature code runs identically in backfill and streaming, and replay compares the online decision payload with later reconstruction.

Splits are forward in time and grouped by account, credential family, or campaign where appropriate. A random row split would place adjacent events from one takeover in train and test. Evaluation includes cold-start users, new devices, and degraded sensors. Visible baselines—a few high-specificity rules, per-identity frequencies, and calibrated logistic regression—show whether graph complexity earns its cost.

Fairness, privacy, and recovery

Geography, schedule, disability accommodations, travel, and employment type can proxy for sensitive traits. Review asks whether a feature is necessary for an attack mechanism and whether a less invasive signal exists. Location precision is reduced when network class suffices; peer groups have minimum sizes; trace access is purpose-limited and audited.

Fairness is not equal challenge rates despite different exposure. Compare calibration, false interventions, recovery time, repeated challenge burden, and attack misses, then change features or policy where differences lack security justification. Recovery is part of control efficacy. If a legitimate traveler cannot recover, the system created an availability incident; if recovery uses weak questions, it becomes an attacker bypass. Recovery events return to the graph as security and friction outcomes.

Graph split drill. A device-ID migration fragments one device into thousands of nodes, causing novelty and challenge rates to spike. Freeze model promotion, compare source cardinality and resolution confidence, replay with corrected mappings, and reimburse users through automatic challenge suppression where corroborating signals are absent.

Adversarial low-and-slow drill. An attacker uses a familiar residential proxy and waits between actions. Test whether credential binding, resource sequence, graph fanout, and post-auth privilege evidence compensate for lost geolocation surprise. Do not simply lower thresholds globally.

Selective-label drill. Analysts only investigate top-ranked episodes for a month. Measure label propensity by score band, launch a safe random audit below threshold, reweight evaluation, and show how the apparent precision was inflated.

Step-up outage drill. The authentication provider fails. High-risk sensitive actions fail closed under a pre-agreed continuity policy; ordinary low-risk sessions degrade to monitoring with short expirations. The incident report distinguishes security exceptions from authentication availability.

Operational SLOs include point-in-time feature freshness, graph resolution latency, decision p95, challenge availability, intervention reversal time, daily review capacity, calibration drift, and outcome-link completeness. On-call dashboards show rates and denominators: a fall in detections can mean fewer attacks, missing events, or a broken join.

Sources and Further Reading

  • NIST, Digital Identity Guidelines SP 800-63B, grounds authenticator assurance, replay resistance, and recovery; risk scoring does not replace strong authentication.
  • NIST, Zero Trust Architecture SP 800-207, supports continuous, resource-aware decisions rather than permanent trust after login.
  • MITRE ATT&CK, Valid Accounts, explains why legitimate credentials make post-authentication sequence and resource evidence essential.
  • Guo et al., On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks, motivates post-hoc calibration, but temporal and population drift require continuing validation.
  • Ratner et al., Snorkel, provides a foundation for estimating latent labels from noisy labeling functions; correlated operational labels must be modeled explicitly.
  • Hernán and Robins, Causal Inference: What If, informs target-trial specification and the separation of prediction from intervention effects.

Interview Practicum

A global company challenges the top 0.5% of workforce sessions. Confirmed takeovers fell 25%, but help-desk calls rose 40%. Administrators complain of repeated prompts. Labels exist almost exclusively for challenged sessions, and a device-telemetry migration occurred halfway through the quarter. The CISO asks whether to expand the system to customers. Design the decision analysis.

Worked Answer

I would refuse the before/after causal claim. The policy selected the labels, the device migration changed features and missingness, and attacker pressure may have changed. First I would reconstruct bitemporal episodes under both identity-resolution versions and quantify event coverage, graph fragmentation, score shifts, challenge propensity, and outcome linkage by week and population.

For predictive quality I would create an independently adjudicated, time-forward sample containing challenged and unchallenged episodes. Random audits below the threshold identify missed compromise and permit inverse-propensity correction. I would evaluate calibration and expected avoidable loss, not accuracy, with separate administrator and device-health strata.

For intervention effect I would define eligible episodes and two outcomes: downstream harmful action and total user time lost, including recovery. Extreme-risk sessions stay protected. In an equipoise band I would randomize between two acceptable timings or challenge mechanisms, analyze intent-to-treat, cap repeat prompts, and monitor compromise, abandonment, help-desk demand, and accessibility. If randomization is unavailable, I would consider a threshold design only after proving the score and other controls were stable around the cutoff.

I would not transfer workforce thresholds to customers. Customer base rates, devices, recovery channels, loss functions, and tolerance differ. I would launch customer shadow scoring, build customer-specific calibration and friction baselines, complete abuse and lockout threat modeling, and test recovery capacity. The executive recommendation would separate: evidence the detector ranks risk; evidence step-up prevents harm; and evidence the customer workflow has acceptable net benefit.

At Principal scope I would also change the operating system: versioned entity resolution, randomized label audits as a permanent budget item, policy-independent outcome collection, a challenge-frequency constraint, and an accountable owner for each population's calibration. That prevents the next quarter from reproducing the same uncertainty.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

What if the CISO needs one threshold tomorrow? Choose a conservative threshold from calibrated expected loss and capacity, retain hard rules for incontrovertible signals, cap repeated challenges, and label it an interim policy with a dated reevaluation.

Why not train on successful challenges as benign? Success proves possession of the requested factor, not that the preceding session was benign; an attacker may abandon or a compromised factor may satisfy the challenge.

How do you handle mixed control? Label the session or credential, not the whole account. Preserve concurrent legitimate and malicious branches in the graph.

Which metric belongs on the executive dashboard? Estimated harmful sessions prevented with an uncertainty interval, paired with hours of user friction and recovery burden, plus telemetry and calibration health.

Key Takeaways

  • Model compromise as temporal control of sessions and credentials, not a permanent user label.
  • Preserve event time, knowledge time, entity confidence, and missingness in the graph.
  • Weak operational signals are useful only when their selection and dependence are explicit.
  • Calibrated risk should drive a capacity-aware intervention policy, not an anomaly leaderboard.
  • Evaluate prevention and friction as causal outcomes with ethical experimentation or carefully bounded quasi-experiments.

Chapter 47: Case Study: AI Vulnerability-Finding Product

An AI scanner does not create value when it emits a plausible paragraph about unsafe code. It creates value when it produces a reproducible, distinct, reachable, correctly prioritized security finding that a developer can fix, and when the fix remains effective. Every transition can fail: generated evidence may be invented, ten reports may describe one root cause, severity may ignore deployment context, a valid report may never reach its owner, and a quick patch may recur elsewhere.

This capstone designs Lumen, a multi-tenant product that analyzes authorized repository snapshots. Lumen combines static program analysis, dependency and configuration facts, and an AI hypothesis generator. The model can propose a vulnerability and a proof strategy; deterministic systems must establish artifact identity, trace evidence, sandboxed reproduction, and policy-compliant disclosure. The product is measured from hypothesis through durable remediation and enterprise risk reduction.

Finding as an evidence dossier

A finding is not a text blob. It is an immutable dossier with versioned claims:

finding(
 finding_id, tenant_id, repo_id, snapshot_sha, detector_release,
 weakness_id, root_cause_key, state, created_at, supersedes_id NULL
)

claim(
 finding_id, claim_type, claim_value, confidence,
 evidence_ids, produced_by, produced_at
)

evidence(
 evidence_id, kind, artifact_digest, source_location,
 derivation, sandbox_run_id NULL, retention_class
)

reproduction(
 sandbox_run_id, image_digest, command_template_id,
 network_mode, fixture_digest, exit_class, sanitizer_signal,
 side_effect_summary, replayable
)

disposition(
 finding_id, actor_role, at_time, decision,
 reason_code, ticket_id NULL, fix_commit NULL
)

Claims include source, sink, dataflow, precondition, reachability, exploit_effect, affected_version, and severity. Each points to evidence such as an AST path, call-graph edge, dependency lockfile, configuration fact, or safe sandbox result. Prose is rendered from claims; it is never the system of record. A reviewer can reject the exploitability claim without discarding the verified source-to-sink path.

Evidence has lineage. If a code location came from generated code or an incomplete build, the dossier says so. Reproduction runs have no production credentials, deny outbound network by default, impose resource limits, and use inert fixtures. For dangerous classes where executable reproduction would be unsafe, a static witness and expert review replace a weaponized proof.

flowchart LR
 S[Authorized snapshot] --> I[Artifact inventory and build graph]
 I --> H[AI hypothesis generator]
 I --> A[Static and dependency analyzers]
 H --> V[Claim verifier]
 A --> V
 V --> R[Safe reproduction sandbox]
 V --> D[(Evidence dossier store)]
 R --> D
 D --> C[Root-cause clustering]
 C --> K[Calibrated ranking]
 K --> U[Developer workflow]
 U --> F[Fix validation]
 F --> O[Survival and recurrence outcomes]
 O --> E[Enterprise value ledger]

Quality taxonomy and evaluation sets

Lumen distinguishes six dimensions:

  1. Validity: the claimed weakness exists in the scanned snapshot.
  2. Reachability: a feasible path reaches the vulnerable code under stated configuration.
  3. Exploitability: an actor satisfying the preconditions can cause the claimed effect.
  4. Severity: technical impact and scope under the customer's environment.
  5. Actionability: the dossier identifies an owner, location, cause, and feasible repair.
  6. Distinctness: the report represents a new remediation unit rather than a duplicate symptom.

The benchmark has three layers. A curated gold set contains seeded and naturally occurring cases with blinded expert adjudication. A repository holdout measures generalization across organizations and time. A production sample estimates performance under real language, framework, and configuration distributions. Training contamination checks compare artifact hashes and lineage; synthetic examples are reported separately because they often have cleaner build systems and simpler paths.

Finding-level precision alone rewards duplicate flooding. Evaluation reports hypothesis precision, root-cause-cluster precision, recall against known cases, severity agreement, replay success, dossier completeness, and developer-confirmed actionable precision. Confidence intervals are clustered by repository because findings in one codebase are dependent.

Deduplication as remediation-unit inference

String similarity is insufficient: two SQL-injection reports can require different fixes, while twenty sink locations can share one unsafe query builder. Lumen constructs a finding graph. Edges encode shared source, sink, call path, package, introduced commit, code-owner boundary, reproduction signature, and learned semantic similarity. A constrained clustering algorithm may merge findings only when they share a plausible remediation unit; high-impact cross-boundary merges require review.

The primary cluster key is a versioned tuple:

\[ k=(repo, snapshot, weakness, root\_cause\_symbol, taint\_origin, fix\_boundary). \]

Cluster quality is assessed pairwise and operationally. Pairwise precision penalizes merging distinct flaws; pairwise recall penalizes duplicate tickets. More important is fix consistency: after one member is repaired, do the others disappear under rescan? A cluster that cannot predict shared remediation is semantically weak even if its descriptions look alike.

Cross-snapshot lineage uses code movement, symbol identity, and patch similarity to distinguish persistence from reintroduction. Closing a finding because line numbers changed is prohibited.

Ranking under developer capacity

Severity is not priority. Lumen estimates expected avoidable loss per unit of remediation effort:

\[ priority_i=\frac{P(exploit_i\mid x_i)\,Impact_i\,Exposure_i\,Fixability_i}{E[effort_i]+\epsilon}. \]

Inputs include dossier confidence, reachable deployment, internet exposure, asset criticality, known exploitation, privilege required, compensating controls, code ownership, and historical fix effort. CVSS remains a standardized description of technical severity; EPSS and CISA KEV provide population-level exploitation evidence; customer context changes the final decision. The model outputs calibrated probability bands and an abstention state when build or deployment evidence is missing.

Ranking is constrained. A tenant may require all critical verified findings shown regardless of predicted effort, reserve capacity for systemic root causes, and cap the number sent to any team. Offline evaluation uses precision and cumulative avoidable-loss gain at realistic review budgets. Online evaluation measures the funnel, not clicks alone.

Developer funnel and product instrumentation

The developer journey has explicit timestamps and loss reasons:

generated -> verified -> clustered -> surfaced -> opened -> accepted -> assigned -> fix_started -> fix_proposed -> validation_passed -> deployed -> recurrence_window_complete.

At each transition, record the eligible denominator. A finding not surfaced due to capacity is different from one surfaced and ignored. Reasons include duplicate, not reachable, accepted risk, wrong owner, insufficient evidence, no feasible fix, and fixed elsewhere. Ticket edits and manual merges are product feedback, not ground truth by themselves.

Core funnel measures include time to first inspection, dossier-open rate, valid-dismissal rate, acceptance conditional on verification confidence, time to owner, time in progress, validation pass rate, deployment lag, and developer minutes per accepted finding. Segment by language, detector, team, tenure, and integration without creating a leaderboard that pressures teams to close findings incorrectly.

Safe runnable Python lab: cluster and rank dossiers

The lab uses synthetic metadata, makes no network calls, and executes no exploit.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from collections import defaultdict

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Finding:
    fid: str
    weakness: str
    root_symbol: str
    fix_boundary: str
    p_exploit: float
    impact: float
    exposure: float
    effort: float

findings = [
 Finding("F1","CWE-89","QueryBuilder.raw","db-lib",.30,9,1.0,3),
 Finding("F2","CWE-89","QueryBuilder.raw","db-lib",.28,9,1.0,3),
 Finding("F3","CWE-79","renderProfile","web-ui",.12,6,.8,1),
 Finding("F4","CWE-89","AdminSearch.sql","admin-api",.08,8,.2,2),
]

clusters = defaultdict(list)
for f in findings:
    clusters[(f.weakness, f.root_symbol, f.fix_boundary)].append(f)

rows = []
for key, members in clusters.items():
    # One remediation unit: use maximum risk, not the sum of duplicate symptoms.
    best = max(members, key=lambda f: f.p_exploit*f.impact*f.exposure/f.effort)
    score = best.p_exploit * best.impact * best.exposure / best.effort
    rows.append((score, ",".join(f.fid for f in members), key[1]))

for score, ids, root in sorted(rows, reverse=True):
    print(f"{ids:5} root={root:16} priority={score:.3f}")

Expected output:

F1,F2 root=QueryBuilder.raw priority=0.900
F3    root=renderProfile    priority=0.576
F4    root=AdminSearch.sql  priority=0.064

The crucial line takes maximum risk within a remediation unit rather than summing duplicates. Summation would reward the scanner for emitting more symptoms. In a production portfolio, correlated loss and multiple independently exploitable paths require a richer aggregation model.

Remediation survival and recurrence

Mean time to remediate is biased when open findings disappear from the calculation. Define origin at the first verified/surfaced time, event at validated deployment, and censoring at observation end, repository archival, or product disconnect—with those mechanisms reported separately. Kaplan-Meier curves estimate the probability a finding remains unresolved:

\[ \hat S(t)=\prod_{t_j\le t}\left(1-\frac{d_j}{n_j}\right). \]

Use cumulative incidence when accepted risk, repository deletion, and remediation compete. A Cox or accelerated-failure-time model can estimate associations with severity, ownership, evidence quality, and suggested-fix availability, but product exposure is confounded: teams receiving richer features may differ systematically. Randomized rollout or stepped-wedge introduction can estimate whether evidence dossiers accelerate validated fixes.

Recurrence is a new manifestation of the same root-cause family after a validated fix and clean window. Measure 30/90/180-day recurrence, vulnerable-code reintroduction, sibling-service recurrence, and bypass of the original patch. Durable remediation may be a shared library change, framework guardrail, test, or training intervention. A team that patches ten endpoints while leaving the unsafe helper intact has fast closure and poor security.

Enterprise value without vanity economics

Enterprise reporting has four layers:

  • Evidence quality: verified distinct findings, calibration, reproduction rate, coverage limits.
  • Workflow: accepted clusters, developer effort, time to validated deployment, integration health.
  • Security outcomes: exposed risk retired, recurrence avoided, systemic fixes, known-exploited coverage.
  • Business value: avoided expected loss ranges, audit evidence, engineering time saved or consumed, renewal-relevant adoption.

Avoid claiming that every critical finding equals a breach prevented. For finding cluster \(i\), estimate incremental expected loss reduction as

\[ \Delta EL_i=[P(A_i\mid no\ fix)-P(A_i\mid fix)]\times Loss_i, \]

with ranges and dependence adjustments. Attribute value only after validated deployment and account for findings that an existing tool or developer would have found. A randomized repository rollout, matched stepped wedge, or credible instrument can estimate incremental discovery and remediation. Customer retention correlations are supportive product evidence, not proof of security benefit.

Suggested fixes and validation gates

An AI-generated patch is a new hypothesis, not remediation evidence. Lumen displays it only when the system can state the intended security invariant and validate against exploit-oriented and regression tests. The patch runs in a disposable branch without repository write access. Existing tests, targeted security tests, static analysis, dependency resolution, and behavior-preservation checks run first. Generated tests are marked and cannot be the sole oracle for a generated fix.

Validation looks for displacement. Escaping one sink may leave an equivalent path; moving validation downstream can create an authorization inconsistency; upgrading a package may select a still-vulnerable transitive version. The post-patch dossier lists invalidated claims, remaining claims, build coverage, and untested surfaces. Lumen abstains where the fix crosses an architectural decision, cryptographic protocol, unsafe-memory interface, or business authorization rule.

Measure acceptance, developer edits, test success, time saved, rollback, and recurrence. Acceptance alone is weak: a convenient patch may be incomplete. Randomized fix offers among eligible low-risk findings can estimate incremental time to validated deployment. The product never auto-merges based only on model confidence.

Multi-tenant isolation and disclosure

Code, embeddings, build artifacts, and evidence remain tenant-scoped. Cache keys include tenant and snapshot; cross-tenant retrieval tests block release. Customer code is not silently added to shared training. Retention and improvement consent are explicit, and support access is time-bounded and audited.

For flaws in shared dependencies, distinguish the customer's affected instance from the upstream vulnerability. Coordinated disclosure reproduces safely, establishes affected versions, avoids premature weaponizable detail, notifies the appropriate maintainer, and gives customers mitigation evidence. Product urgency and finding counts do not override safe disclosure.

Failure drills

Hallucinated dossier drill. The narrative cites a dataflow edge absent from deterministic evidence. Quarantine the detector release, prevent unsupported prose from rendering, replay affected dossiers, and search for the same claim template. The claim/evidence foreign-key check must fail before customer exposure.

Duplicate storm drill. A parser change produces 40,000 variants. Freeze notification, compare root-cause cardinality and fix consistency, restore the previous clusterer, and ensure billing and executive metrics use remediation units rather than raw findings.

Unsafe reproduction drill. A proposed proof attempts outbound access. The sandbox denies it, destroys the run, preserves metadata, and routes the case to static validation. The model never receives credentials to “make the proof work.”

Closure illusion drill. Findings close after a file rename and recur on rescan. Rebuild cross-snapshot lineage, reopen affected clusters without penalizing developers, and correct survival origin/event logic.

Field Case: Building a Data-Science Assurance Layer for sec-pr

This section reports an implemented validation project for sec-pr, a pull-request cybersecurity review application. The case is useful because it exposes a common category error in security products: teams often mistake operational volume for validated effectiveness. A thousand scans prove that a system ran. They do not prove that its findings were correct, that it found most eligible vulnerabilities, or that it reduced risk without imposing excessive review burden.

The engineering innovation was therefore not another detector. It was a closed evidence loop that joined a working cybersecurity application to a governed data-science layer:

sec-pr scan and workflow data
        ↓
immutable identity, hashes, versions, and provenance
        ↓
normalization, completeness checks, and quarantine
        ↓
human adjudication and benchmark contracts
        ↓
precision, recall, calibration, slices, burden, and drift
        ↓
minimum-evidence release decision

The final arrow is deliberately conditional. A dashboard is not entitled to publish an effectiveness number merely because a formula can be evaluated. The denominator, label maturity, sample size, population definition, and observation window must first satisfy the metric contract.

Decision objective and estimands

The project did not ask the vague question, “Is sec-pr good?” It decomposed that question into decisions:

  1. Is the evidence platform fit for controlled engineering use?
  2. For which repositories, languages, vulnerability classes, change types, and safety contexts is detector effectiveness supported?
  3. What is the false-interruption burden on developers?
  4. What eligible changed code was not inspected successfully?
  5. Does a candidate scanner version improve security yield without regressing critical cohorts or workflow reliability?
  6. Is the evidence mature enough to promote, hold, roll back, or continue observing?

These decisions require different estimands. Posted-finding precision requires adjudicated posted findings. Recall requires independently reviewed eligible changed code, including clean pull requests and confirmed misses. Coverage requires the full eligible PR-iteration population. Operational reliability requires workflow events such as scans, comments, replies, votes, rescans, and closure. None of these denominators can be substituted for another.

Four linked analytical grains

The canonical design separated four grains that are frequently collapsed in production databases:

GrainIdentityQuestion answered
PR iterationorganization, project, repository, PR, iterationWhat exact changed-code population was eligible?
Scan runPR iteration plus scanner, prompt, policy, and execution versionWhat system behavior produced the observations?
Finding candidatescan plus stable finding identity and dispositionWhat vulnerability claim was generated, suppressed, duplicated, or posted?
Workflow eventactor, action, target, event time, and provenanceWhat happened after the prediction?

This separation prevents three serious errors. First, rescans are not mistaken for new pull requests. Second, mutable current state is not mistaken for historical evidence. Third, a posted comment is not mistaken for an independently validated vulnerability.

Implemented evidence corpus

The implementation audit verified the following state:

Record or checkVerified resultCorrect interpretation
PR iterations1,287An iteration-aware evaluation population was reconstructed.
Scan runs1,428Historical scanner executions were normalized.
Finding candidates1,098Candidate claims were available for governed review.
Label-queue items1,098Every candidate could enter the human-review workflow.
Evidence artifacts566Observed artifacts were indexed with provenance and hashes.
Benchmark contracts564Versioned benchmark definitions were registered.
Reconstructed workflow events15A limited historical workflow record was recovered explicitly.
Metric snapshots5Metric state and maturity could be persisted reproducibly.
Unresolved quarantine records278Unreliable records were isolated rather than silently accepted.
Invented validity labels0Missing outcome truth remained missing.
Invented missed findings0The recall denominator was not fabricated.
Database integrityokThe SQLite evidence store passed structural integrity checking.
Foreign-key errors0No broken canonical relationships were detected.
Verification41 Python tests, 3 frontend tests, production build, 5 browser-verified routesThe scoped engineering release suite passed.

These numbers are intentionally reported as engineering evidence, not as a detector score. The most scientifically important zeros are the zero invented labels and zero invented misses. They show that the implementation preferred an honest unknown over a polished but fictitious metric.

Quarantine is part of the measurement system

The 278 unresolved records were not deleted, coerced into a convenient schema, or counted as valid observations. They were quarantined with reason and provenance. Typical causes in systems like this include incomplete composite identity, missing iteration linkage, malformed historical artifacts, unresolved duplicate identity, or inadequate evidence for a semantic mapping.

Quarantine changes the analytical contract. Every published result should expose at least:

eligible population
− structurally ineligible records
− quarantined unresolved records
− immature labels
= mature analytical denominator

This reconciliation makes missingness visible. It also supports repair: a quarantined record can later be corrected and replayed idempotently without rewriting the raw artifact.

Ground truth as an append-only workflow

The project used evidence maturity rather than a single mutable is_valid column:

  • Gold: strong independent confirmation, such as qualified reviewer agreement or reviewer plus demonstrated reproduction.
  • Silver: validated operational evidence with sufficient rationale.
  • Bronze: provisional evidence, including an unresolved assertion or weak single-source judgment.
  • Unknown: insufficient evidence.

Labels are events. Corrections append a new decision with reviewer role, timestamp, rationale, evidence reference, and superseded label. This supports agreement measurement, conflict adjudication, and retrospective reconstruction of what was known at release time.

The 1,098-item review queue demonstrates workflow readiness, not completed truth. Until qualified adjudication matures, precision and severity-agreement claims remain gated. Recall requires an additional stream: independent review of eligible changed code that did not produce posted findings. Reviewer disagreement is measured rather than hidden, using raw agreement and a chance-corrected statistic where the sample supports it.

Metric contracts and fail-closed publication

Each measure was designed as a contract containing:

  • decision and owner;
  • numerator and denominator;
  • inclusion and exclusion rules;
  • label maturity requirement;
  • grouping and cohort dimensions;
  • minimum sample size;
  • interval or uncertainty method;
  • version dependencies;
  • freshness and observation-window requirement;
  • status such as mature, provisional, or insufficient_evidence.

Precision uses mature adjudicated posted findings and should be accompanied by a binomial interval such as Wilson's. Recall uses confirmed issues found divided by all confirmed issues in independently reviewed eligible code. Calibration compares confidence with observed validity and can use reliability diagrams, Brier score, or expected calibration error after adequate labels accumulate. Burden measures invalid interruptions and review minutes per eligible PR. Drift is decomposed into input, prediction, outcome, operational, and policy drift so that a changing repository mix is not confused with a degraded detector.

One benchmark run was executed. Its result was insufficient_evidence. This was a successful safety behavior: the benchmark pipeline ran, evaluated its evidence requirements, and refused to manufacture a pass or failure. In high-stakes analytics, an explicit non-result can be the correct result.

Shadow comparison and release logic

Candidate versions run in a structurally read-only shadow path. They cannot comment on live pull requests, cast votes, mutate trackers, or trigger production rescans. A valid comparison freezes the exact eligible input and records both versions' scanner, prompt, policy, registry, dependency, and benchmark versions.

A promotion decision should combine:

  1. no critical safety regression;
  2. mature evidence in required cohorts;
  3. paired or otherwise comparable evaluation;
  4. bounded developer burden;
  5. operational SLO compliance;
  6. no unresolved data-integrity blocker;
  7. documented rollback conditions.

The independent implementation review returned GO FOR ENGINEERING RELEASE. This means the evidence platform was fit for controlled ingestion, adjudication, benchmarking, dashboarding, and release governance. It does not mean that sec-pr precision, recall, calibration, subgroup performance, or long-term drift were established. The distinction is not legalistic fine print; it is the central result of the validation project.

Reproducibility protocol

An engineer reproducing a metric snapshot should be able to recover:

  1. the immutable source artifacts and checksums;
  2. the canonical schema and migration version;
  3. the exact population query and exclusions;
  4. scanner, prompt, policy, registry, and benchmark versions;
  5. label events and maturity rules available at computation time;
  6. the metric implementation version;
  7. the resulting numerator, denominator, interval, cohort, and maturity state.

The operational database used serialized SQLite writes for the pilot, with integrity and foreign-key verification. PostgreSQL was identified as the scale-out boundary rather than pretending that a single-writer pilot store was an enterprise endpoint. Aggregate views avoid exposing source snippets, while evidence drill-through remains subject to repository authorization. Credentials and personal identities are excluded or pseudonymized in analytical exports.

What the field case changed in the product conversation

Before the validation layer, stakeholders could discuss scan counts, findings, and anecdotal fixes. After it, they could ask better questions:

  • Which population did this score represent?
  • How many observations were quarantined or unlabeled?
  • Was recall measured against independently reviewed clean code?
  • Did performance differ for authentication, cryptography, injection, or sensitive logging?
  • Did a new prompt improve yield by increasing noise?
  • Was the apparent improvement a detector change, a repository-mix change, or a policy change?
  • What evidence supports promotion, and what evidence is still absent?

That transition—from activity reporting to falsifiable decision support—is the real data-science contribution.

Field-case interview questions and answers

Question: You have 1,098 scanner findings but no mature labels. What can you report?

Answer: Report the finding population, its provenance, disposition completeness, queue status, data-quality exclusions, and label maturity. Do not report precision. Create a stratified adjudication plan, define reviewer qualification and conflict resolution, and publish precision only after the metric contract's maturity and sample gates are satisfied.

Question: Why can posted findings estimate precision but not recall?

Answer: Posted findings reveal claims the scanner made. Recall also needs issues the scanner did not report. Its denominator therefore requires independent review of eligible changed code, including apparently clean PRs, plus a governed process for confirmed misses.

Question: Is quarantining 278 records evidence of poor engineering?

Answer: It is evidence of incomplete historical data and functioning quality controls. The engineering failure would be silently coercing those records into the analytical population. The operational response is to classify causes, repair recoverable records, measure quarantine rate by source, and prevent recurrence at ingestion.

Question: How do you explain “GO FOR ENGINEERING RELEASE” beside “effectiveness not established”?

Answer: They answer different questions. The first says the validation machinery, controls, tests, and evidence paths are fit for controlled use. The second says the outcome evidence is not yet mature enough to quantify detector quality. A professional assurance system must be able to release measurement infrastructure before it has accumulated the future observations that infrastructure is designed to govern.

Question: What is the most novel aspect of the system?

Answer: The closed evidence loop. A real cybersecurity application emits workflow evidence; an assurance digital thread preserves identity and provenance; governed human truth and statistical methods test performance; and explicit evidence gates feed promotion or hold decisions. Detection, measurement, and release governance are integrated without allowing the evaluation path to mutate production behavior.

Sources and Further Reading

  • NIST, SSDF SP 800-218, frames vulnerability discovery as part of a secure development lifecycle; this chapter extends measurement through validated deployment and recurrence.
  • MITRE, CWE, supplies weakness semantics useful for claims and clustering, but CWE identity alone does not establish a shared fix boundary.
  • FIRST, CVSS v4.0, standardizes technical severity inputs; it is intentionally not treated as a complete remediation priority.
  • FIRST, EPSS, estimates exploitation probability for published CVEs. Its population-level signal complements, but cannot replace, code reachability and customer exposure.
  • CISA, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, provides strong evidence of exploitation in the wild and should create portfolio constraints rather than merely add score points.
  • NIST, AI RMF 1.0, motivates explicit validity, reliability, transparency, and monitoring claims for the AI components of the product.
  • Kaplan and Meier, Nonparametric Estimation from Incomplete Observations, provides the censoring-aware basis for remediation survival analysis.

Interview Practicum

An AI scanner's dashboard shows 12,000 “critical” findings and 96% precision on a seeded benchmark. Customers accept only 8% of surfaced findings. One large customer says half are duplicates, while sales claims the count demonstrates value. You have six weeks before renewal season and may not run exploit code against customer environments. Redesign the product measurement and recommend what ships.

Worked Answer

I would stop using raw critical count as value and decompose the failure. The benchmark may be contaminated or unrepresentative; precision may be measured per emitted symptom; severity may omit reachability; and acceptance may reflect both quality and workflow. I would sample production findings across languages, customers, scores, accepted and dismissed states, then conduct blinded adjudication of validity, reachability, exploitability, actionability, severity, and distinctness.

I would make the dossier the product contract. Every displayed claim must reference deterministic source, path, configuration, or safe sandbox evidence. Unsupported claims abstain. Since customer execution is prohibited, validation uses authorized snapshots, inert fixtures, static witnesses, and isolated product-owned test repositories. The UI exposes evidence gaps rather than inventing certainty.

Next I would cluster around remediation units using root symbol, dataflow origin, fix boundary, reproduction signature, and snapshot lineage. I would evaluate pairwise merge/split errors and fix consistency. Ranking would use calibrated exploitability, exposure, impact, confidence, and effort under customer capacity, with mandatory lanes for verified known-exploited or policy-critical items.

The six-week ship should be narrow: evidence-backed dossiers, cluster-level counts, a calibrated high-confidence queue, clear abstention, and funnel instrumentation. I would not ship autonomous fixes or an avoided-breach dollar counter. Renewal reporting would show distinct verified clusters, accepted clusters, validated deployments, median and survival-based remediation, systemic fixes, recurrence, developer effort, and coverage limitations.

At Principal level I would align incentives: sales cannot quote unverified raw counts; detector teams are scored on cluster precision and durable fixes, not output volume; product owns time-to-owner and evidence usability; research owns held-out generalization; and security owns safe reproduction policy. Then I would propose a staggered customer rollout to estimate incremental acceptance and remediation relative to the previous workflow.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

What if deduplication hides two exploitable paths? Preserve member dossiers and path evidence inside the remediation cluster. Merge workflow, not truth; split when fixes or exploit preconditions differ.

How do you value a systemic fix? Count retired affected paths and estimate incremental loss reduction once, with dependence, rather than multiplying value by every symptom.

Should developer dismissal be a negative label? No. It is a disposition requiring a reason. Wrong owner, duplicate, risk acceptance, and invalidity have different learning meaning.

What is the release stop condition? Any unsupported evidence claim, cross-tenant artifact exposure, unsafe reproduction escape, or severe calibration failure in a material language segment.

Key Takeaways

  • The atomic product object is an evidence-linked, versioned dossier—not generated prose.
  • Measure distinct remediation units so duplicate output cannot masquerade as coverage or value.
  • Rank by calibrated, contextual avoidable loss under capacity and policy constraints.
  • Instrument the full developer funnel through validated deployment, survival, and recurrence.
  • Enterprise value requires incremental evidence and uncertainty, not “findings times breach cost.”

Chapter 48: Case Study: Evidence-Driven Security Program

An enterprise security program is usually described as a list of tools, controls, incidents, and compliance percentages. Those objects do not compose into evidence. A green control dashboard can coexist with an expanding attack path; fewer incidents can reflect prevention, attacker quiet, or broken sensors; a risk score can conceal assumptions that no executive agreed to.

This final capstone designs an evidence system for Meridian, a global software and payments company. It integrates the book's semantic contracts, telemetry engineering, threat models, detection measurement, vulnerability prioritization, causal evaluation, AI assurance, production reliability, team design, and decision communication. The goal is not a universal cyber number. It is a traceable chain from business assets and plausible threats through control claims and observations to decisions, uncertainty, and accountable work.

Semantic architecture: facts before dashboards

Meridian defines a small enterprise security ontology. Core entities are BusinessService, Asset, Identity, DataClass, ThreatScenario, AttackPath, Control, ControlClaim, Evidence, Observation, Finding, Incident, Decision, and Owner. Every metric declares its population, event time, knowledge time, grain, exclusions, source health, and version.

Canonical facts are append-only. Corrections supersede prior records; they do not silently rewrite history. Operational systems retain local schemas, while semantic adapters map them into governed facts. This avoids forcing endpoint, cloud, identity, and application telemetry into one lossy mega-table.

flowchart TB
 subgraph Sources
  CM[Asset/identity/config]
  TM[Security telemetry]
  WK[Workflow and finance]
 end
 CM --> SC[Versioned semantic contracts]
 TM --> SC
 WK --> SC
 SC --> FF[(Canonical fact and lineage layer)]
 FF --> EG[(Claims and evidence graph)]
 FF --> FS[Point-in-time feature products]
 FS --> AN[Detection, vulnerability, and causal analytics]
 AN --> EG
 EG --> TP[Threat portfolio]
 TP --> DR[Decision registry]
 DR --> EX[Executive narratives and roadmap]
 EX --> DR

A metric definition resembles an API contract. For example, identity_compromise_harm_30d specifies an episode population, verified harmful outcomes within 30 days, label maturity, intervention status, and excluded test tenants. Its dashboard cannot substitute raw alert count without changing the metric version.

Data quality is risk-weighted. Completeness for production control-plane logs receives a tighter SLO than completeness for low-risk laboratory endpoints. Health dimensions include expected volume, entity join rate, latency, schema conformity, clock skew, duplication, and outcome linkage. A sensor-health incident annotates dependent evidence so downstream reports do not treat absence as safety.

Control claims and evidence graph

“MFA is deployed” is an implementation fact, not a security claim. Meridian expresses a control as falsifiable propositions:

control_claim(
 claim_id, control_id, subject_scope, threat_edge,
 proposition, target, valid_from, valid_to,
 claim_owner, review_frequency, status
)

evidence_assertion(
 assertion_id, claim_id, evidence_type, artifact_uri,
 observed_at, population_start, population_end,
 result, uncertainty_low, uncertainty_high,
 freshness_deadline, producer, method_version
)

dependency(
 upstream_claim_id, downstream_claim_id,
 dependency_type, rationale
)

An identity claim might state: “For workforce administrator access to production, phishing-resistant authentication interrupts credential replay in at least 99% of eligible attempts, with telemetry coverage above 99.5%.” Evidence can include configuration attestations, sampled access logs, replay tests, red-team results, exceptions, and outage history. Each item has scope and freshness. A policy document alone cannot satisfy an effectiveness claim.

The graph separates four evidence classes:

  • Design evidence: architecture, policy, threat analysis, and test specification.
  • Implementation evidence: configuration, deployment, inventory, and attestation.
  • Operating evidence: logs, sampling, SLOs, exceptions, and failure recovery.
  • Outcome evidence: attack interruption, incident impact, remediation, and causal estimates.

Claim confidence is not a naive average. Suppose implementation depends on sensor coverage and policy enforcement. The confidence in the conjunction cannot exceed its weakest required dependency. Correlated evidence from the same source receives less weight than independent evidence. One usable conservative aggregation is

\[ C(claim)=\min_{d\in required}C(d)\times Freshness\times ScopeCoverage, \]

with uncertainty retained, not rounded into traffic-light theater. The graph permits queries such as “Which high-loss attack paths depend on a stale identity-provider assertion?” and “Which executive claims rely on the same failing asset inventory?”

Threat portfolio and control coverage

Meridian manages threat scenarios rather than an undifferentiated risk register. A scenario states actor, objective, entry condition, attack path, affected services, loss mechanisms, current controls, observability, and plausible frequency/severity ranges. Examples include cloud-control-plane takeover, software supply-chain compromise, payment credential theft, destructive ransomware, and AI-agent misuse.

Attack paths are directed graphs. A control maps to an edge only when a falsifiable claim explains how it prevents, detects, delays, or recovers that transition. Coverage has dimensions: population scope, time, implementation, demonstrated effectiveness, and independence. Five tools observing one edge do not imply fivefold protection.

Scenario loss is a distribution:

\[ L_s=I_s\times D_s+R_s+C_s, \]

where \(I_s\) is business interruption per unit time, \(D_s\) duration, \(R_s\) response/recovery cost, and \(C_s\) customer, legal, or contractual consequence. Frequency and loss ranges come from internal episodes, near misses, external evidence, expert elicitation, and stress tests. Monte Carlo simulation can propagate uncertainty, but the result remains conditional on the scenario model.

Prioritization uses marginal risk reduction per constrained unit, adjusted for strategic dependencies:

\[ Value(j)=\frac{E[L\mid current]-E[L\mid control_j]}{Cost_j}\times Enablement_j. \]

This does not reduce the portfolio to a greedy ratio. Some investments—asset identity, telemetry lineage, strong authentication, safe deployment—enable many later controls. The roadmap therefore balances immediate loss reduction, foundational leverage, regulatory obligations, and concentration risk.

Detection, incidents, and vulnerabilities in one portfolio

Detection metrics connect to scenario edges. Report eligible attack opportunities, sensor coverage, detection probability with intervals, time from first observable event to decision, analyst capacity, containment time, and missed/late evidence. Alert volume is a workload measure.

Incident outcomes use severity-adjusted business harm, time to containment and recovery, recurrence, and control-learning closure. Incident counts are shown with exposure and sensor health. A postmortem creates or updates graph evidence; it does not close until systemic actions have owners and validation criteria.

Vulnerabilities are clustered into remediation units and joined to deployment exposure, business service, exploit evidence, and compensating controls. The queue optimizes avoidable loss under engineering capacity, while mandatory policy lanes remain visible. Survival and recurrence reveal whether teams retire root causes or merely close tickets.

Safe runnable SQL lab: find unsupported executive claims

This SQLite lab builds a miniature claims/evidence graph and queries stale or insufficient assertions. It uses no production data.

CREATE TABLE claims(
 claim_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, scenario TEXT, proposition TEXT,
 min_coverage REAL, max_age_days INTEGER, executive_visible INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE evidence(
 evidence_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, claim_id TEXT, observed_date TEXT,
 coverage REAL, result TEXT, independent_source TEXT
);

INSERT INTO claims VALUES
('C1','cloud takeover','Admin MFA blocks replay',0.995,30,1),
('C2','supply chain','Release artifacts are provenance-verified',0.990,14,1),
('C3','ransomware','Tier-0 recovery meets 8-hour objective',0.950,90,1);
INSERT INTO evidence VALUES
('E1','C1','2026-07-28',0.998,'pass','idp-log'),
('E2','C1','2026-07-29',0.997,'pass','red-team'),
('E3','C2','2026-06-01',0.999,'pass','ci-config'),
('E4','C3','2026-07-15',0.910,'pass','recovery-test');

WITH latest AS (
 SELECT c.claim_id, c.scenario, c.proposition, c.min_coverage, c.max_age_days,
        MAX(e.observed_date) AS last_seen,
        MIN(e.coverage) AS demonstrated_coverage,
        COUNT(DISTINCT e.independent_source) AS independent_sources
 FROM claims c LEFT JOIN evidence e USING(claim_id)
 WHERE c.executive_visible=1 GROUP BY c.claim_id
)
SELECT claim_id, scenario,
 CASE
  WHEN last_seen IS NULL THEN 'NO_EVIDENCE'
  WHEN julianday('2026-08-20')-julianday(last_seen) > max_age_days THEN 'STALE'
  WHEN demonstrated_coverage < min_coverage THEN 'INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE'
  WHEN independent_sources < 2 THEN 'SINGLE_SOURCE'
  ELSE 'SUPPORTED'
 END AS status
FROM latest ORDER BY claim_id;

Expected output:

C1|cloud takeover|SUPPORTED
C2|supply chain|STALE
C3|ransomware|INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE

The query is intentionally conservative: it uses minimum demonstrated coverage and requires two independent sources. In production, evidence applicability is interval- and population-specific, and dependence is more nuanced than counting source names. Still, this simple test catches a common governance failure: a current dashboard backed by stale evidence.

Executive reporting as decision support

The quarterly executive report begins with decisions, not telemetry. A one-page portfolio view contains:

  1. material scenario movement and why;
  2. controls whose evidence strengthened, weakened, or expired;
  3. realized incidents and near misses linked to scenarios;
  4. leading exposure changes such as internet-facing privilege or unsupported software;
  5. investments requiring acceptance, acceleration, or stop decisions;
  6. uncertainty and data-health exceptions.

Every statement is tagged as fact, estimate, assumption, or recommendation. Ranges replace false precision. The report may say: “Cloud takeover exposure likely decreased after phishing-resistant administrator authentication; implementation evidence covers 99.8% of eligible access and red-team replay was blocked, but two break-glass paths lack independent testing.” That is more actionable than “identity risk: 72/100.”

Board reporting uses fewer scenarios and emphasizes loss mechanisms, resilience, concentration, trend evidence, and management decisions. Operational drill-down remains available through the graph. Compliance mappings are generated from claims and evidence but do not become the enterprise risk model: passing a control test and reducing a material threat are related, not identical.

Operating model and measurement governance

A small central security data-science and evidence team owns ontology, causal standards, shared platforms, and portfolio synthesis. Embedded analysts own domain features and decisions in identity, cloud, product security, detection, and resilience. Security engineering owns control operation; business-service owners own risk decisions; internal audit independently tests selected claims.

Every production metric has a named owner, semantic version, review cadence, source SLO, and retirement condition. Every model has point-in-time reproducibility, calibration monitoring, rollback, and an intervention policy. Every experiment has an estimand and ethical boundary. The decision registry records the evidence available, alternatives considered, expected outcome, owner, review date, and what would reverse the decision.

The program avoids performance traps. Analysts are not rewarded for alert counts, red teams for raw findings, or engineering teams for ticket closure alone. Shared outcomes include demonstrated attack-path interruption, durable remediation, reduced recovery time, evidence freshness, and decision turnaround—balanced by user friction, privacy, cost, and reliability.

Twelve-month roadmap

Quarter 1: establish truth and choose the portfolio

  • Approve the ontology, metric contract template, evidence classes, and decision registry.
  • Identify the top five threat scenarios with business owners and loss ranges.
  • Inventory telemetry dependencies and define risk-weighted source SLOs.
  • Build canonical identity, asset, service, and control identifiers; quantify unresolved joins.
  • Baseline current incident harm, detection coverage, vulnerability survival, and control-evidence freshness.

Exit criteria: scenario owners agree on attack paths; 80% of Tier-0 services map to accountable assets and identities; executive claims expose source and freshness; known data gaps have funded owners.

Quarter 2: prove two vertical slices

  • Deliver an identity-compromise slice from event contract through intervention and friction measurement.
  • Deliver a software-supply-chain slice from build provenance through release control claims and recovery drill.
  • Launch randomized label audits and independent evidence sampling.
  • Connect vulnerability remediation units to services and deployment exposure.
  • Train domain teams to write falsifiable claims and uncertainty-aware decision memos.

Exit criteria: both slices support point-in-time replay, have tested failure modes, and produce a decision that changes resource allocation or policy.

Quarter 3: evaluate controls and scale operations

  • Run causal or quasi-experimental evaluations for two high-cost controls.
  • Deploy detection-capacity optimization and remediation survival reporting.
  • Automate claim freshness, scope, and dependency checks.
  • Conduct cloud takeover, ransomware recovery, and coding-agent containment drills.
  • Establish model release gates, calibration review, and rollback across security analytics.

Exit criteria: at least two controls have credible effect and friction estimates; stale executive claims automatically downgrade; drill actions are validated rather than merely assigned.

Quarter 4: institutionalize portfolio decisions

  • Produce the first evidence-linked annual threat portfolio and budget options.
  • Quantify risk reduction ranges and foundational enablement from completed investments.
  • Retire vanity metrics and duplicate dashboards through metric-contract governance.
  • Add audit sampling and board drill-down to the evidence graph.
  • Review team topology, skills, privacy controls, retention, and next-year scenario changes.

Exit criteria: the budget memo traces proposed spending to scenarios, claims, evidence gaps, expected outcomes, and owners; executives can inspect uncertainty; next-year priorities follow measured residual exposure rather than tool renewal dates.

Failure drills

Executive metric contradiction. Incident reporting says ransomware recovery improved while recovery exercises show Tier-0 regression. Trace definitions, populations, and censoring; suspend the aggregate claim; publish the contradiction and decision needed. Negative evidence is not a communications defect.

Semantic breaking change. A cloud provider changes principal identifiers, collapsing join coverage. Quarantine dependent metrics, version the adapter, replay the affected period, and annotate every evidence assertion generated during degradation.

Control monoculture. Three “independent” claims rely on one identity provider. Simulate provider compromise or outage, update dependency edges, and fund a recovery or alternate-verification path. Tool count is not defense independence.

Roadmap capture. A loud stakeholder requests an AI dashboard unrelated to top scenarios. Require a decision, user, evidence gap, and expected portfolio effect. Prototype only if it competes successfully against committed work; novelty is not priority.

Sources and Further Reading

  • NIST, Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, supplies Govern/Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover outcomes. The evidence graph makes those outcomes falsifiable rather than treating framework categories as metrics.
  • NIST, Risk Management Framework SP 800-37 Rev. 2, informs lifecycle authorization, continuous monitoring, and accountable risk decisions.
  • NIST, Security and Privacy Controls SP 800-53 Rev. 5, provides a control catalog; this chapter distinguishes catalog mapping, implementation evidence, operating evidence, and outcome evidence.
  • NIST, Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments SP 800-30 Rev. 1, supports threat, vulnerability, likelihood, and impact reasoning while preserving uncertainty.
  • MITRE, ATT&CK, supports attack-path and detection mappings. Technique coverage does not by itself prove prevention or detection effectiveness.
  • Open Group, Open FAIR Standard, offers a quantitative loss-event vocabulary useful for scenario ranges; estimates remain conditional on evidence and assumptions.
  • NIST, AI RMF 1.0, extends governance to AI-enabled controls and products, including validity, transparency, monitoring, and accountability.

Interview Practicum

You join a company after a material cloud breach. The board wants one cyber-risk score in 30 days. Security owns 140 dashboards, audit reports 92% control compliance, asset inventory joins only 68% of cloud resources to a business service, and the CISO must submit next year's budget in eight weeks. Design the response without promising a mature quantitative program in a month.

Worked Answer

I would not manufacture a scalar. In 30 days I would produce a decision-grade provisional portfolio. First, reconstruct the breach as a scenario and attack path, then select four or five material scenarios with business owners: likely cloud takeover, supply chain, ransomware, payment-data theft, and a company-specific case. For each I would state assets, entry conditions, loss mechanisms, controls, evidence, gaps, and uncertainty.

The 68% join rate is not a footnote; it bounds every service-level claim. I would prioritize Tier-0 and externally exposed resources, measure unresolved populations, and create a temporary “unknown ownership” risk segment rather than dropping those assets. The 92% compliance figure would be decomposed into design, implementation, operation, and outcome evidence. I would test freshness and independence for the claims most relevant to the breach.

For the board, I would present scenario ranges and confidence, recent movement, concentration, control evidence that survived or failed, recovery readiness, and three decisions. If a visual summary is required, I would use ordinal evidence states with drill-down, not arithmetic that implies unsupported precision. I would explicitly label facts, estimates, assumptions, and recommendations.

For the eight-week budget, I would compare options by marginal scenario reduction, foundational enablement, obligations, cost, and time to evidence. Likely first investments are identity and asset semantics, control-plane telemetry, strong administrator authentication, tested recovery, and a claims/evidence layer—not another dashboard. Each funded item receives an owner, falsifiable claim, measurement plan, and stop/review date.

At Principal level, I would use the crisis to simplify governance: freeze creation of uncontracted metrics, register executive claims, establish source SLOs, select two end-to-end vertical slices, and define a 12-month roadmap. I would tell the board what can be known in 30 days, what cannot, and which instrumentation will reduce uncertainty. Credibility comes from traceability and bounded claims, not a polished number.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

What if the board insists on a number? Provide explicitly modeled scenario loss ranges and, if necessary, a portfolio distribution with assumptions and sensitivity—not an opaque 0–100 score. Pair it with the largest uncertainty drivers.

How do you choose the first vertical slice? Select a material scenario with an imminent decision, usable telemetry, an intervention owner, and measurable harm/friction. Avoid choosing only the easiest data.

Can compliance evidence populate the graph? Yes, with scope, time, method, and evidence class. A passed audit sample supports a bounded assertion; it does not automatically prove attack-path effectiveness.

How do you show program value after one year? Demonstrated control effects, retired exposure, faster containment/recovery, durable remediation, fresher independent evidence, and better decisions—alongside cost, friction, privacy, and remaining uncertainty.

Key Takeaways

  • Build enterprise security measurement on versioned semantic facts, not dashboard names.
  • Express controls as falsifiable, scoped claims connected to fresh and independent evidence.
  • Manage a threat-scenario portfolio with attack paths, loss ranges, dependencies, and residual uncertainty.
  • Executive reporting should expose decisions, evidence changes, assumptions, and contradictions.
  • A credible roadmap alternates foundational data work with end-to-end decisions that prove practical value.

Field lesson: platform evidence can mature before outcome evidence

The sec-pr assurance program established a canonical population of 1,287 PR iterations, 1,428 scan runs, 1,098 candidate findings, 566 evidence artifacts, and 564 benchmark contracts. It also exposed 278 unresolved records through quarantine and preserved unknown outcomes instead of fabricating labels. For program leaders, this is a useful maturity pattern: first make the evidence supply chain observable and governed; then acquire adjudicated outcomes; only then authorize effectiveness and investment claims. Chapter 47 presents the complete vertical slice.
