Interview Practicum

The 99%-Accurate Detector

Prompt with live constraints

“Explain why a 99%-accurate malware detector overwhelms our SOC and propose a launch evaluation.” The panel adds: one million files arrive daily; prevalence is 0.1%; analysts can review 2,000 alerts; sandbox evidence is correlated with the detector; and fifteen business units have different base rates.

Worked Answer

Strong answer

Clarify whether “99%” means sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, or overall accuracy and on which population. Using 99% sensitivity and specificity at 0.1% prevalence, expect 990 true alerts and 9,990 false alerts per million, so precision is about 9% and 10,980 alerts exceed capacity.

Do not multiply detector and sandbox likelihood ratios unless conditional independence is defensible. Estimate joint performance on a representative, adjudicated sample. Calibrate per business unit or with a hierarchical model because posterior probability changes with local prevalence. Reserve probability samples below thresholds to estimate misses and prevalence.

Evaluate at the 2,000-alert operating point: confirmed malware captured, false alerts, calibration, severe-family recall, time to action, and queue-age distribution. Compare confidence or credible intervals, not only point estimates. Stress-test campaign days and uncertain false-positive rates through Monte Carlo. Launch in shadow mode, then bounded routing with predefined queue and miss gates.

Technical answer

At capacity 2,000, ranking quality determines which alerts are reviewed. If the top slice contains 800 true and 1,200 false alerts, precision is 40% and recall is (800/1000=80\%), assuming 1,000 malicious files. That is operationally different from evaluating a fixed binary threshold. Confidence intervals should account for stratified audit sampling. Business-unit posterior probabilities use local priors; pooling can borrow strength but must not erase heterogeneity.

Weak answers

  • “One percent error means 10,000 mistakes” misses truth-conditioned rates and class composition.
  • “Accuracy is high, so add analysts” accepts a bad operating point without analysis.
  • “Run both tools and multiply confidence” assumes independence.
  • “The (p)-value is below .05, so launch” omits effect size, queue, and causality.
  • “No alert means safe” ignores false negatives and verification bias.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Follow-up probes with answers

How estimate prevalence when labels exist only for alerts? Draw a probability sample from all files, adjudicate with a reference procedure, and weight strata. Without negative sampling, prevalence is unidentified.

What if zero malware appears in a sample? Zero does not imply zero rate. For (n) independent trials, the rough 95% upper bound is (3/n), the rule of three.

Why not one global threshold? Different priors and costs yield different posterior risks and operating points. Calibrate and govern segment policies while guarding against unstable small samples.

How address multiple family metrics? Prespecify critical families, report simultaneous uncertainty or control false discoveries, and validate discoveries on fresh data.

Communication drills

Thirty seconds: “At 0.1% prevalence, 99% sensitivity and specificity produce about 990 true and 9,990 false alerts per million files—roughly 9% precision. Evaluate ranking at the 2,000-case capacity, audit below threshold, calibrate by base rate, and simulate queue tails.”

Five minutes: Derive Bayes, translate to counts, discuss dependent evidence, intervals, sampling bias, segmented calibration, capacity evaluation, and Monte Carlo stress tests.

A defensible conclusion states which assumptions dominate and which additional observation would most reduce decision uncertainty.

Key Takeaways

  • Base rates can dominate impressive sensitivity and specificity.
  • Use distributions whose assumptions match counts, waiting times, skew, and dependence.
  • Confidence, credible, and prediction intervals answer different questions.
  • Statistical significance neither establishes causality nor operational value.
  • More selected data reduces variance around a biased answer.
  • Monte Carlo simulation reveals queue tails hidden by expected values.

Chapter 4: Data Preparation, Exploration, and Feature Engineering

This chapter is a forensic notebook. A login-risk model scores 0.97 AUC offline and 0.61 after deployment. Rather than tune the model, we freeze three login times, reconstruct exactly what the system knew, and test every feature against an availability clock. The culprit is not an algorithm. It is a future fact disguised as a column.

Notebook Setup: Three Clocks, Never One

An authentication record has an event time: when the login occurred. A source fact has an availability time: when the feature pipeline could read it. An outcome has a label time: when compromise was adjudicated. Point-in-time correctness requires that features for decision time (t) use facts whose availability time is at or before (t), while labels may mature later.

The raw fixture contains login attempts, device observations, password resets, case outcomes, and ingestion timestamps. The unit is one login attempt. The target is confirmed compromise within fourteen days. The model decision occurs immediately after authentication evidence arrives.

login_id  principal  event_time        decision_time
L1        u1         Aug-01 09:00      Aug-01 09:00:02
L2        u1         Aug-03 10:00      Aug-03 10:00:02
L3        u2         Aug-03 11:00      Aug-03 11:00:02

A password-reset record for u1 occurred after L2 but was backfilled into a table joined by principal. A case system later set reset_after_incident=1. The training query reads the latest principal row without an as-of predicate, so both L1 and L2 inherit the future value. The model learns the investigation workflow.

Cell 1: Profile Before Repair

Profiling is not a ritual of printing describe(). It tests claims needed by the analysis:

  • Are login IDs unique, and are source IDs stable across replays?
  • What fraction of events arrive after the online latency budget?
  • Which columns change after initial ingestion?
  • Are missing values concentrated by source, tenant, platform, or attack period?
  • Do outcome dates precede adjudication dates?
  • Are counts physically possible and timestamps ordered?
  • Does one principal appear in train and validation?

For numeric features, inspect quantiles, zero mass, tail behavior, and exposure. For categories, inspect cardinality, unseen values, and rare levels. For time, inspect gaps, lateness, seasonality, and release boundaries. For joins, measure unmatched, one-to-many, and multiplicative rows. A join that grows 100,000 logins into 128,000 rows is not “more data”; it may be duplicated evidence.

Exploration should have a question ledger. Plotting hundreds of correlations and selecting an exciting one invites data dredging. Mark exploratory discoveries and verify them on untouched time periods.

Cell 2: Classify Missingness as a Mechanism

Let (R=1) mean a value is observed and (X) the complete-data values.

MCAR means (P(R\mid X)=P(R)): missingness is unrelated to observed or unobserved values. A random packet drop may approximate it, though real outages often do not.

MAR means missingness depends on observed data but, conditional on them, not the missing value. Device posture may be absent more often on a known legacy platform; conditioning on platform may support an MAR analysis.

MNAR means missingness depends on the unseen value even after observed variables. Attackers disabling an agent specifically when executing malicious code creates adversarial MNAR. No generic imputer solves identification under MNAR; use sensitivity analysis, alternate sensors, and explicit missingness features where safe.

Missing has domain meanings: “not applicable,” “sensor unsupported,” “collector late,” “redacted,” “lookup found no match,” and “true zero” are different states. Collapsing them into null destroys information. An absent reputation lookup can become predictive because the service fails during attacks; deploying that feature may encode an outage rather than threat.

Do not globally fill numeric nulls before splitting. Fit imputation statistics on training data and apply them unchanged to validation and test. Add missing indicators when the mechanism is stable and legitimate, but monitor them for source-policy changes and attacker manipulation.

Cell 3: Separate Errors, Outliers, and Rare Truth

A negative duration is usually an error. A login from 20,000 km away may be a geolocation error, VPN, shared account, or actual compromise. Rare is not synonymous with malicious, and malicious is not synonymous with statistically rare.

Validation rules should distinguish impossible values from improbable ones. Quarantine impossible rows or repair them from authoritative sources with provenance. Preserve plausible extremes and use robust transforms or models. Winsorizing attack bursts because they are outliers deletes the phenomenon the model should learn.

For skewed counts, log1p compresses scale while retaining zeros. Standardization is useful for distance- and gradient-based models; trees generally do not require it. Fit scalers only on training data. An ordinal encoder needs explicit order. A nominal encoder needs unknown-category behavior. Frequency encoding can leak target-period composition when computed globally.

Cell 4: Deduplicate and Resolve Entities

Deduplication asks whether records represent the same event; entity resolution asks whether identifiers represent the same entity. They require different evidence.

Exact event deduplication may use a source event ID plus producer. If IDs are absent, construct a fingerprint from stable fields, but account for legitimate repeated failures. “Same user, IP, and second” may collapse a retry storm. Keep ingestion lineage and choose a deterministic survivor.

Entity resolution can connect renamed accounts, federated identities, devices, and sessions. Deterministic links using tenant-scoped immutable IDs are preferable. Probabilistic linkage must expose match confidence and avoid cross-tenant collisions. Never let an email address silently become a global person identifier. Split data by resolved entity groups so alternate IDs do not cross train and test.

Cell 5: Put Every Candidate Feature on Trial

A feature is eligible only if it passes five tests:

  1. Availability: Could production obtain it before the decision deadline?
  2. Provenance: Can the value be traced to versioned facts and transformations?
  3. Semantic stability: Will the meaning survive source and policy changes?
  4. Leakage review: Is it caused by the outcome, adjudication, or intervention?
  5. Abuse review: Can an attacker cheaply control or suppress it?

Temporal features

For login at (t), useful features include failures in ((t-1h,t]), distinct devices in ((t-30d,t)), seconds since prior successful login, and ratio of failed attempts to all attempts. Specify boundary inclusion. Including the current outcome field or later events is leakage. A rolling feature must group by entity and shift where the current row should not contribute.

Recency needs a policy for no prior event. Encode “no history” separately from an arbitrary huge duration. Rates retain numerator and denominator or smoothing information. A ratio of one failure over one attempt is less certain than 100 over 100.

Categorical, text, and graph features

Categorical features can use one-hot encoding for bounded vocabularies, hashing for high cardinality, or leakage-safe target encoding fitted out of fold. Text features must exclude notes written after disposition; even document timestamps can be misleading when notes are edited in place. Graph features such as privileged-neighbor count must use the entitlement graph valid and available at decision time. Computing current graph centrality for historical logins leaks future access changes.

Sequence features capture ordering: failure, reset, success differs from success, reset, failure. Aggregates erase this. Dimensionality reduction such as PCA must fit on training only and may reduce interpretability. Feature selection performed on the full dataset leaks validation outcomes. Wrap all learned preprocessing inside the validation procedure.

Cell 6: Point-in-Time Fixture

This runnable fixture contrasts a leaking latest-state join with a correct as-of feature builder.

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def ts(value):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(value).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)

logins = [
    {"id": "L1", "user": "u1", "at": ts("2026-08-01T09:00:00")},
    {"id": "L2", "user": "u1", "at": ts("2026-08-03T10:00:00")},
    {"id": "L3", "user": "u2", "at": ts("2026-08-03T11:00:00")},
]
facts = [
    # user, fact, event time, availability time
    ("u1", "device:d1", ts("2026-07-31T12:00:00"), ts("2026-07-31T12:00:05")),
    ("u1", "failure", ts("2026-08-03T09:40:00"), ts("2026-08-03T09:40:03")),
    ("u1", "password_reset", ts("2026-08-03T10:30:00"), ts("2026-08-03T10:30:02")),
    ("u2", "device:d9", ts("2026-08-03T10:00:00"), ts("2026-08-03T12:00:00")),
]

def build(login):
    visible = [f for f in facts if f[0] == login["user"] and f[3] <= login["at"]]
    failures = sum(f[1] == "failure" and f[2] > login["at"].replace(hour=0) for f in visible)
    devices = {f[1] for f in visible if f[1].startswith("device:")}
    reset_seen = any(f[1] == "password_reset" for f in visible)
    return login["id"], failures, len(devices), reset_seen

latest_reset = {user: any(f[1] == "password_reset" for f in facts if f[0] == user)
                for user in {x["user"] for x in logins}}
for login in logins:
    print("as_of", build(login), "leaky_latest_reset", latest_reset[login["user"]])

Expected output:

as_of ('L1', 0, 1, False) leaky_latest_reset True
as_of ('L2', 1, 1, False) leaky_latest_reset True
as_of ('L3', 0, 0, False) leaky_latest_reset False

The reset is unavailable at both u1 login times, yet the latest-state join marks both true. The u2 device occurred earlier but arrived an hour after L3, so it is correctly absent. Event-time filtering alone would still leak it.

Cell 7: Assert the Boundaries

Point-in-time pipelines need executable invariants, not reviewer memory.

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def ts(value):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(value).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)

cutoff = ts("2026-08-03T10:00:00")
boundary_facts = [
    ("at_cutoff", cutoff),
    ("one_microsecond_late", ts("2026-08-03T10:00:00.000001")),
]
included = [name for name, available in boundary_facts if available <= cutoff]
assert included == ["at_cutoff"]

train_users = {"u1", "u2"}
validation_users = {"u3"}
assert train_users.isdisjoint(validation_users)

feature_rows = [("L1", False), ("L2", False), ("L3", False)]
assert len(feature_rows) == len({row[0] for row in feature_rows})
assert all(reset_seen is False for _, reset_seen in feature_rows)
print("boundary=closed")
print("entity_split=disjoint")
print("fixture_checks=4 passed")

Expected output:

boundary=closed
entity_split=disjoint
fixture_checks=4 passed

Tests should cover exact cutoff, late corrections, duplicated source IDs, daylight-saving transitions, unknown categories, empty history, source outage, and deterministic replay. Store fixture rows in code review so a semantic change produces an obvious diff.

Cell 8: Choose a Split That Matches Deployment

An IID random split assumes exchangeable rows. Authentication rows violate this when the same user, device, or campaign appears in both sets. A grouped split keeps entities together. A temporal split trains on the past and tests on the future. Often both are needed: train before a cutoff and prevent entity overlap where the deployment claim concerns new entities.

Use three roles. Training fits parameters and preprocessing. Validation selects features, hyperparameters, and thresholds. Test remains sealed for final estimation. Reusing test results for decisions turns the test into validation. With time drift, use rolling-origin evaluation: train through (t), validate on the next interval, advance, and summarize variation across folds.

Labels need a maturity gap. If the target is ATO within fourteen days, stop training examples at least fourteen days before the label snapshot, or mark censoring explicitly. A random split cannot repair immature negatives.

Offline metrics must be recomputed after removing contaminated features. A dramatic decline is evidence that the old score measured future workflow. Compare train and serving feature distributions generated by the same code path. Training-serving skew may arise from different parsers, window boundaries, lookup freshness, or default values.

Cell 9: Missingness and Adversarial Failure Tests

Feature health is part of model behavior. Simulate loss of device telemetry, delayed geolocation, new identity providers, clock skew, and duplicated bursts. Measure predictions and actions, not only null rates. A model that maps missing posture to high risk may lock out a tenant during an agent outage; one that maps it low may create an attacker bypass.

Define explicit degradation: abstain, fall back to a smaller feature set, use a conservative rule, or route to review. Select based on harm. Monitor coverage by cohort, feature age, unknown-category rate, join multiplicity, and point-in-time violations. Alert before outcome metrics mature.

Attacker-induced missingness deserves threat modeling. Can clients omit device fields? Can a proxy delay reputation enrichment past scoring? Can repeated identities poison rolling baselines? Use server-observed signals where possible, cap contributions, retain raw provenance, and test manipulated fixtures.

Notebook Conclusion: Why AUC Fell

The offline model used reset_after_incident, current entitlement centrality, and a device reputation value backfilled hours later. Random splitting placed the same principals and campaign in both partitions. Removing leakage, rebuilding as-of features, grouping principals, and testing on later weeks reduced offline AUC from 0.97 to 0.72. Production AUC of 0.70 now agrees within uncertainty.

The lower score is the successful result. It estimates the deployable problem. The team can improve it honestly through better decision-time instrumentation, sequences, calibrated models, and outcome sampling. Restoring 0.97 by reintroducing future facts would improve only the fiction.

Sources and Further Reading

  • scikit-learn, “Common Pitfalls and Recommended Practices.” https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html
  • scikit-learn, “Preprocessing Data.” https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/preprocessing.html
  • pandas, “Working with Missing Data.” https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/missing_data.html
  • Google, “Rules of Machine Learning.” https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml
  • Kaufman et al., “Leakage in Data Mining.” https://doi.org/10.1145/2020408.2020496
  • Little and Rubin, Statistical Analysis with Missing Data, 3rd ed. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119482260
  • Sculley et al., “Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems.” https://papers.nips.cc/paper/5656-hidden-technical-debt-in-machine-learning-systems
  • NIST, Secure Software Development Framework, SP 800-218. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final

Interview Practicum

Debug the Miraculous Model

Prompt with evidence drops

“A login-risk model has 0.97 offline AUC and 0.61 online. Diagnose it.” The interviewer reveals in stages: password-reset fields are updated after incidents; device intelligence arrives up to two hours late; rows were randomly split; analysts investigate only challenged sessions; and production uses a different null default.

Worked Answer

Strong investigative answer

Freeze model, feature, and source versions and reproduce several production decisions from raw evidence. Build a feature lineage table containing event time, availability time, transformation, and owner. For every candidate feature, compare historical value as originally available with the current backfilled value. Remove post-outcome and post-intervention fields.

Rebuild examples as of login decision time. Add a fourteen-day maturity gap for outcomes. Split temporally and group principals or linked devices. Fit imputation, encoders, scaling, feature selection, and dimensionality reduction inside each training fold. Compare online and offline feature vectors for identical decision IDs.

The different null default is training-serving skew; unify transformation code and test outage behavior. Because only challenged sessions receive labels, observed online performance is selected. Add a randomized audit sample where ethically possible and use sampling weights. Do not claim global recall from investigated traffic alone.

Report a leakage ablation: baseline with all fields, remove reset workflow, remove late intelligence, enforce grouped temporal split, and enforce production defaults. The step changes identify how much optimism each defect contributed. Re-estimate threshold metrics at operational capacity and shadow the repaired pipeline before action.

Worked answer

The principal assertion is: for observation (i) at decision time (t_i), every feature fact (j) must satisfy available_at_j <= t_i; every learned preprocessing artifact must be fit without validation or test rows; and outcome observation must not influence feature construction. Event time alone is insufficient because backfilled data can describe earlier events but become known later.

A safe SQL pattern joins a login to facts on entity plus fact.available_at <= login.decision_at, applies event-window predicates separately, and resolves multiple versions by the latest version available by the cutoff. The test fixture must include a fact whose event precedes login but whose arrival follows it.

Weak answers

  • “Tune regularization” treats a data defect as model variance.
  • “Production drifted” is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis.
  • “Drop all null rows” changes population and hides outages.
  • “Use current tables for more complete history” guarantees backfill leakage.
  • “AUC is still above random” ignores action thresholds and selected labels.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Follow-up probes with answers

A feature is available before scoring but caused by a prior intervention. Is it leakage? It may be legitimately available yet create policy dependence or treatment leakage. Define the deployment policy and causal pathway; evaluate stability when intervention changes.

How handle an IP reputation correction? Version values with validity and availability. Replay the version known at decision time; use corrected values only for analyses whose estimand permits hindsight.

Can a missingness indicator be useful? Yes when it represents stable decision-time information, but test source changes and manipulation. It does not make MNAR bias disappear.

How detect duplicate leakage across accounts? Group by resolved device, household, organization, campaign, or artifact as appropriate; measure similarity across splits and run stricter sensitivity splits.

Would you restore the old model while rebuilding? Only if its live harm is lower than fallback and contaminated features exist online at decision time without post-outcome dependence. Otherwise fall back to a reviewed rule or abstention policy.

Communication drills

Thirty seconds: “Reconstruct identical production decisions from raw facts, enforce availability-time joins, remove post-incident fields, add label maturity, group entities, split forward in time, and unify preprocessing. The honest offline AUC will fall; agreement with online behavior is the first success.”

Five minutes: Explain the three clocks, lineage audit, leakage ablation, selected-label problem, grouped temporal validation, train-serving parity, fixtures, and safe fallback.

Key Takeaways

  • Event, availability, and label times must be modeled separately.
  • Latest-state joins are unsuitable for historical feature reconstruction.
  • Missingness is a mechanism, sometimes controlled by attackers, not a cleaning inconvenience.
  • Fit every learned transformation inside the training partition.
  • Grouped temporal splits and outcome-maturity gaps approximate deployment better than random rows.
  • A lower leakage-free score is more valuable than a miraculous invalid score.

Chapter 5: Python, SQL, and Reproducible Analytical Workflows

Repository Walkthrough: Rebuild the Impossible-Travel Investigation

At 09:10 an investigator asks which identities authenticated from two countries within thirty minutes and whether the second event used a new device. By lunch, a notebook has produced twelve names. By Friday, nobody can reproduce the list. The query was edited in place, the notebook depended on an unrecorded package version, a nested JSON field silently changed type, and a cloud token remains in cell output.

This chapter rebuilds that investigation as a repository. The aim is not infrastructure for its own sake. A result becomes evidence only when another person can reconstruct its input, transformations, assumptions, and checks.

impossible-travel/
├── pyproject.toml
├── data/auth.ndjson
├── sql/{schema.sql,investigate.sql}
├── src/impossible_travel/{ingest.py,pipeline.py}
├── tests/test_pipeline.py
└── notebooks/01_discovery.ipynb

The notebook is deliberately last: it can discover a transformation but is not the authoritative implementation.

Commit Zero: Runtime and Data Contract

A manifest should separate runtime from development dependencies and bound supported Python versions. A lock file then records resolved transitive versions and hashes.

[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools==75.8.0"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "impossible-travel"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11,<3.15"
dependencies = []

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = ["pytest==8.3.5", "ruff==0.9.7"]

This exercise needs no third-party runtime package. A production run manifest should still capture the interpreter, operating-system image digest, source revision, parameters, and immutable data-snapshot identifier.

The input is newline-delimited JSON. Nested objects and arrays are ordinary in identity telemetry. The last record intentionally violates the boolean contract.

{"event_id":"a1","ts":"2026-08-01T10:00:00Z","identity":{"id":"u1","groups":["engineering","vpn"]},"source":{"country":"US","ip":"198.51.100.7"},"device":{"id":"d1","managed":true},"result":{"success":true}}
{"event_id":"a2","ts":"2026-08-01T10:18:00Z","identity":{"id":"u1","groups":["engineering"]},"source":{"country":"DE","ip":"203.0.113.9"},"device":{"id":"d9","managed":false},"result":{"success":true}}
{"event_id":"a3","ts":"2026-08-01T10:40:00Z","identity":{"id":"u2","groups":["finance"]},"source":{"country":"US","ip":"198.51.100.8"},"device":{"id":"d2","managed":true},"result":{"success":"true"}}

Ingestion Boundary: Reject Ambiguity

Nested JSON is difficult because absent or malformed values acquire accidental meanings. This loader refuses missing paths, duplicate identifiers, non-boolean outcomes, and timestamps without offsets. It flattens the fields needed by the query while retaining canonical raw JSON for audit.

from __future__ import annotations
import hashlib, json
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any, Iterable

def require(record: dict[str, Any], *path: str) -> Any:
    value: Any = record
    for key in path:
        if not isinstance(value, dict) or key not in value:
            raise ValueError(f"missing JSON path: {'.'.join(path)}")
        value = value[key]
    return value

def parse_line(line: str) -> tuple[object, ...]:
    record = json.loads(line)
    success = require(record, "result", "success")
    if type(success) is not bool:
        raise ValueError("result.success must be a JSON boolean")
    stamp = datetime.fromisoformat(require(record, "ts").replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    if stamp.utcoffset() is None:
        raise ValueError("ts must include an offset")
    raw = json.dumps(record, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return (require(record, "event_id"), stamp.isoformat(),
            require(record, "identity", "id"), require(record, "source", "country"),
            require(record, "device", "id"), int(require(record, "device", "managed")),
            int(success), raw)

def load_lines(lines: Iterable[str]) -> list[tuple[object, ...]]:
    rows = [parse_line(line) for line in lines if line.strip()]
    ids = [row[0] for row in rows]
    if len(ids) != len(set(ids)):
        raise ValueError("duplicate event_id")
    return rows

def snapshot_id(path: Path) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()[:12]

The exact outcome for a3 is:

ValueError: result.success must be a JSON boolean

Converting the string to True would conceal a producer regression. Explicit failure is cheaper than a plausible wrong answer.

SQL That Exposes Its Plan

SQLite stores the normalized subset. Raw JSON remains available for forensic review, but every query need not repeat deep extraction.

CREATE TABLE auth_event (
 event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, ts TEXT NOT NULL, identity_id TEXT NOT NULL,
 country TEXT NOT NULL, device_id TEXT NOT NULL,
 managed INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(managed IN (0,1)),
 success INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(success IN (0,1)), raw_json TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX auth_identity_ts ON auth_event(identity_id, ts);

LAG compares each success with the immediately preceding success for that identity. The correlated subquery determines whether the current device appeared earlier.

WITH ordered AS (
 SELECT event_id, identity_id, ts, country, device_id,
   LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY identity_id ORDER BY ts,event_id) previous_ts,
   LAG(country) OVER (PARTITION BY identity_id ORDER BY ts,event_id) previous_country
 FROM auth_event WHERE success=1
), candidates AS (
 SELECT *, ROUND((julianday(ts)-julianday(previous_ts))*1440,1) minutes_apart,
   NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM auth_event p
     WHERE p.identity_id=ordered.identity_id AND p.device_id=ordered.device_id
       AND p.ts<ordered.ts) new_device
 FROM ordered
)
SELECT identity_id,previous_country,country,minutes_apart,device_id,new_device
FROM candidates
WHERE previous_country<>country AND minutes_apart BETWEEN 0 AND 30
ORDER BY identity_id,ts;

After correcting a3 to the JSON boolean true, exact output is:

identity_id  previous_country  country  minutes_apart  device_id  new_device
u1           US                DE       18.0           d9         1

This is a candidate, not proof of compromise. VPN egress and carrier routing can change apparent country without travel.

Inspect properties, not decorative SQL

Run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN. SQLite wording varies by release, so assert a useful property instead of snapshotting every character:

import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE auth_event(
  event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, identity_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  ts TEXT NOT NULL, country TEXT NOT NULL, device_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  success INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX auth_identity_ts ON auth_event(identity_id, ts);
""")
investigation_sql = """
SELECT identity_id, ts, country
FROM auth_event INDEXED BY auth_identity_ts
WHERE identity_id = 'u1' AND ts >= '2026-08-01T00:00:00+00:00'
ORDER BY identity_id, ts
"""
plan = connection.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + investigation_sql).fetchall()
assert "auth_identity_ts" in "\n".join(row[-1] for row in plan)

In a warehouse, first bound the base scan by event-date partitions and project only needed columns. Then inspect partitions pruned, bytes read, cardinality estimates, join distribution, spill, and sort stages. A thirty-day query that scans five years because its date predicate appears too late is an analytical defect, not merely a slow database.

Independent Python Implementation

Parity is more convincing when Python does not call the SQL implementation.

from datetime import datetime

def find_country_jumps(rows: list[tuple[object, ...]]) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    seen: dict[str, set[str]] = {}; prior: dict[str, tuple[datetime,str]] = {}
    findings: list[dict[str, object]] = []
    for row in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (str(r[2]),str(r[1]),str(r[0]))):
        _, ts_text, identity, country, device, _, success, _ = row
        if not success: continue
        ts = datetime.fromisoformat(str(ts_text)); key = str(identity)
        known = seen.setdefault(key, set())
        if key in prior:
            previous_ts, previous_country = prior[key]
            minutes = (ts-previous_ts).total_seconds()/60
            if previous_country != country and 0 <= minutes <= 30:
                findings.append({"identity_id":identity,"previous_country":previous_country,
                    "country":country,"minutes_apart":round(minutes,1),
                    "device_id":device,"new_device":str(device) not in known})
        known.add(str(device)); prior[key]=(ts,str(country))
    return findings

The tie-breaker event_id matters. If SQL orders tied timestamps differently from Python, the engines can disagree nondeterministically.

Tests That Protect Meaning

Tests should cover parsing, temporal logic, duplicate handling, SQL/Python parity, plan properties, and idempotent reruns. unittest keeps the fixture runnable in this repository.

from __future__ import annotations
import hashlib, json
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any, Iterable

def require(record: dict[str, Any], *path: str) -> Any:
    value: Any = record
    for key in path:
        if not isinstance(value, dict) or key not in value:
            raise ValueError(f"missing JSON path: {'.'.join(path)}")
        value = value[key]
    return value

def parse_line(line: str) -> tuple[object, ...]:
    record = json.loads(line)
    success = require(record, "result", "success")
    if type(success) is not bool:
        raise ValueError("result.success must be a JSON boolean")
    stamp = datetime.fromisoformat(require(record, "ts").replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    if stamp.utcoffset() is None:
        raise ValueError("ts must include an offset")
    raw = json.dumps(record, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return (require(record, "event_id"), stamp.isoformat(),
            require(record, "identity", "id"), require(record, "source", "country"),
            require(record, "device", "id"), int(require(record, "device", "managed")),
            int(success), raw)

def load_lines(lines: Iterable[str]) -> list[tuple[object, ...]]:
    rows = [parse_line(line) for line in lines if line.strip()]
    ids = [row[0] for row in rows]
    if len(ids) != len(set(ids)):
        raise ValueError("duplicate event_id")
    return rows

def snapshot_id(path: Path) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()[:12]

from datetime import datetime

def find_country_jumps(rows: list[tuple[object, ...]]) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    seen: dict[str, set[str]] = {}; prior: dict[str, tuple[datetime,str]] = {}
    findings: list[dict[str, object]] = []
    for row in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (str(r[2]),str(r[1]),str(r[0]))):
        _, ts_text, identity, country, device, _, success, _ = row
        if not success: continue
        ts = datetime.fromisoformat(str(ts_text)); key = str(identity)
        known = seen.setdefault(key, set())
        if key in prior:
            previous_ts, previous_country = prior[key]
            minutes = (ts-previous_ts).total_seconds()/60
            if previous_country != country and 0 <= minutes <= 30:
                findings.append({"identity_id":identity,"previous_country":previous_country,
                    "country":country,"minutes_apart":round(minutes,1),
                    "device_id":device,"new_device":str(device) not in known})
        known.add(str(device)); prior[key]=(ts,str(country))
    return findings

import unittest

GOOD = [
'{"event_id":"a1","ts":"2026-08-01T10:00:00Z","identity":{"id":"u1"},"source":{"country":"US"},"device":{"id":"d1","managed":true},"result":{"success":true}}',
'{"event_id":"a2","ts":"2026-08-01T10:18:00Z","identity":{"id":"u1"},"source":{"country":"DE"},"device":{"id":"d9","managed":false},"result":{"success":true}}']

class PipelineTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_jump(self):
        result=find_country_jumps(load_lines(GOOD))
        self.assertEqual(result[0]["minutes_apart"],18.0)
        self.assertIs(result[0]["new_device"],True)
    def test_string_boolean(self):
        bad=GOOD[0].replace('"success":true','"success":"true"')
        with self.assertRaisesRegex(ValueError,"JSON boolean"): parse_line(bad)
    def test_duplicate(self):
        with self.assertRaisesRegex(ValueError,"duplicate"): load_lines([GOOD[0],GOOD[0]])

if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()

Expected output:

...
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 3 tests

OK

Do not convert every empirical expectation into a brittle assertion. “Exactly twelve findings” fails when legitimate late events arrive. Monitor input count, null rate, identity cardinality, and finding rate within documented tolerances; reserve hard failure for broken schemas and impossible values. Monitoring detects change. Tests define invalidity.

Secrets Are Inputs, Not Notebook Content

Use a workload identity or secret manager. Local code should fail without printing the secret:

import os
def warehouse_token() -> str:
    token=os.environ.get("SECURITY_WAREHOUSE_TOKEN")
    if not token: raise RuntimeError("SECURITY_WAREHOUSE_TOKEN is not configured")
    return token

Avoid credentials in committed .env files, command arguments visible in process listings, query URLs, exception traces, and notebook output. Prefer short-lived credentials, least-privilege read roles, separate development and production identities, and audited access. Fixtures should replace personal identifiers and IP addresses unless their retention is necessary and approved.

Notebook Exit Criteria

A notebook is useful while the analyst asks which transformation explains the observation. It becomes hazardous when hidden state is treated as a scheduled pipeline. Promote work when the answer is recurring, shared, used for enforcement, or expensive enough that silent drift matters.

Promotion means moving logic into typed functions; replacing mutable downloads with snapshot IDs; parameterizing the observation interval instead of using implicit “now”; storing reviewed SQL with deterministic ordering; recording revision, runtime, parameters, counts, and snapshot hash; adding schema, parity, idempotence, and plan checks; scheduling with a service identity, timeout, bounded retries, and alerts; and publishing atomically from staging only after validation.

{"run_id":"2026-08-02T06:00Z","source_revision":"8c31f2a","input_snapshot":"70dc8a7c8225","window_start":"2026-07-03T00:00:00Z","window_end":"2026-08-02T00:00:00Z","input_rows":8420911,"findings":37,"status":"published"}

Retry only likely transient failures. A schema violation will not heal on attempt three. Backfills accept explicit intervals and must produce the same state twice. Alert on stale successful output as well as exceptions: a green job that published zero bytes is unhealthy.

Reproducibility Under Real Failure

The happy path is the least interesting test of a pipeline. Consider a scheduler that reads a date partition, writes findings, and crashes after the write but before it records success. If the retry appends, every finding is duplicated. Give the output a natural idempotency key—perhaps (identity_id, current_event_id, rule_version)—and write with an upsert or transactional replace. When the transformation itself changes, increment the rule version rather than silently overwriting historical meaning.

Late data creates a different problem. Suppose event a2 arrives today but belongs to yesterday. Reprocessing only today's partition misses its relationship to a1; appending it to yesterday changes yesterday's result. A bounded correction policy should identify which input partitions can still change, rebuild the affected output interval, and publish a new revision. The run manifest should distinguish observed_at, event_time, and published_at so an auditor can reconstruct both operational knowledge and corrected history.

Data snapshots require more than a file name. A useful snapshot descriptor includes object URI or table version, content hash where feasible, extraction query revision, inclusive and exclusive time boundaries, row count, schema fingerprint, and source retention policy. If regulations prohibit retaining raw security data, retain a governed reference and enough aggregate evidence to verify the analysis without copying restricted content into the repository.

Test categories have different owners

A unit test belongs close to a function and runs on every change. A contract test confirms that the producer and consumer agree about field names, types, enums, and timestamp semantics. A data-quality test checks a particular snapshot for broken invariants. A statistical test watches distributional movement without asserting that movement is necessarily wrong. An integration test exercises database transactions, permissions, and serialization. A replay test processes a historical interval end to end and compares a versioned result.

Combining these into one “pipeline passed” flag makes diagnosis slower. A new country code may violate an outdated enum but be valid data; a large fall in volume may be a collector outage; a changed finding count may be the intended result of a rule revision. Each failure should name its violated assumption, observed value, expected boundary, snapshot, and remediation owner.

Tests also need adversarial cases. Use a timestamp exactly at the thirty-minute boundary, two events with identical timestamps, reversed arrival order, a failed login between two successes, a device seen only after the candidate event, Unicode identity values, missing country, and an input line large enough to stress memory. The expected behavior must be stated before implementation. Boundary fixtures prevent a future refactor from changing BETWEEN 0 AND 30 into a subtly different policy.

Cost-Aware Baselines Without Semantic Drift

Precomputation is safe only when the aggregate retains sufficient information. A daily table with login_count, device_count, and last_country cannot reproduce an impossible-travel sequence: ordering inside the day has been destroyed. Conversely, daily count, sum, minimum, and maximum can support many rolling summaries exactly. Decide physical grain from the hardest required query, not from storage fashion.

Query optimization should proceed as an experiment. Record the reference query's plan and answer on a fixed snapshot. Change one factor—predicate placement, index, clustering key, materialized daily aggregate, or join strategy. Measure wall-clock time, compute or bytes scanned, peak memory or spill, and answer parity. A query that is twice as fast but loses late-arriving records is not optimized; it computes a different function.

Parameterization deserves equal care. Bind values through the database driver rather than formatting identity strings into SQL. Maintain an allowlist when a parameter selects a column or ordering direction, because bind parameters generally represent values, not SQL identifiers. Log a redacted parameter manifest: time bounds and rule version are useful; access tokens and full lists of sensitive identities are not.

Finally, distinguish reproducible from repeatable. A run is repeatable when the same operator can execute it again. It is reproducible when an independent operator can obtain the same result from the recorded materials. It is robust when reasonable changes—machine, batch size, event arrival order—do not change meaning. A mature analytical repository aims for all three and documents the cases, such as nondeterministic approximate algorithms, where exact equality is neither possible nor required.

A final peer-review checklist should be answerable from the repository alone: What question and interval were evaluated? Which snapshot supplied the records? Which fields can be absent? Which ordering resolves timestamp ties? Which query plan was accepted? Which outputs are exact versus approximate? Which principal can read the source and publish the result? How does an operator rerun one interval without touching others? If any answer exists only in the original analyst's memory, the workflow is not ready to become shared evidence.

Sources and Further Reading

  1. Python Packaging Authority, Writing pyproject.toml.
  2. Python Software Foundation, unittest.
  3. SQLite, Query Planning and Window Functions.
  4. NIST, Secure Software Development Framework, SP 800-218.
  5. NIST, Digital Identity Guidelines, SP 800-63.
  6. OWASP, Secrets Management Cheat Sheet.
  7. The Twelve-Factor App, Config.
  8. Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, O'Reilly, 2017.

Interview Practicum

The Baseline Query Melts the Warehouse

Panel prompt

“A query computes each identity's thirty-day authentication baseline across billions of events. It takes four hours and spills. Analysts need twenty minutes.” The panel then reveals that events arrive forty-eight hours late and no new database will be approved.

Worked Answer

Strong answer as constraints arrive

Ask for the plan, physical layout, daily volume, identity cardinality, skew, freshness requirement, and exact statistics. Counts, quantiles, sequences, and distinct devices do not have identical aggregation properties.

Require predicates that prune partitions, project only baseline columns, and verify pruning. Check whether service identities cause skew. Align clustering or sort order with identity and event time if supported. For mergeable features, materialize daily identity aggregates and combine thirty bounded partitions. Means merge from sum and count; variance from count, mean, and second moment. Exact distinct counts and quantiles do not merge like sums, so either retain sufficient detail or document sketch error.

Rebuild the last two or three daily partitions for the late-data correction horizon, then recompute affected rolling outputs. If raw sequence features are necessary, use aggregates to identify candidates and read raw events only for them. Compare old and new outputs per identity on a frozen replay; investigate mismatches by lateness, null pattern, and high-volume identity. The launch gate includes parity or declared approximation tolerance, bytes scanned, spill, and wall time.

Optimization shortcuts that fail

“Use Spark” ignores the platform constraint and may preserve the scan. “Add an index” is incomplete for a columnar warehouse. “Cache it” omits invalidation. “Sample one percent” can erase rare identities and corrupt individual baselines.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Warehouse follow-ups

Exact distinct devices are mandatory—what then? Maintain bounded identity-device membership at a daily grain and compute distinctness over thirty partitions, accepting its cost. Never call a probabilistic sketch exact.

What belongs in the on-call page? Run ID, failed stage, interval, snapshot, last successful publication, count deltas, and sanitized-log link—never credentials or raw sensitive events.

Thirty-second answer: “I would prove partition pruning, replace repeated raw scans with recomputable daily aggregates, rebuild the late-data horizon, and demonstrate semantic parity on an immutable replay before changing production.”

Key Takeaways

  • Reproducibility joins identified code, runtime, parameters, and immutable input.
  • Validate nested JSON before coercion; plausible conversions hide telemetry regressions.
  • SQL performance starts with bounded scans and inspected plans.
  • Independent SQL and Python implementations enable semantic parity tests.
  • Tests distinguish impossible data from unusual data; pipelines must survive retries and backfills.
  • A recurring or consequential notebook should graduate into a package and monitored pipeline.

Chapter 6: Visualization, Communication, and Analytical Storytelling

Redesign Studio: Four Charts Enter, One Decision Leaves

The wall display says alert volume is down 42 percent. The security vice president calls the program green. An analyst points out that confirmed compromises doubled. Both statements are true, and the dashboard has made them appear contradictory because it visualizes production rather than exposure, quality, or consequence.

This chapter is a critique studio. Each station begins with a chart that can be computed correctly and still mislead. We calculate the replacement, specify visual encodings, and state what the display permits a reader to conclude. There is no generic dashboard architecture here. The unit of work is a visual claim.

Station 1: Replace the Alert Mountain

Suppose two weeks have these counts:

week  eligible_logins  alerts  reviewed  confirmed_compromises
W1    2,000,000        1,000   900       20
W2    3,500,000          580   540       42

A bar chart of alerts celebrates a fall from 1,000 to 580. Its denominator is invisible, review coverage changed, and the outcome moved in the opposite direction. Calculate rates per 100,000 eligible logins and precision among reviewed alerts:

rows = [
    {"week":"W1","eligible":2_000_000,"alerts":1_000,"reviewed":900,"confirmed":20},
    {"week":"W2","eligible":3_500_000,"alerts":580,"reviewed":540,"confirmed":42},
]
for r in rows:
    r["alert_rate"] = 100_000*r["alerts"]/r["eligible"]
    r["compromise_rate"] = 100_000*r["confirmed"]/r["eligible"]
    r["review_precision"] = r["confirmed"]/r["reviewed"]
    print(r["week"], f'{r["alert_rate"]:.2f}', f'{r["compromise_rate"]:.2f}',
          f'{100*r["review_precision"]:.2f}%')

Exact output:

W1 50.00 1.00 2.22%
W2 16.57 1.20 7.78%

The redesign is a small multiple, not a dual-axis chart: alert rate and confirmed-compromise rate get separate aligned panels with the same weekly x-axis; review precision appears as a third panel. Each mark includes numerator and denominator in its tooltip or adjacent annotation. The decision memo now reads: alert burden per login fell sharply, reviewed-alert yield increased, yet observed compromise incidence rose 20 percent. That combination calls for a coverage investigation, not a green status.

Rare-event denominators

Never divide by “all traffic” when only a subset could generate the event. A privileged-action detector should use eligible privileged actions, not HTTP requests. A phishing report rate might use delivered messages or active mailboxes depending on the question; those denominators answer different questions. Display the population definition and observation window beside the chart.

When denominators are small, raw rates jump. For 1 compromise in 100 logins, the observed rate is 1 percent, but uncertainty is wide. Wilson's 95 percent interval for a binomial proportion is

\[ \frac{\hat p+z^2/(2n)\;\pm\;z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n+z^2/(4n^2)}}{1+z^2/n}. \]

The following code computes it without a statistics package:

from math import sqrt
def wilson(k: int, n: int, z: float=1.96) -> tuple[float,float]:
    p=k/n; d=1+z*z/n
    c=(p+z*z/(2*n))/d
    h=z*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n+z*z/(4*n*n))/d
    return c-h,c+h
print(tuple(round(100*x,2) for x in wilson(1,100)))

Expected output is (0.18, 5.45). Plot the point with this interval; do not give a tiny team the same visual certainty as a population of millions.

Station 2: Audit the Geometry

Three common choices create false drama or false calm.

Truncated bars. Bars encode length from a baseline. Showing values 96 and 100 on an axis beginning at 95 makes a four-percent change occupy eighty percent of the drawing. Begin ordinary bars at zero. If the meaningful question is deviation from a service objective, use a dot plot centered on the objective and label the transformation.

Dual axes. Mapping alert count to a left axis and compromise loss to an independently scaled right axis lets the author manufacture apparent correlation. Use vertically aligned panels or normalize both to a clearly named baseline index. If indexed values are used, preserve raw values in labels.

Log scales. A log scale is useful when values span orders of magnitude, such as host byte counts from 100 to 100,000,000. It turns equal ratios into equal distances. It is invalid for zero and awkward for signed differences. Label powers explicitly and explain that the distance from 100 to 1,000 equals the distance from 1,000 to 10,000. For an executive ranking of absolute financial exposure, a log axis may visually understate the largest item; use it only when multiplicative comparison is the task.

A composition chart also deserves suspicion. A pie chart of alert categories can show that 60 percent are phishing, but it cannot show that total alerts tripled. A stacked area chart makes only its baseline category easy to compare. Prefer direct lines for a few categories or a heat map when category-by-time density is the actual question.

Station 3: Put Calibration on Trial

A classifier assigns probabilities, but the dashboard shows only ROC AUC. In rare-event work, a model may rank well while producing probabilities that cannot support staffing or automated action.

Use ten equal-width probability bins or, when predictions cluster, quantile bins with displayed boundaries. Within bin \(b\), calculate mean predicted probability and observed event frequency:

\[ \operatorname{ECE}=\sum_b \frac{n_b}{N}\left|\bar p_b-\bar y_b\right|. \]

pred = [0.02,0.04,0.08,0.12,0.18,0.55,0.62,0.76,0.84,0.93]
truth = [0,0,0,0,1,0,1,1,1,1]
bins = [(0,.2),(.2,.6),(.6,1.0001)]
ece=0
for lo,hi in bins:
    idx=[i for i,p in enumerate(pred) if lo<=p<hi]
    mp=sum(pred[i] for i in idx)/len(idx)
    oy=sum(truth[i] for i in idx)/len(idx)
    ece += len(idx)/len(pred)*abs(mp-oy)
    print(f"[{lo:.1f},{hi:.1f}) n={len(idx)} predicted={mp:.3f} observed={oy:.3f}")
print(f"ECE={ece:.3f}")

Exact output:

[0.0,0.2) n=5 predicted=0.088 observed=0.200
[0.2,0.6) n=1 predicted=0.550 observed=0.000
[0.6,1.0) n=4 predicted=0.787 observed=1.000
ECE=0.196

The reliability diagram plots observed rate against predicted probability with a 45-degree reference. Add bin counts below it: a point based on four cases must not look as authoritative as one based on forty thousand. ECE is a summary, not a substitute for the diagram; binning choices can hide local failure.

For discrimination under class imbalance, show the precision-recall curve and label the prevalence baseline. ROC plots can remain useful for comparing ranking across thresholds, but a low false-positive rate multiplied by millions of benign events may still overwhelm operations. Mark the deployed threshold and annotate its precision, recall, alerts per day, and confidence interval.

Station 4: Separate Drift into Questions

“The model drifted” conflates at least three displays.

  1. Input drift: did feature distributions change? For categorical device posture, show shares by category and an “unknown” category rather than dropping missing values. For a numeric feature, overlay empirical cumulative distributions or use fixed, meaningful bins.
  2. Prediction drift: did the score distribution move? Show quantiles over time, with deployment and policy changes annotated.
  3. Performance drift: conditional on matured labels, did precision, recall, calibration, or cost change? Align each metric to the event cohort date, not the date on which its delayed label arrived.

Population Stability Index is often overinterpreted. For reference distribution shares \(r_i\) and current shares \(c_i\),

\[ PSI=\sum_i(c_i-r_i)\log(c_i/r_i). \]

from math import log
reference=[.70,.20,.10]; current=[.50,.30,.20]
parts=[(c-r)*log(c/r) for r,c in zip(reference,current)]
print([round(x,4) for x in parts], round(sum(parts),4))

Expected output:

[0.0673, 0.0405, 0.0693] 0.1772

This says the binned distribution differs; it does not identify cause, harm, or a universal retraining threshold. Show category contributions so reviewers can see what moved. Fix bins from the reference interval and handle zero shares with a declared smoothing rule.

Station 5: Draw a Causal Effect Without Hiding Time

A security-key rollout begins in week 5. A before/after line for treated employees drops from 8 to 4 compromises per 100,000 logins. That does not establish an effect if the untreated group fell from 6 to 3 during the same incident lull.

The difference-in-differences estimate is

\[ (4-8)-(3-6)=-1 \]

compromise per 100,000 logins. The redesign shows treated and comparison rates across all weeks, an intervention marker, pre-period trend, and a second panel of estimated weekly treatment effects with confidence intervals. Do not plot only the aggregate pre/post bars: they conceal pre-trend failure and timing.

If rollout timing varies, an event-study display aligns units by time relative to adoption. Include leads before treatment; nonzero pre-treatment coefficients warn that parallel trends may be implausible. State whether intervals account for clustering. A visual recommendation should say “consistent with one fewer compromise per 100,000 under the stated comparison,” not “security keys prevented every observed decline.”

Accessibility Review at the Door

Color is redundant, never sole meaning. Use line style, point shape, direct labels, or texture in addition to hue. A red/green status display excludes many readers and turns uncertainty into traffic lights. Prefer a blue/orange palette with text labels such as “within range” and “outside range.”

Meet WCAG contrast requirements for text and essential graphical objects. Avoid low-contrast gridlines competing with data. Provide concise alt text that states the chart's question, principal pattern, exception, and uncertainty. Preserve reading order and data tables for keyboard and screen-reader users. Do not rely on hover for denominators or threshold values.

Example alt text: “Weekly confirmed-compromise rate rose from 1.00 to 1.20 per 100,000 eligible logins while alert rate fell from 50.00 to 16.57. Review precision rose from 2.22 to 7.78 percent. The display does not determine why compromise incidence increased.”

Studio Critique: Match Display to Audience

An investigator needs event-level drill-down and reversible filters. A model owner needs cohort-aligned calibration, drift, threshold, and latency diagnostics. An executive needs the decision, affected population, magnitude, uncertainty, and alternatives. Giving all three audiences the same wall of tiles is not consistency; it is refusal to edit.

For a decision memo, lead with a complete sentence: “Observed compromise incidence increased despite lower alert burden; hold the proposed coverage reduction until the missing segment is explained.” Follow with the smallest figure that supports the sentence, then limitations and requested action. Avoid “data storytelling” that assigns motives to an attacker or causal credit to a control without evidence.

Critique Bench: Questions Before Pixels

Before accepting a chart, conduct a five-minute verbal review. What comparison must the reader make: position, length, angle, area, color, or animation? Position on a shared scale is generally easier to compare than area or angle, which is why a sorted dot plot often beats bubbles or a pie. What data disappeared through aggregation? Which records were excluded? Does the visual encode an outcome, a proxy, or an operational activity? What action would change if the pattern reversed?

Then inspect the calculation. Confirm time zones and whether weekly buckets are calendar weeks or rolling seven-day windows. Check whether a “daily average” is the mean of tenant averages—which weights small and large tenants equally—or total events divided by total exposure. If customers have radically different sizes, show both the population-weighted rate and the distribution of tenant rates. Simpson's paradox can make the aggregate improve while every important segment worsens because the mixture changed.

Uncertainty is not limited to confidence intervals. Labels may be incomplete, identity resolution may merge people, and controls may change what becomes observable. Encode maturity with open points, hatching, or a separate recent-period band rather than extending a confident line into unresolved cohorts. Annotate known instrumentation changes on the time axis. A vertical line labeled “collector v3 deployed” often explains more than another anomaly color.

Small multiples require disciplined scales. Shared scales support comparison but can flatten a small segment; free scales expose within-segment shape but prohibit magnitude comparison. State the choice. Sorting categories by value helps ranking; preserving a stable semantic order helps repeated scanning. Do not reorder severity levels alphabetically or let a dashboard resort them each refresh.

Network diagrams deserve a special warning. A force-directed hairball converts node count into visual authority while edge overlap hides paths. Begin with the question. For reachability, show the few typed paths to the protected resource. For neighborhood review, use an ego graph with degree limits. For group comparison, an adjacency matrix or summarized edge counts may be clearer. Label edge direction and time validity; otherwise a visually connected node can imply access that never existed simultaneously.

The final review is linguistic. Titles should make claims, subtitles should define population and period, and annotations should distinguish observation from explanation. “Compromise rate increased after rollout” is descriptive. “Rollout caused compromise” is causal. A responsible display never smuggles the second sentence through the grammar of the first.

Export matters too. Review the figure at presentation size, on a grayscale printer, at 200 percent zoom, and in the document where it will actually appear. A dashboard tooltip cannot rescue a screenshot pasted into an incident report. Preserve a machine-readable table beside static exports, record the query and snapshot used to generate them, and put the generation timestamp somewhere less prominent than the event-time coverage. “Updated today” does not mean the underlying labels are current.

When animation is proposed, ask whether motion reveals transition or merely attracts attention. A scrubber can help inspect an evolving attack path; autoplaying points usually obstruct comparison and creates inaccessible content. Prefer stable views with selectable time states and a textual summary of what changed.

  4. W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2.
  5. NIST, Visualizing Information for Cybersecurity.
  6. Brier, “Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability,” Monthly Weather Review, 1950.

Interview Practicum

The Executive Demands One Light

Prompt with live evidence

“Alert volume is down 42 percent, precision is up, compromise incidence is also up, and the executive wants one red/green indicator.” Then the interviewer reveals that only 60 percent of alerts have matured labels and the product launch doubled eligible login volume.

Worked Answer

Strong response

Decline the false compression while meeting the need for a decision. Offer a headline state tied to an explicit action—“coverage review required”—plus three supporting measures: compromise rate per eligible login, alert burden per analyst hour, and reviewed-alert precision with label maturity. Recalculate all count metrics using eligible exposure. Separate mature cohorts from recent incomplete ones and show their denominators.

Use aligned small multiples, not a weighted score whose weights conceal tradeoffs. If governance insists on a status, define it from preapproved conditions: for example, red if the mature compromise-rate interval exceeds the guardrail, amber if label maturity is insufficient, and green only when outcome and operational guardrails pass. The state must carry an “insufficient evidence” condition; missing labels are not green.

Misleading executive compromises

An average of normalized metrics allows a favorable alert decline to cancel rising harm. A dual-axis chart can visually force agreement. Showing counts ignores the launch-driven exposure change. Picking red “to be safe” avoids the analytical question and eventually destroys trust in status signals.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Display-review follow-ups

What if compromise labels arrive sixty days late? Freeze performance panels by event cohort and maturity; use leading operational measures separately, never as if they were confirmed outcomes.

What if the executive has ten seconds? State the action and reason: “Do not reduce coverage: confirmed compromise per eligible login is higher, and 40 percent of recent labels are unresolved.”

How would you test the redesign? Give representative analysts and leaders decision tasks, measure whether they identify the correct direction and denominator, audit accessibility, and compare decisions—not aesthetic preference.

Key Takeaways

  • Chart rates against the population that could experience the event and display numerator, denominator, and uncertainty.
  • Calibration, discrimination, drift, and causal effect answer different questions and require different displays.
  • Visual geometry carries assumptions: zero baselines, log scales, binning, and dual axes are analytical decisions.
  • Accessibility requires redundant encoding, contrast, alt text, and non-hover access to essential values.
  • A decision display should preserve conflict when the evidence conflicts; a single score must not make harm disappear.

Chapter 7: Machine Learning Methods and Selection

Benchmark Notebook: Three Models, One Review Queue

The product requirement is not “maximize AUC.” Each hour, a login service produces more suspicious sessions than investigators can review. The team can inspect the top 25 sessions in a batch. Missing a malicious login costs far more than reviewing a benign one, yet an uncalibrated probability cannot safely drive an automatic challenge.

We will build an imbalanced temporal fixture, compare logistic regression, a decision tree, and histogram gradient boosting, calibrate the selected model, and evaluate ranking, capacity, cost, stability, and interpretation. The fixture is synthetic so its mechanism is visible; the validation design is intended for real data.

Fixture: Make Time and Base Rate Visible

Each row represents a login. Features available at decision time are failed attempts in the preceding hour, device age, distance from the user's usual region, ASN rarity, and whether the session has strong authentication. Attack prevalence rises in the final period and the relationship between distance and attack changes slightly—a small regime shift.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.frozen import FrozenEstimator

rng=np.random.default_rng(27); n=6000
day=np.repeat(np.arange(60),100)
failed=rng.poisson(0.7,n); device_age=rng.exponential(120,n)
distance=rng.gamma(1.5,350,n); asn_rare=rng.binomial(1,.08,n)
strong_auth=rng.binomial(1,.62,n)
logit=-4.7+0.72*failed-0.004*np.minimum(device_age,365)+0.0015*distance
logit += 1.45*asn_rare-1.2*strong_auth+0.8*((distance>900)&(device_age<7))
logit += .035*np.maximum(day-44,0)
prob=1/(1+np.exp(-logit)); y=rng.binomial(1,prob)
X=np.c_[failed,device_age,distance,asn_rare,strong_auth]
train=day<45; test=day>=45
print(X.shape, int(y.sum()), f"train={y[train].mean():.4f}", f"test={y[test].mean():.4f}")

With the specified seed, expected output in the companion environment is:

(6000, 5) 177 train=0.0284 test=0.0327

The positive class is rare, and prevalence differs across time. A random split would leak future regime composition into training and produce a deceptively stable estimate. The first 45 days are development data; the last 15 form a locked temporal test.

Metrics Before Models

Let the review capacity be \(k=25\) per 1,500-event test period. For scores \(s_i\), precision at \(k\) is positives among the largest \(k\) scores divided by \(k\); recall at \(k\) divides by all positives. A cost policy assigns 1 unit to a benign review and 40 units to a missed malicious login.

import numpy as np

def top_k(y, score, k=25):
    chosen=np.argsort(score)[-k:]
    tp=int(y[chosen].sum()); positives=int(y.sum())
    return tp/k, tp/positives, chosen

def queue_cost(y, score, k=25, review_cost=1, miss_cost=40):
    precision, recall, chosen=top_k(y,score,k)
    tp=int(y[chosen].sum()); fp=k-tp; fn=int(y.sum())-tp
    return fp*review_cost+fn*miss_cost, {"tp":tp,"fp":fp,"fn":fn}

Average precision summarizes the precision-recall ranking across thresholds and should be read against prevalence. ROC AUC remains informative about pairwise ranking but can look excellent while top-of-queue precision is unusable. Brier score evaluates squared probability error; calibration curves will reveal where errors occur.

The operational metric is not accuracy. Predicting every event benign already achieves about 96.7 percent accuracy on the test period and catches nothing.

Contenders and an Honest Search

Logistic regression is the low-variance, inspectable baseline. Scaling is inside its pipeline so each fold estimates scaling only on its training portion. The shallow tree captures thresholds and interactions but is prone to instability. Histogram boosting can learn nonlinearities and interactions with regularization.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.frozen import FrozenEstimator

rng=np.random.default_rng(27); n=6000
day=np.repeat(np.arange(60),100)
failed=rng.poisson(0.7,n); device_age=rng.exponential(120,n)
distance=rng.gamma(1.5,350,n); asn_rare=rng.binomial(1,.08,n)
strong_auth=rng.binomial(1,.62,n)
logit=-4.7+0.72*failed-0.004*np.minimum(device_age,365)+0.0015*distance
logit += 1.45*asn_rare-1.2*strong_auth+0.8*((distance>900)&(device_age<7))
logit += .035*np.maximum(day-44,0)
prob=1/(1+np.exp(-logit)); y=rng.binomial(1,prob)
X=np.c_[failed,device_age,distance,asn_rare,strong_auth]
train=day<45; test=day>=45

def top_k(y, score, k=25):
    chosen=np.argsort(score)[-k:]
    tp=int(y[chosen].sum()); positives=int(y.sum())
    return tp/k, tp/positives, chosen

def queue_cost(y, score, k=25, review_cost=1, miss_cost=40):
    precision, recall, chosen=top_k(y,score,k)
    tp=int(y[chosen].sum()); fp=k-tp; fn=int(y.sum())-tp
    return fp*review_cost+fn*miss_cost, {"tp":tp,"fp":fp,"fn":fn}

models={
 "logistic": Pipeline([("scale",StandardScaler()),
     ("model",LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000,class_weight="balanced",C=.2))]),
 "tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4,min_samples_leaf=30,
     class_weight="balanced",random_state=27),
 "boosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=120,max_leaf_nodes=15,
     learning_rate=.06,l2_regularization=2.0,random_state=27)
}

for model in models.values(): model.fit(X[train],y[train])
for name,model in models.items():
    score=model.predict_proba(X[test])[:,1]
    p,r,_=top_k(y[test],score)
    cost,parts=queue_cost(y[test],score)
    print(name, f"AP={average_precision_score(y[test],score):.3f}",
          f"ROC={roc_auc_score(y[test],score):.3f}",
          f"P@25={p:.3f}",f"R@25={r:.3f}",f"cost={cost}",parts)

Expected output for the pinned fixture is:

logistic AP=0.357 ROC=0.870 P@25=0.560 R@25=0.286 cost=1411 {'tp': 14, 'fp': 11, 'fn': 35}
tree AP=0.107 ROC=0.757 P@25=0.200 R@25=0.102 cost=1780 {'tp': 5, 'fp': 20, 'fn': 44}
boosting AP=0.169 ROC=0.821 P@25=0.280 R@25=0.143 cost=1698 {'tp': 7, 'fp': 18, 'fn': 42}

These numbers must be regenerated when library versions change; that is why the environment is part of the result. Logistic regression wins this fixture at the actual review capacity. The higher-capacity models overfit a small positive class and unstable interactions. The relevant advantage is seven more discoveries than the tree in the first 25 and 369 lower cost units—not a vague claim that linear models are always safer.

Nested validation for tuning

The locked test cannot select hyperparameters. On the 45-day development interval, an outer temporal split estimates generalization and an inner temporal split selects settings. The inner folds must precede their validation windows.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.frozen import FrozenEstimator

rng=np.random.default_rng(27); n=6000
day=np.repeat(np.arange(60),100)
failed=rng.poisson(0.7,n); device_age=rng.exponential(120,n)
distance=rng.gamma(1.5,350,n); asn_rare=rng.binomial(1,.08,n)
strong_auth=rng.binomial(1,.62,n)
logit=-4.7+0.72*failed-0.004*np.minimum(device_age,365)+0.0015*distance
logit += 1.45*asn_rare-1.2*strong_auth+0.8*((distance>900)&(device_age<7))
logit += .035*np.maximum(day-44,0)
prob=1/(1+np.exp(-logit)); y=rng.binomial(1,prob)
X=np.c_[failed,device_age,distance,asn_rare,strong_auth]
train=day<45; test=day>=45

outer=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=3)
grid={"max_leaf_nodes":[7,15],"learning_rate":[.04,.08],"l2_regularization":[1.,4.]}
outer_ap=[]
for outer_train,outer_valid in outer.split(X[train]):
    search=GridSearchCV(
        HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=100,random_state=27),grid,
        scoring="average_precision",cv=TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=3),n_jobs=1)
    search.fit(X[train][outer_train],y[train][outer_train])
    score=search.best_estimator_.predict_proba(X[train][outer_valid])[:,1]
    outer_ap.append(average_precision_score(y[train][outer_valid],score))
print([round(x,3) for x in outer_ap], round(float(np.mean(outer_ap)),3))

Expected output:

[0.161, 0.222, 0.099] 0.161

Variation across outer folds is itself evidence. Report the fold distribution and dates, not only the mean. If multiple events belong to one identity or campaign, time splitting alone may still leak entity-specific patterns. Use grouped temporal blocks or purge an interval around fold boundaries when feature windows overlap.

Probability Repair Without Test Leakage

Class weighting changes the training objective and often distorts raw probabilities. Calibration requires data not used to fit the base model. Reserve the last portion of development data for calibration or use cross-validated calibration within development. Never fit the calibrator on the locked test.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.frozen import FrozenEstimator

rng=np.random.default_rng(27); n=6000
day=np.repeat(np.arange(60),100)
failed=rng.poisson(0.7,n); device_age=rng.exponential(120,n)
distance=rng.gamma(1.5,350,n); asn_rare=rng.binomial(1,.08,n)
strong_auth=rng.binomial(1,.62,n)
logit=-4.7+0.72*failed-0.004*np.minimum(device_age,365)+0.0015*distance
logit += 1.45*asn_rare-1.2*strong_auth+0.8*((distance>900)&(device_age<7))
logit += .035*np.maximum(day-44,0)
prob=1/(1+np.exp(-logit)); y=rng.binomial(1,prob)
X=np.c_[failed,device_age,distance,asn_rare,strong_auth]
train=day<45; test=day>=45

fit_days=day<35; calibration_days=(day>=35)&(day<45)
base=Pipeline([("scale",StandardScaler()),
    ("model",LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000,class_weight="balanced",C=.2))])
base.fit(X[fit_days],y[fit_days])
calibrated=CalibratedClassifierCV(FrozenEstimator(base),method="isotonic")
calibrated.fit(X[calibration_days],y[calibration_days])
raw=base.predict_proba(X[test])[:,1]
fixed=calibrated.predict_proba(X[test])[:,1]
print(f"raw Brier={brier_score_loss(y[test],raw):.4f}")
print(f"calibrated Brier={brier_score_loss(y[test],fixed):.4f}")
print(f"mean predicted={fixed.mean():.4f} observed={y[test].mean():.4f}")

Expected output:

raw Brier=0.1569
calibrated Brier=0.0263
mean predicted=0.0280 observed=0.0327

Isotonic calibration can overfit when positives are scarce. Compare sigmoid calibration, inspect reliability bins with counts, and bootstrap by time block. Calibration does not improve ranking by design; it makes a score more interpretable as probability. A ranking queue may choose the uncalibrated model if ordering is best, while an automated step-up policy needs trustworthy probabilities and separate safety review.

Interpretation as Falsifiable Investigation

For logistic regression, standardized coefficients show direction and relative log-odds association, conditional on the feature set. They do not prove causes. Correlated variables can exchange coefficient magnitude.

For any model, permutation importance measures the performance decrease after shuffling one feature on a held-out set. It fails when correlated features substitute for one another and becomes misleading if shuffling creates impossible combinations. Partial dependence averages predictions over synthetic feature changes; accumulated local effects can behave better with correlated features but still describe the fitted model, not the world.

A security review should pair global and local analysis:

  • inspect performance by strong-auth status, device-age bands, region, customer, and time;
  • retrieve representative true positives, false positives, and false negatives;
  • perturb inputs within valid ranges and check monotonic expectations where policy requires them;
  • look for proxies such as geography standing in for customer or workforce population;
  • explain the final queue with observed feature values and comparison cases, not a causal story.

The fixture intentionally makes strong authentication protective. If local explanations repeatedly claim strong authentication increases risk, investigate correlation, encoding, and interaction before writing prose around the model.

Model Choice Beyond the Scoreboard

The benchmark does not automatically crown boosting.
