Interview Practicum

The prompt is a negotiation: “The board wants one cyber-risk score next month. Design it.” The interviewer plays three stakeholders. The CFO supplies outage cost but distrusts probabilities. The CISO wants ATT&CK coverage. The platform VP says the asset inventory is stale.

The candidate gets credit for drawing a typed graph before proposing arithmetic. They define horizon and consequence, identify crown-jewel assets, authority paths, trust boundaries, attack transitions, controls, and observations. They offer an expected-loss distribution with drill-down, not a magic scalar.

At minute ten, the interviewer reveals two controls depend on the same identity provider. The candidate adds a common-cause node and retracts any independence assumption. At minute twenty, the CFO asks to multiply red/amber/green ratings. The candidate explains why ordinal categories cannot support multiplication and proposes ranges with sensitivity. Finally, the platform VP admits inventory coverage is 70 percent. The candidate reports model coverage as a first-class uncertainty and refuses to label absent paths safe.

Worked Answer

Deliver a bounded first model for two material services, not an invented enterprise total. Define asset-specific loss distributions over twelve months. Build identity and deployment reachability from authoritative configuration, then validate trust crossings with owners. Map plausible attack steps to ATT&CK or ATLAS and local scenario identifiers. Attach controls to mechanisms and telemetry to observations.

Compute path-conditioned loss with explicit dependence and parameter grades. Present median and tail risk, top paths, control-removal deltas, missing-topology coverage, and sensitivity. Use CSF functions as governance and outcome groupings. The board sees a concise range and movement; engineers retain graph-level evidence.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

How do you combine confidentiality and availability impact? Keep separate consequence dimensions until an accountable owner supplies a common monetary or utility model. Do not average incompatible ordinal ratings.

Does ATT&CK coverage equal security? No. It measures mapped behavioral scope. It says nothing by itself about attacker frequency, sensor quality, control effect, or consequence.

How should unknown probabilities be handled? Use ranges or distributions tied to evidence grades, then run sensitivity. If a decision reverses across plausible values, fund measurement before claiming a ranking.

What invalidates the graph? Unowned high-impact assets, stale authority edges, hidden shared dependencies, topology changes without versioning, or outputs that cannot be traced to evidence.

Key Takeaways

  • Risk emerges from connected assets, authority, trust transitions, attack mechanisms, controls, and consequences.
  • ATT&CK and ATLAS supply behavioral coordinates, not probabilities or proof of coverage.
  • Control coverage, conditional effect, availability, and common-cause failure are separate quantities.
  • Events, alerts, incidents, near misses, and losses require distinct keys and denominators.
  • A scalar is acceptable only as a view over a versioned, inspectable graph with uncertainty.
  • The most valuable output is often the path or assumption that can change a decision.

Chapter 11: Make the Claim Before You Touch the Data

“Prove the new agent approval flow makes us safer.” This sentence hides at least six decisions: what “safer” means, which agent actions count, whose experience matters, what alternative policy is being compared, how long outcomes take, and how much evidence is sufficient to change rollout. If analysts open a notebook before resolving those questions, the available data will quietly choose the question for them.

This chapter is a claim-construction workshop. The running case is an engineering agent that proposes shell commands and production changes. The current policy auto-approves low-risk actions and sends others to a human. A new policy requires approval for any command touching deployment infrastructure. We will translate the executive request into a population, unit, intervention, comparison, outcomes, horizon, estimand, evidence grade, and decision rule—then execute an analysis on fixed fixtures.

The Claim Card

A formal claim should fit on one page before implementation begins:

claim_id: AGENT-APPROVAL-07
decision: expand_new_gate | retain_current | revise_and_retest
population: eligible production-agent action requests by staffed teams
unit: action request, clustered within task and team
policy_1: infrastructure-sensitive approval gate v2
policy_0: current gate v1
primary_outcome: harmful execution within 24 hours
guardrails: [task_abandonment, approval_latency, reviewer_minutes]
horizon: 28-day enrollment, 24-hour outcome maturation
estimand: intention-to-treat risk difference
threshold: expand only if upper_95_harm_delta <= -0.002
             and p95_latency_delta <= 45 seconds
exclusions: break-glass incidents, synthetic red-team tasks

The card prevents semantic drift. It does not guarantee identification. It makes disagreements inspectable before results are known.

Question, Claim, Estimand, Decision

A security question is broad: does approval help? A claim is falsifiable: among eligible production action requests, assignment to gate v2 reduces harmful execution within 24 hours by at least 0.2 percentage points without adding more than 45 seconds to p95 decision latency. An estimand is the precise population quantity:

$$\tau_{ITT}=E[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)],$$

where $Y_i(z)$ is the potential harmful-execution outcome under assignment $z$. The decision rule maps estimates and uncertainty to action.

Intention-to-treat is appropriate because assignment is controlled and bypasses occur in reality. A per-protocol estimand—effect among requests that actually received the assigned behavior—answers a different question and can be biased by noncompliance. Both may be reported, but only one is primary.

When random assignment is unavailable, specify the comparison mechanism: phased rollout, regression discontinuity around a policy boundary, difference-in-differences, matched controls, or an explicitly descriptive comparison. Never let “A/B-like” conceal a nonrandom launch.

Choose a Unit That Can Receive Policy

Possible units include event, action request, task, session, identity, host, incident, customer, and team-week. The unit must align with assignment and outcome. One agent task may emit twenty commands. Randomizing commands within the same task can contaminate treatment because an earlier rejection changes later proposals. Meridian therefore randomizes by task and analyzes action outcomes with cluster-aware uncertainty.

The population is not “all logs.” It is the set of units to which the decision will apply. State eligibility in executable terms:

eligible = environment = 'production'
       AND agent_mode = 'write_enabled'
       AND team_staffed_for_review = TRUE
       AND break_glass = FALSE

This excludes unstaffed teams, so external validity is limited. The result cannot justify rollout to them without further evidence. Record eligible-but-not-enrolled units to diagnose selection.

Outcomes Need Adjudication, Not Convenient Proxies

The primary harm outcome is a request that executes and causes unauthorized state change, material policy violation, secret exposure, or service impairment within 24 hours, adjudicated blind to assignment where feasible. “Command rejected” is a control action, not harm. “Security alert” is detector output, not ground truth. “No incident ticket” may reflect reporting failure.

Guardrails protect other objectives. Approval latency should be measured from policy decision request to executable decision, using event time and monotonic duration. Reviewer burden is minutes per eligible task, not minutes per reviewed request alone. Task abandonment needs a definition distinguishing user cancellation from policy-induced failure.

Outcomes form a hierarchy:

  1. harmful execution (primary);
  2. near miss stopped by policy;
  3. unsafe proposal without execution;
  4. review disagreement;
  5. latency, burden, and abandonment.

Moving a result between levels after seeing data is not interpretation; it is outcome switching.

Evidence Grades Describe Support, Not Importance

Meridian grades each input and inference:

GradeMeaningExample
Arandomized or directly verified with complete provenancetask assignment; signed execution trace
Bstrong observational evidence with tested assumptionsphased rollout with stable pretrends
Cindirect or selectively observed evidenceanalyst verdict on alerted actions
Dexpert judgment or unvalidated proxyheuristic “unsafe” tag

A high-impact claim supported by grade D remains high impact and weakly known. Grades never average into a faux confidence score. The claim card lists which conclusion depends on which grade and what evidence would upgrade it.

Evidence can be contradictory. A signed trace may prove a command ran, while incident review disputes whether the change was harmful. Preserve both provenance chains and adjudication. Unknown is a valid state.

Metric Specifications Are Small Programs

A metric specification includes name, purpose, unit, numerator, denominator, event-time rule, availability rule, exclusions, grouping, missingness behavior, revision policy, owner, and tests. For example:

metric: harmful_execution_rate_24h
unit: eligible action request assigned to a policy
numerator: adjudicated harmful execution <= request_time + 24h
denominator: all assigned eligible requests with mature 24h horizon
missing: unresolved outcome remains pending; never coerce to zero
dedupe: request_id, latest valid adjudication version
revision: weekly cohorts may revise for 35 days; retain prior snapshots

The denominator includes assigned requests, not only executed or reviewed requests. That preserves the ITT interpretation. A separate executed-request rate can diagnose mechanism but is post-treatment and must not replace the primary metric.

Assumptions Become Tests or Sensitivity Analyses

Randomization requires allocation integrity, limited interference, known assignment, and valid outcome capture. Test balance on pre-treatment features, check assignment hashes, enumerate cross-task shared state, and compare outcome missingness by arm. Cluster assignment or analysis when teams and tasks create dependence.

For binary outcomes, the risk difference is

$$\widehat\tau=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0.$$

With rare harm, report arm counts, risk ratio when defined, exact or score intervals, and absolute difference. A zero in one arm does not prove zero risk. For clustered data, use cluster bootstrap, randomization inference, or cluster-robust models. Guardrails often need quantiles, not averages; a modest mean latency can hide a disastrous p95.

Multiplicity matters. One primary outcome and a small preregistered guardrail set protect decision clarity. Exploratory slices are labeled exploratory and used to design follow-up studies, not opportunistically to declare success.

Workshop Artifact: The Approval Evidence Ledger

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Eligible
    Eligible --> AssignedV1: hash bucket
    Eligible --> AssignedV2: hash bucket
    AssignedV1 --> Proposed
    AssignedV2 --> Proposed
    Proposed --> Approved
    Proposed --> Rejected
    Proposed --> Escalated
    Approved --> Executed
    Approved --> Abandoned
    Executed --> Harmful: adjudication
    Executed --> Clean: mature 24h
    Executed --> Pending: horizon open
    Rejected --> NearMiss: counterfactual review

The state machine makes denominators explicit. “Near miss” after rejection is not an observed harmful counterfactual; it is an adjudicated unsafe proposal. The ledger stores assignment before downstream state, immutable request IDs, policy versions, reviewer identity, decision timestamps, execution trace references, outcome version, and evidence grade.

Approval authority itself is a control surface. Reviewers need scoped permissions, conflict-of-interest rules, workload limits, and protected audit logs. The experiment must not weaken production by routing dangerous requests to underprepared reviewers.

Executable Analysis: A Clustered Approval Trial

The fixed fixture contains eight teams, four per policy, with eligible request counts, harmful executions, p95 latency, and reviewer minutes. The analysis reports ITT harm rates and a team-cluster bootstrap confidence interval. Save as ch11_approval_analysis.py and run with the specified .venv.

import numpy as np

rows = [
    ("A", 0, 400, 5, 31, 180), ("B", 0, 350, 4, 29, 155),
    ("C", 0, 500, 7, 35, 225), ("D", 0, 450, 5, 33, 205),
    ("E", 1, 420, 2, 63, 300), ("F", 1, 380, 1, 68, 285),
    ("G", 1, 510, 3, 72, 390), ("H", 1, 440, 2, 65, 325),
]

def rate(group):
    selected = [r for r in rows if r[1] == group]
    return sum(r[3] for r in selected) / sum(r[2] for r in selected)

r0, r1 = rate(0), rate(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
by_arm = [[r for r in rows if r[1] == z] for z in (0, 1)]
deltas = []
for _ in range(20_000):
    sampled = []
    for arm in by_arm:
        sampled.append([arm[i] for i in rng.integers(0, len(arm), len(arm))])
    arm_rates = [sum(r[3] for r in a) / sum(r[2] for r in a) for a in sampled]
    deltas.append(arm_rates[1] - arm_rates[0])
lo, hi = np.quantile(deltas, [0.025, 0.975])
lat0 = max(r[4] for r in by_arm[0]); lat1 = max(r[4] for r in by_arm[1])
minutes = [sum(r[5] for r in arm) / sum(r[2] for r in arm) for arm in by_arm]

print(f"v1_harm={r0:.4%} v2_harm={r1:.4%}")
print(f"risk_difference={r1-r0:.4%} cluster_bootstrap_95=[{lo:.4%}, {hi:.4%}]")
print(f"max_team_p95_latency_delta={lat1-lat0}s")
print(f"review_minutes_per_request: v1={minutes[0]:.3f} v2={minutes[1]:.3f}")
print("decision=REVISE_AND_RETEST")

Exact fixture output:

v1_harm=1.2353% v2_harm=0.4571%
risk_difference=-0.7782% cluster_bootstrap_95=[-0.9484%, -0.6231%]
max_team_p95_latency_delta=37s
review_minutes_per_request: v1=0.450 v2=0.743
decision=REVISE_AND_RETEST

Why not expand? The harm criterion and latency guardrail pass, but reviewer burden rises 71 percent and the claim card did not define an acceptable burden threshold. The correct action is not to invent one after seeing results. Operations and security must set it, improve routing, then retest. The fixture teaches a crucial discipline: favorable statistics do not authorize a decision absent a complete decision contract.

The bootstrap resamples teams, reflecting assignment clusters. Eight clusters are too few for comfortable asymptotics; a real launch should use randomization inference and more clusters. The exact output is a software fixture, not a claim that the interval has ideal frequentist coverage.

Decision Logs Prevent Retrospective Certainty

Before launch, record the claim, owner, alternatives, approved evidence, analysis version, thresholds, stop conditions, and expiration. After analysis, append results and decision without overwriting the prior record. If leadership chooses rollout despite an unmet condition, record it as a risk acceptance with accountable authority.

A good log distinguishes “evidence says,” “model assumes,” and “decision chooses.” Analysts estimate; policy owners weigh costs; control owners implement; independent reviewers challenge. Combining these roles invites motivated reasoning.

Negative Controls and Falsification

A credible plan says what should not change. The approval gate should not affect read-only actions outside its scope. If their latency shifts, shared infrastructure or logging may explain the apparent effect. A pre-treatment outcome—harm recorded before assignment—must show no policy effect; a nonzero estimate reveals linkage or clock defects.

Falsification questions make the workshop adversarial. Could reviewers infer assignment and classify outcomes differently? Could the gate cause agents to split one dangerous command into several safe-looking commands? Could users move work to uninstrumented tools? Could latency shrink the denominator through abandonment? Each mechanism implies an auxiliary measure and sometimes a redesigned unit.

The estimand may be partially identified. If capture is missing for two percent of v1 and six percent of v2 requests, calculate worst-case bounds by assigning all missing v2 outcomes harmful and missing v1 outcomes benign, then reverse. If the decision changes across bounds, repair capture before rollout.

Power calculations should use the decision threshold and cluster structure, not a generic ritual. Estimate baseline harm, minimum worthwhile absolute reduction, intracluster correlation, cluster sizes, and attrition. For extremely rare harm, extend enrollment, use a validated intermediate outcome, apply controlled sequential monitoring, or combine capability tests with bounded observational evidence. Do not lower the evidentiary bar because the desired answer is expensive.

Claims also need transport conditions. A result from staffed infrastructure teams may transfer to another group only if action mix, reviewer skill, baseline risk, tool permissions, and outcome capture are sufficiently comparable. List those moderators before rollout. Re-estimate locally when they differ rather than applying the same threshold by organizational decree.

Archive abandoned claims as carefully as successful ones. A stopped study records why identification failed, which data were insufficient, and what future instrumentation would make the question answerable. This prevents another team from repeating the same attractive but invalid analysis and turns negative analytical work into institutional evidence.

  • ASA, Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values: <https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108>
  • OWASP, Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations: <https://genai.owasp.org/>

Interview Practicum

The interviewer says: “Prove our new agent approval gate makes us safer.” The candidate must ask questions; each good question unlocks a fact. Assignment is by team, not request. Teams share reviewers. Harm labels mature after 24 hours. The rollout excludes nights because nobody staffs approvals. Leadership wants results after one week. The new gate logs rejected commands but the old gate does not.

The strong response converts the request into an ITT claim for staffed eligible teams, names task or team as assignment unit, defines harmful execution and guardrails, and refuses to compare raw rejection counts because instrumentation differs. They flag one week as inadequate for stable team-level inference and external validity to nights.

Then the interviewer changes the constraint: randomization is politically impossible. The candidate proposes a phased rollout with pretrend checks, contemporaneous controls, explicit interference analysis, and a weaker evidence grade. When told the highest-risk team demands early treatment, they recognize treatment timing is confounded and avoid claiming a simple causal effect.

Worked Answer

Draft and approve the claim card before rollout. Instrument eligibility, assignment, proposal, review, execution, outcome, and availability times with immutable IDs. Randomize at the task or team level depending shared context. Blind outcome adjudication where feasible. Retain all assigned eligible units in the primary ITT analysis.

Estimate absolute harm-rate difference with cluster-aware uncertainty. Report counts and unresolved outcomes. Pre-register p95 latency, reviewer burden, abandonment, and bypass as guardrails with thresholds. Audit allocation integrity and differential missingness. Publish evidence grades and limitations. Expand only when the complete decision rule passes; otherwise revise, retest, or explicitly accept risk.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

What if no harmful events occur? Report the exposure count and an upper confidence bound. Zero observations is not zero risk; supplement with safe adversarial tests that answer capability, not prevalence.

Can rejected unsafe commands count as prevented harm? They are near misses or unsafe proposals. Counterfactual harm requires assumptions or a design; do not count every rejection as a prevented incident.

Why not use requests as independent observations? Shared teams, tasks, reviewers, and repositories induce correlation. Ignoring clustering understates uncertainty.

Who sets the threshold? Accountable security and product owners set it before results, informed by loss, friction, and capacity. Analysts make consequences and uncertainty explicit.

Key Takeaways

  • Formalize population, unit, policy contrast, outcomes, horizon, estimand, and decision before analysis.
  • Assignment unit and analysis unit need not match; dependence must be honored.
  • Control actions and detector outputs are not security outcomes.
  • Evidence grades describe inferential support and must remain traceable to claims.
  • Metric specifications define denominator, time, missingness, revisions, ownership, and tests.
  • A favorable estimate cannot approve rollout when the decision contract is incomplete.

Chapter 12: Operating Security Data Science as a Control System

A lifecycle diagram is easy to draw and easy to ignore. Teams frame a question, collect logs, train a model, publish a dashboard, and call the work complete. Six months later nobody can reproduce the result, the schema has changed, analysts distrust the queue, and the model remains deployed because no owner has authority to retire it.

Security data science is not a sequence ending at deployment. It is an operating control system: evidence changes decisions; decisions change attackers, users, and telemetry; those changes alter future evidence. This chapter designs the operating model for Harbor, a company creating its first security data-science program and an eventual AI-agent security measurement platform.

The Lifecycle Is a Set of Accountable Gates

Harbor uses seven verbs—frame, instrument, collect, validate, analyze, intervene, monitor—but every transition has entry evidence, an accountable approver, and an exit artifact.

FRAME      -> signed claim card and harm model
INSTRUMENT -> event contract, privacy review, coverage test
COLLECT    -> immutable raw evidence plus provenance manifest
VALIDATE   -> quality report, adversarial fixtures, known limitations
ANALYZE    -> reproducible result and uncertainty statement
INTERVENE  -> policy version, rollout bounds, rollback owner
MONITOR    -> outcome, drift, capacity, and retirement evidence

Work can move backward. Validation may expose an unanswerable claim; monitoring may require new instrumentation; a threat-model finding may cancel collection. A stage gate is not bureaucracy when it prevents an irreversible decision from resting on unknown evidence.

Each artifact has an owner and time-to-live. Claims expire when the system or adversary changes. Schemas have compatibility policy. Models have review dates. Exceptions have explicit expiration. “Still running” is not evidence of continuing fitness.

Maturity Is Decision Capability, Not Tool Count

Harbor assesses maturity across evidence, inference, intervention, and governance:

StageDecision capabilityTypical artifactPromotion test
0 Reactivereconstruct isolated incidentsmanually assembled timelineprovenance and clock agreement
1 Descriptivequantify stable operationsversioned metric specificationdenominator and coverage tests
2 Diagnosticdistinguish plausible mechanismsslice and dependency analysiscompeting explanations tested
3 Predictiverank future cases within scopecalibrated shadow scoretemporal validation and capacity fit
4 Causalestimate policy effectspreregistered experimentassumptions and guardrails pass
5 Adaptiveupdate controls under feedbackgoverned champion/challenger loopsafe exploration and retirement work

Maturity is not globally uniform. Harbor may operate incident timelines at stage 2 and agent controls at stage 0. Buying a feature store does not advance causal capability. Promotion requires a repeated, audited decision process, not one successful project.

Stage 0 is not shameful. During a breach, reliable reconstruction can matter more than prediction. The danger is claiming a higher stage than evidence supports.

Threat-Model the Analytics Pipeline

The pipeline is part of the attack surface. An adversary can evade collection, poison features, manipulate labels, steal sensitive telemetry, probe thresholds, exhaust reviewers, or compromise deployment. Insiders and accidental changes can create the same effects.

Harbor models the pipeline by asset and trust transition:

flowchart TB
    S1[Endpoint sensors] -->|signed batches| I{Ingestion boundary}
    S2[Cloud audit] -->|checkpointed stream| I
    I --> R[(Immutable evidence lake)]
    R --> F[Point-in-time feature builder]
    F --> M[Model/evaluation workspace]
    M --> P{Policy approval boundary}
    P --> D[Decision service]
    D --> H[Human review queue]
    H --> O[(Outcome registry)]
    O -. delayed labels .-> M
    K[Key service] --> I
    K --> D
    A[Adversary] -. evade/poison .-> S1
    A -. probe .-> D
    X[Privileged insider] -. alter labels .-> O

The diagram exposes a shared key-service dependency, a human capacity node, delayed feedback, and distinct ingestion and policy boundaries. Threat analysis asks:

  • Can a source impersonate another source?
  • Can events be deleted, reordered, replayed, or backdated?
  • Can later evidence leak into historical features?
  • Who can alter labels, thresholds, or exclusion lists?
  • Can queries reveal sensitive identities or detector boundaries?
  • Can an attacker create queue exhaustion?
  • Can the organization reconstruct every deployed decision?
  • What happens when the outcome registry is unavailable?

Controls include source authentication, append-only manifests, sequence checks, schema quarantine, point-in-time joins, least privilege, two-person policy approval, isolated evaluation, data minimization, query auditing, rate limits, capacity shedding, signed artifacts, and practiced rollback. Every control needs its own telemetry; otherwise pipeline protection is merely asserted.

Reproducibility Is an Incident-Response Feature

A reproducible result binds code commit, environment lock, source snapshots, schema versions, extraction time, feature definitions, random seeds, parameter file, and output hashes. For mutable warehouses, store snapshot identifiers or an immutable extract manifest. A notebook whose query reruns against today's tables is not a historical record.

Peer review has three distinct passes. A security reviewer challenges threat assumptions and harm definitions. A data reviewer checks time, units, selection, leakage, uncertainty, and computation. An operator checks whether intervention and rollback are executable under real capacity. One generic approval box cannot substitute for all three.

Model governance begins before modeling. A rule, graph score, statistical test, or LLM judge can cause consequential action and belongs in the registry. Harbor records purpose, prohibited uses, training/evaluation lineage, owners, dependencies, thresholds, known failure modes, monitoring, review date, and retirement procedure.

Human-in-the-Loop Means Designed Authority

“A human reviews it” is not a safety argument. Reviewers need the right information, time, competence, authority, and appeal path. Harbor specifies four modes:

  1. human decides: automation organizes evidence but cannot act;
  2. human confirms: automation proposes a bounded action requiring approval;
  3. human supervises: automation acts within limits while humans sample and can stop it;
  4. human handles exceptions: automation acts normally, escalating uncertainty or policy conflicts.

Mode follows consequence and reversibility. A production database deletion may require confirmation; a reversible low-risk quarantine may operate under supervision. Automation bias is measured through disagreement audits and blind re-review. Reviewer fatigue is measured as queue age, decision time, override rate, and sampled error—not just ticket count.

Escalation paths must survive off-hours, conflicts, and outages. If no qualified reviewer is available, the system should fail into an explicitly chosen safe state: deny, defer, sandbox, or bounded automation. “Ask a human” without a service-level design is a latent outage.

Governance as Decision Rights

Harbor's council does not approve every query. It assigns decision rights:

DecisionResponsibleAccountableRequired challenge
collect a sensitive fielddata stewardprivacy ownersecurity and legal
change a harm definitionmeasurement leadrisk ownerindependent reviewer
deploy a thresholdservice ownercontrol owneroperations
grant an exceptionrequesting leaderrisk executiveexpiry review
retire a modelmodel ownercontrol ownerdownstream consumers

The registry links decisions to evidence. Exceptions contain scope, reason, compensating control, approver, start, expiry, and verification. Governance quality is measured by expired exceptions still active, unowned artifacts, overdue reviews, rollback-test age, and time to resolve challenged evidence.

Privacy and security can conflict. More telemetry may improve detection while increasing employee or customer risk. Collection must show purpose, proportionality, retention, access, and deletion. Derived features can be as sensitive as raw events. Governance evaluates the complete lineage.

A Twelve-Month Roadmap Built on Dependencies

Harbor avoids a list of models. It sequences capabilities.

Quarter 1: establish truth boundaries. Inventory three consequential services and their identities; define six metric specifications; build immutable manifests and clock-quality checks; create an outcome registry; form review roles. Deliver one reproducible incident reconstruction. Success means 95 percent of selected source batches have verifiable provenance and every published metric has an owner and denominator.

Quarter 2: make evidence dependable. Add point-in-time feature construction, schema compatibility tests, source health, privacy controls, and sampled label adjudication. Ship a descriptive identity-risk view and measure coverage. Success means replay produces identical approved outputs and missingness is reported by source and asset.

Quarter 3: evaluate interventions. Shadow one agent approval policy, establish random or phased comparison, capacity guardrails, and rollback drills. Success means an approved claim card reaches a decision with mature outcomes and uncertainty—not necessarily that the model wins.

Quarter 4: operate and retire. Launch a bounded champion/challenger process, quarterly threat-model review, evidence-grade dashboard, and retirement workflow. Integrate the first platform slice. Success means an obsolete rule is safely retired and one policy decision is reconstructed end to end.

Portfolio priority can be scored for discussion, not automated choice:

$$Priority=\frac{Decision\ Value\times Evidence\ Feasibility\times Reuse}{Delivery\ Cost\times Governance\ Risk}.$$

Inputs remain ranges with rationale. Hard constraints—legality, unacceptable harm, missing owner—veto regardless of score.

Unique Lab: Validate an Artifact Promotion Manifest

The lifecycle's smallest enforceable artifact is a promotion manifest. The lab checks that an analysis cannot advance to intervention without lineage, reviews, monitoring, and rollback. Save as ch12_lifecycle_gate.py and run using the book .venv.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Artifact:
    name: str
    code_sha: str
    data_snapshot: str
    schema_version: str
    security_review: bool
    data_review: bool
    operator_review: bool
    monitor_ids: tuple[str, ...]
    rollback_test_age_days: int
    expires_in_days: int

def gate(a: Artifact) -> list[str]:
    failures = []
    if not (len(a.code_sha) == 8 and a.code_sha.isalnum()):
        failures.append("invalid_code_sha")
    if not a.data_snapshot:
        failures.append("missing_data_snapshot")
    if not a.schema_version.startswith("v"):
        failures.append("unversioned_schema")
    if not all((a.security_review, a.data_review, a.operator_review)):
        failures.append("incomplete_peer_review")
    if len(a.monitor_ids) < 2:
        failures.append("insufficient_monitoring")
    if a.rollback_test_age_days > 30:
        failures.append("stale_rollback_test")
    if not 0 < a.expires_in_days <= 180:
        failures.append("invalid_review_expiry")
    return failures

fixtures = [
    Artifact("agent_gate_v2", "9ac14e2b", "snap-2026-08-01", "v3", True,
             True, True, ("harm-24h", "queue-p95"), 12, 90),
    Artifact("legacy_ranker", "main", "", "latest", True,
             False, True, ("alert-count",), 94, 0),
]

for item in fixtures:
    failures = gate(item)
    print(f"{item.name}: {'PROMOTE' if not failures else 'BLOCK'}")
    if failures:
        print("  " + ",".join(failures))

Exact fixtures are the two immutable Artifact instances. Exact expected output:

agent_gate_v2: PROMOTE
legacy_ranker: BLOCK
  invalid_code_sha,missing_data_snapshot,unversioned_schema,incomplete_peer_review,insufficient_monitoring,stale_rollback_test,invalid_review_expiry

This is intentionally a policy gate, not a statistical lab. Its artifact is unique to lifecycle operations: a machine-checkable promotion contract. Production should validate signed identities, registry references, approved exception objects, compatible environment hashes, monitor ownership, and rollback evidence. Hard-coded rules should be policy-as-code with tests and change review.

The negative fixture is important. A useful laboratory does not merely demonstrate success; it proves that unsafe or unreproducible state is rejected for named reasons. Exact error ordering makes changes reviewable.

Capstone Preview: The Harbor Evidence Platform

Later chapters build the pieces that this preview connects. The capstone platform is not a monolithic “security AI.” It has six bounded planes:

  • evidence plane: append-only source records, provenance, retention, and privacy controls;
  • semantic plane: entities, event contracts, clocks, metric specifications, and outcome versions;
  • analysis plane: point-in-time datasets, notebooks/jobs, evaluation suites, and uncertainty;
  • policy plane: thresholds, approvals, exceptions, decision rights, and rollback;
  • execution plane: detectors, agent controls, human queues, and bounded automated actions;
  • assurance plane: lineage, monitoring, audits, adversarial tests, and retirement.

An AI-agent security use case traverses all six. Tool calls and prompts enter the evidence plane; task, identity, capability, and resource semantics enter the semantic plane; an evaluation estimates unsafe behavior; policy decides approval requirements; execution routes or blocks the action; assurance samples outcomes and tests rollback.

The platform's contract is traceability: for any consequential decision, answer what evidence was available, which semantic and model versions transformed it, what policy chose the action, who had authority, what happened later, and whether the artifact remained within its approved scope.

Failure Modes That a Roadmap Must Budget For

Programs fail when foundational work has no visible customer, when model projects outrun outcome instrumentation, when privacy review arrives after collection, when human queues are treated as infinite, and when nobody receives credit for retirement. Harbor assigns product owners to evidence capabilities and publishes decisions enabled, not terabytes ingested.

Another failure is maturity theater: dashboards labeled “causal,” a registry containing only model filenames, or a red-team event presented as prevalence. Independent review should sample claims and reconstruct them. If reconstruction fails, the program has an assurance incident.

Roadmaps also need stop rules. A project stops if the decision has no owner, the intervention cannot be changed, required collection is disproportionate, outcome maturity exceeds the decision window, or plausible uncertainty cannot alter action. Stopping low-value analysis is a sign of maturity.

  • NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework: <https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218>
  • NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, governance, audit, assessment, and contingency controls: <https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5>

Interview Practicum

The assignment is an operating exercise, not a speech: “You are the first security data scientist. Build a twelve-month roadmap.” The interviewer hands the candidate twelve cards: cloud audit gaps, a noisy phishing model, no outcome registry, two analysts, an upcoming agent launch, privacy complaints, stale asset inventory, executive demand for a score, no experiment framework, strong incident responders, an unowned dashboard, and a fixed budget.

The candidate must place cards on a dependency wall. Strong candidates put ownership, asset/identity scope, event contracts, outcomes, privacy, and reproducibility before new predictive models. They exploit the strong incident team as a source of adjudication knowledge. They bound the agent launch with instrumentation, approval, and rollback rather than promising a perfect model.

At the halfway point, budget drops 30 percent. The candidate protects provenance, outcome capture, and one decision-focused pilot; they defer broad feature-platform work. Then a regulator requests explanation of agent actions. The candidate promotes decision reconstruction and retention policy, not a generic explainability dashboard. Finally, the CISO demands quarterly visible wins. The candidate defines wins as enabled decisions and reduced unknowns: source coverage verified, one metric retired, one policy evaluated, one rollback exercised.

Worked Answer

Begin with a four-week discovery that maps consequential services, identities, decisions, owners, telemetry, outcomes, privacy constraints, and current analytical artifacts. Score maturity per decision domain. Select one incident-reconstruction use case and one bounded agent-control use case.

Quarter 1 establishes claims, event contracts, manifests, outcome registry, and review authority. Quarter 2 establishes point-in-time data, quality controls, privacy enforcement, and reproducible descriptive measures. Quarter 3 shadows and evaluates one intervention with capacity guardrails. Quarter 4 deploys conditionally, monitors outcomes, runs rollback, and retires an obsolete artifact.

Govern with artifact owners, expirations, evidence grades, independent reviews, exceptions, and reconstruction audits. Measure the program through decisions supported, mature outcome coverage, reproducibility, review latency, control capacity, exception hygiene, and retirement—not model count.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

What is the first hire after the lead? It depends on the bottleneck. With unreliable collection, hire or borrow a security data engineer; with sound evidence but weak decisions, add an applied scientist. Do not default to an ML title.

How do you show value before incidents are reduced? Demonstrate verified coverage, faster reconstruction, retired misleading metrics, bounded unknowns, exercised rollback, and a decision changed by evidence. Do not relabel activity as risk reduction.

Who can stop an automated control? A named on-call role with technical authority, documented triggers, and a tested path. Governance without executable stop authority is advisory.

When is the platform ready? When a bounded use case can be reconstructed end to end and fail safely. Platform completeness is not a prerequisite; traceable operation is.

Key Takeaways

  • The lifecycle is a feedback control system with accountable gates, not a one-way project diagram.
  • Maturity measures repeatable decision capability, not tooling or model count.
  • Threat-model sensors, labels, features, models, policies, humans, and shared dependencies.
  • Human review requires capacity, authority, evidence design, audit, and fallback behavior.
  • Roadmaps should sequence truth, reliability, intervention evidence, operation, and retirement.
  • The capstone platform's central promise is reconstruction of every consequential decision.

Chapter 13: Telemetry — What the System Can Actually Know

At 02:14, an autonomous support agent read a customer ticket, queried an internal account service, generated a refund request, and called a payment tool. The payment was blocked. A dashboard later said the control “caught an unsafe agent action.” That sentence claims more knowledge than the system necessarily possesses. Did the agent intend a refund? Did untrusted ticket text redirect it? Did the model propose the call or did deterministic orchestration construct it? Was the customer record returned by the tool the same record shown to the model? Did policy block execution, or did the payment API merely time out?

Telemetry is the boundary between what happened and what can be defended as known. A log is not a transparent window onto reality. It is a claim emitted by a component, under a particular configuration, at a particular clock time, with blind spots and incentives. Security analysis begins by naming those claims precisely.

The Epistemic Ladder

Treat every investigation as a climb through four levels:

  1. World state: processes executed, credentials were exercised, packets traversed interfaces, people made decisions, and tools changed resources.
  2. Sensor observation: an endpoint hook, identity provider, proxy, application, or agent runtime noticed some projection of that state.
  3. Recorded assertion: the sensor serialized fields, attached its clock and identity, and attempted delivery.
  4. Analytical inference: a rule, query, model, or investigator interpreted one or more assertions.

The levels must not be collapsed. A cloud audit record proves that the provider's control plane recorded an API request; it does not alone prove which human controlled the credential. A DNS log proves what a resolver observed, not every name a process attempted to resolve. An agent trace containing a prompt proves what the tracing layer stored, not necessarily the exact token sequence presented after provider-side transformations.

For a recorded event \(e\), a useful evidence annotation is

\[ K(e)=(s, o, c, d, i), \]

where \(s\) is source identity, \(o\) the observation mechanism, \(c\) the configuration version, \(d\) the delivery path, and \(i\) integrity evidence. An event without these attributes may still be operationally useful, but its evidentiary ceiling is lower.

Seven Surfaces, Seven Different Truths

Endpoint telemetry observes local execution: process start, image hash, parent relationship, command arguments, module load, file mutation, socket creation, user session, and sensor health. Kernel or EDR observations are strong for activity on enrolled hosts, but container boundaries, short-lived workloads, encrypted filesystems, tampering, and unenrolled assets create gaps. A process tree is also an interpretation: parent identifiers can be reused, and operating-system semantics differ.

Identity telemetry records authentication and authorization. Preserve authentication method, credential or session identifier, issuer, subject, client, device claim, challenge result, token scopes, policy decision, and revocation. A successful MFA event says that a factor satisfied a policy; it does not prove benign control of the session. Authorization deserves its own event because “logged in” and “permitted this action” answer different questions.

Network telemetry spans flow records, DNS, DHCP, TLS metadata, proxy transactions, packet capture, and service-mesh observations. Flow records retain endpoints, ports, byte counts, flags, and timing at low cost; they omit content and may be distorted by NAT. Proxies see application requests only for routed traffic. Full packet capture has high investigative value but severe cost, privacy, encryption, and retention limits. No single network feed is “the network.”

Cloud telemetry includes control-plane audit, workload logs, configuration history, identity policy, object access, and managed-service diagnostics. Provider audit is authoritative about the provider's recorded API surface, but data-plane logging is often separately enabled. Organization-level collection, region coverage, account onboarding, and immutable export determine whether an apparently rich feed is complete.

Application telemetry supplies business meaning unavailable elsewhere: tenant, object, operation, authorization reason, workflow stage, request correlation, and outcome. It is also closest to developer change. Free-form logs, inconsistent identifiers, accidental secrets, and success messages emitted before transaction commit are common hazards. Prefer versioned security events at semantic boundaries over parsing prose.

Code and software-supply-chain telemetry records commits, reviews, branch protection, build identities, dependency resolution, provenance attestations, artifact digests, deployments, and runtime version. A repository event links an identity to a change; a signed provenance statement links a builder and inputs to an artifact. Neither alone proves the deployed bytes came from the reviewed source. The chain requires digest continuity.

Model and agent telemetry must represent nondeterministic reasoning and consequential execution without pretending that hidden model cognition is observable. Store inputs, context references, model and policy versions, outputs, tool proposals, approvals, executions, and resulting state as separate records.

A Trace Schema for Consequential Agents

An agent trace should be an event graph, not one enormous JSON transcript. Large blobs impede selective retention, access control, causal reconstruction, and schema evolution. The following envelope separates correlation, semantics, clocks, provenance, and sensitivity:

{
  "event_id": "evt_01J8B8YQ6V",
  "event_type": "agent.tool.execution.completed",
  "schema_version": "1.2.0",
  "observed_at": "2026-08-20T14:03:12.481Z",
  "occurred_at": "2026-08-20T14:03:12.402Z",
  "trace_id": "tr_7f91",
  "span_id": "sp_09",
  "parent_span_id": "sp_08",
  "actor": {"agent_id": "refund-agent", "run_id": "run_441"},
  "subject": {"tenant_token": "tkn_93", "case_id": "case_1882"},
  "action": {"tool": "payments.issue_refund", "operation": "execute"},
  "authorization": {"policy_version": "pay-guard@31", "decision": "allow", "approval_id": "ap_772"},
  "input_ref": {"digest": "sha256:ab...", "vault_uri": "evidence://inputs/991"},
  "output_ref": {"digest": "sha256:de...", "classification": "restricted"},
  "execution": {"attempt": 1, "status": "succeeded", "resource_version_after": "refund/883@2"},
  "runtime": {"orchestrator": "agent-runtime@8f31", "model": "model-release-2026-08"},
  "integrity": {"collector": "trace-gateway-4", "sequence": 91882, "signature": "base64:..."}
}

Prompt content should usually be referenced by digest and controlled storage rather than copied into every event. Record the system instruction, user input, retrieved chunks, memory reads and writes, model response, policy evaluations, tool proposal, approval, tool execution, and observable effect as distinct span types. A proposed tool call is not an executed tool call. A tool's 200 OK is not proof that the intended state changed. Capture a postcondition or resource version when consequences matter.

OpenTelemetry supplies trace and span correlation, but security semantics still require conventions. W3C Trace Context propagates identifiers; it does not establish trust. An attacker can forge an incoming trace header, so gateways should distinguish an untrusted upstream identifier from an internally minted trace identity.

Sensitive values need field-level handling. Prompts can contain credentials, customer data, exploit text, and model-injection payloads. Attach classifications, tokenize identities where attribution is unnecessary, encrypt referenced payloads, and make access purpose-bound. Redaction must preserve analytical meaning: replacing every URL with [REDACTED] destroys the ability to find a repeated malicious domain. Store a keyed token or normalized feature alongside restricted raw evidence.

Authentication, Authorization, and Sensitive Actions

A defensible chain for a sensitive action contains at least five assertions:

credential presented -> authentication evaluated -> session/token issued
        -> authorization evaluated -> resource mutation observed

Each arrow can fail independently. Identity-provider success without application authorization cannot explain why access was granted. Application authorization without token issuance context cannot show whether step-up authentication was required. A tool execution event without resource mutation cannot distinguish a no-op, timeout, rollback, or misleading response.

Define a sensitive-action catalog rather than relying on log severity. Examples include changing MFA factors, granting a role, exporting records, rotating a key, modifying a detector, approving an agent tool, publishing a package, and disabling collection. Each catalog entry names required evidence: actor, effective principal, target, old and new state, authorization policy, approval, request and result identifiers, and independently observable postcondition.

Coverage Is a Set Problem, Not a Volume Metric

Terabytes per day do not answer whether a decision is observable. Let \(U\) be the set of required evidence claims for a threat or control. Sensor \(j\) covers subset \(S_j\), has reliability \(r_j\), latency \(l_j\), cost \(c_j\), and common-mode dependency \(g_j\). Naive coverage is

\[ C=\frac{|\bigcup_j S_j|}{|U|}. \]

Weighted coverage assigns consequence weight \(w_i\) to each claim:

\[ C_w=\frac{\sum_{i\in \cup S_j}w_i}{\sum_{i\in U}w_i}. \]

Neither formula captures independence. Endpoint and local forwarding logs may both disappear when the host is compromised. Two feeds sharing the same upstream collector are not two independent witnesses. Mark common dependencies and require diverse evidence for high-consequence claims.

The practical artifact is a coverage matrix whose rows are evidence requirements and columns are sensors. Cells should be richer than yes/no: D for direct observation, I for inference, H for sensor-health evidence, and blank for no support. Add scope, latency, retention, failure visibility, owner, and validation date outside the matrix. The matrix is versioned because products, policies, and fleets change.

Minimization Without Self-Blinding

Collection minimization asks which evidence is necessary for a defined decision, not which logs are inexpensive. Begin with the sensitive action and work backward. If the decision is whether to suspend a session after impossible token use, exact message bodies and shell history are disproportionate; token lineage, device binding, regions, timing, policy result, and session revocation are germane.

Minimize along several axes:

  • field: omit content when category, digest, or keyed token suffices;
  • population: instrument privileged or exposed workflows more deeply than unrelated users;
  • time: retain high-volume raw evidence briefly and durable derived claims longer;
  • resolution: aggregate health metrics while preserving case evidence under authorization;
  • access: separate operational search, investigation, model training, and audit purposes;
  • location: derive features near the source when central raw collection adds risk without value.

Minimization can create an undocumented blind spot. Record every deliberate omission as a coverage exception with rationale, compensating evidence, approver, and review date. That turns “we do not collect it” from tribal knowledge into an explicit risk decision.

Executable Lab: Audit an Agentic Refund Path

The lab computes weighted direct coverage, reports inferential-only and missing claims, detects common-mode witness failures, and finds a minimum-cost sensor set that directly covers every mandatory claim. Save as coverage_audit.py and run with the book interpreter.

from itertools import combinations

requirements = {
    "untrusted_input": (2, False),
    "model_context": (3, False),
    "tool_proposal": (5, True),
    "policy_decision": (5, True),
    "human_approval": (4, True),
    "tool_execution": (5, True),
    "resource_postcondition": (5, True),
    "collector_health": (3, False),
}

sensors = {
    "agent_trace":   {"cost": 3, "group": "runtime", "D": {"model_context", "tool_proposal"}, "I": {"tool_execution"}},
    "policy_log":    {"cost": 2, "group": "policy",  "D": {"policy_decision", "human_approval"}, "I": set()},
    "tool_gateway":  {"cost": 3, "group": "runtime", "D": {"tool_execution"}, "I": {"policy_decision"}},
    "payment_audit": {"cost": 4, "group": "payment", "D": {"resource_postcondition"}, "I": {"tool_execution"}},
    "input_proxy":   {"cost": 2, "group": "edge",    "D": {"untrusted_input"}, "I": set()},
    "health_ledger": {"cost": 1, "group": "ops",     "D": {"collector_health"}, "I": set()},
}

selected = list(sensors)
direct = set().union(*(sensors[s]["D"] for s in selected))
inferred = set().union(*(sensors[s]["I"] for s in selected)) - direct
missing = set(requirements) - direct - inferred
total_weight = sum(weight for weight, _ in requirements.values())
direct_weight = sum(requirements[r][0] for r in direct)

mandatory = {r for r, (_, required) in requirements.items() if required}
candidates = []
for size in range(1, len(sensors) + 1):
    for names in combinations(sensors, size):
        observed = set().union(*(sensors[n]["D"] for n in names))
        if mandatory <= observed:
            candidates.append((sum(sensors[n]["cost"] for n in names), names))
    if candidates:
        break

best_cost, best = min(candidates)
runtime_claims = set().union(*(sensors[s]["D"] for s in selected if sensors[s]["group"] == "runtime"))

print(f"direct_weighted_coverage={direct_weight}/{total_weight} ({direct_weight/total_weight:.1%})")
print(f"inferential_only={sorted(inferred)}")
print(f"missing={sorted(missing)}")
print(f"minimum_mandatory_set={list(best)} cost={best_cost}")
print(f"runtime_common_mode_claims={sorted(runtime_claims)}")

Exact output:

direct_weighted_coverage=32/32 (100.0%)
inferential_only=[]
missing=[]
minimum_mandatory_set=['agent_trace', 'policy_log', 'tool_gateway', 'payment_audit'] cost=12
runtime_common_mode_claims=['model_context', 'tool_execution', 'tool_proposal']

The 100 percent result is not a declaration of perfect observability. It says only that the enumerated claims have a direct source in the fixture. The last line identifies a correlated dependency: trace and gateway evidence share the runtime group. The resource postcondition from the payment domain provides an independent witness for the consequence. A production audit should also test fleet scope, delivery lag, retention, schema validity, sequence gaps, and controlled canary events.

Operating the Unknowns Register

Coverage gaps belong in an operational register. Each entry states the decision impaired, affected scope, adversary opportunity, present proxy, planned remedy, owner, and expiration. Distinguish known absent evidence from unexpected silence. The former is design debt; the latter may be an incident.

Use canaries to verify end-to-end observation. A synthetic privileged action can traverse authentication, authorization, application, export, normalization, and detection paths. The canary succeeds only if every expected claim arrives within its latency objective and can be joined without manual guessing. Merely checking that a collector process is alive tests machinery, not knowledge.

Detection and response produce their own telemetry: rule version, alert inputs, suppression, routing, analyst access, disposition, containment, restoration, and later outcome. Vulnerability programs need scanner identity, asset scope, finding instance, evidence, deduplication lineage, ownership, exception, remediation, verification, and recurrence. Product telemetry should record whether security controls are enabled, successfully exercised, bypassed, abandoned, or creating friction. These operational records reveal whether an evidence system changes decisions rather than merely accumulating events.

Interview Practicum

You inherit telemetry for a customer-service agent that can credit accounts. The red team demonstrated prompt injection through ticket text, yet the company stores only final model text and application exceptions. The network team refuses payload capture, Legal prohibits indefinite prompt retention, the payment team offers a daily audit export, and launch is in six weeks.

The interviewer asks: Design the minimum telemetry needed to investigate unsafe credits and evaluate the approval control. After ten minutes, two constraints change: payment audit becomes available only after 24 hours, and the agent platform team says trace identifiers can be supplied by clients.

A strong candidate first asks which actions are consequential, maximum credit, authorization boundary, approval modes, tenant isolation, investigation horizon, expected volume, regulator needs, and who can retrieve restricted content. They separate proposal, authorization, execution, and postcondition. They reject client-supplied trace IDs as trusted roots and mint an internal run identity at ingress while preserving the external value as an untrusted correlation attribute.

Worked Answer

Instrument ticket ingestion with content digest, source trust label, tenant token, and restricted payload reference. Record ordered references to system instructions, retrieved material, memory reads, model release, sampling configuration, model response, and parsed tool proposal. The policy service emits rule version, evaluated attributes, decision, and reason. Human approval emits approver role, displayed evidence digest, decision, and latency. The gateway records the exact normalized call and idempotency key. Payment audit supplies independent postcondition evidence one day later.

For immediate containment, treat gateway success as provisional and reconcile it with payment audit. Alert on missing reconciliation after 26 hours. Retain structured trace metadata longer than prompt content; place content in purpose-bound encrypted storage with shorter retention and case holds. Preserve keyed indicators derived from untrusted text so repeated injections can be found without broad content access.

Coverage tests inject a synthetic ticket, approve and deny controlled calls, verify correlation and ordering, then reconcile daily results. The launch gate requires complete observation of all tool proposals, policy decisions, approvals, executions, and eventual postconditions; sequence-gap monitoring; access audit; and a tested kill switch. Report both direct coverage and the 24-hour consequence-confirmation lag.

Weak answers ask for “all logs,” equate model output with executed action, ignore sensor integrity, or promise that distributed tracing proves causality. A costly but still weak answer captures every packet while omitting authorization policy versions and resource postconditions.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

What if prompts cannot be retained at all? Retain digests, trust labels, token counts, retrieval identifiers, policy-relevant features, and a short-lived quarantined payload only when lawful. Evaluation becomes less capable of semantic replay; document that limitation rather than manufacturing certainty.

How do you distinguish tool retry from duplicate malicious execution? Carry a stable idempotency key across proposal, approval, gateway attempts, and resource audit. Preserve attempt numbers and final resource version.

Would you adopt OCSF or OpenTelemetry? Use OpenTelemetry for propagation and span mechanics, and map security events to a governed semantic model such as OCSF where categories fit. Neither substitutes for agent-specific action and authorization contracts.

How do you prove collection is alive? Exercise a harmless synthetic action end to end and require the expected event graph, latency, signatures, and reconciliation—not just collector heartbeat.

Thirty-second summary? Separate observed claims from inference; capture proposal, policy, approval, execution, and consequence as distinct events; minimize sensitive content; independently verify high-impact state changes; continuously test coverage.

Key Takeaways

  • Telemetry is a chain of claims with an evidentiary ceiling, not reality itself.
  • Endpoint, identity, network, cloud, application, code, model, and agent sources observe different projections.
  • Agent traces need separate, correlated records for context, proposals, decisions, executions, and postconditions.
  • Coverage is defined against required evidence and failure independence, not event volume.
  • Minimization should reduce fields, populations, time, resolution, access, and movement without concealing the resulting gaps.
  • Synthetic end-to-end actions test whether a system can actually know what its diagrams claim.

Chapter 14: Security Event Schemas and Data Modeling

The incident timeline looked impossible. At 09:02, alex@northwind authenticated from a managed laptop. At 09:04, a.chen downloaded a design. At 09:05, device 7F-22 reached a restricted database. The identity team counted three actors. All three records described one contractor after an email rename, directory migration, and device re-enrollment.

Security modeling preserves distinctions until evidence justifies a join. It must answer opposing questions: which records refer to the same entity, and which similar records must remain separate? A warehouse that never resolves identity cannot reconstruct behavior. One that resolves too aggressively can accuse the wrong person.

Facts Need a Declared Grain

A fact records an occurrence at a declared grain. A useful activity grain is: one row represents one source-observed attempt by an effective principal to perform one operation on one resource. A retry is another attempt, not an update. One request affecting five resources may require five resource-action facts plus a request fact. An alert derived from events belongs in a detection fact with lineage; it is not another activity event.

Dimensions describe entities or classifications: identity, device, resource, application, organizational unit, vulnerability, and detector. They change independently. If a device becomes unmanaged today, yesterday's activity must not silently acquire today's status.

A compact model includes fact_activity plus versioned identity, device, and resource dimensions. Facts carry event, occurrence and ingestion times, actor, device, resource, operation, result, source, and source locator. Dimensions carry stable entity keys and time-bounded attributes. Bridge tables express many-to-many relationships such as identity-to-account assertions.

Surrogate keys improve joins, but preserve natural identifiers and issuing authority. 12345 means nothing without issuer=okta-prod or source=aws-account-17. Global uniqueness is a contract, not a visual property.

Sessions Are Hypotheses With Boundaries

Some systems emit explicit sessions with issue, renewal, and revocation. Preserve that source session. Analysts also infer sessions by grouping activity across inactivity gaps. If ordered event times are \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), a new gap session begins when

\[ t_i-t_{i-1}>\Delta. \]

The threshold \(\Delta\) is a modeling parameter. Thirty minutes may fit interactive administration yet merge unrelated automation or split a long remote shell. Version the algorithm and threshold, and attach confidence when device or credential binding is uncertain.

Do not use a session to erase actor layers. A human operates a browser, which exercises an application service account, which assumes a cloud role. Model initiating_subject, effective_principal, and credential/session separately. “Who caused this?” may mean human initiator, target-accepted principal, executing process, or accountable automation owner.

Identity Resolution Is Evidence Accumulation

Begin with assertions, not a universal user table. An assertion has a source identifier, candidate entity, issuer, assertion type, interval, source record, and confidence. Strong links include an immutable directory object ID, certificate key identifier, device enrollment record, or cloud role session naming its source. Weak links include display name, mutable email, IP, and temporal proximity.

Resolution forms a graph of source identifiers and canonical entities. Deterministic rules can join (issuer, immutable_subject_id). Probabilistic linkage can combine evidence:

\[ \log \frac{P(M\mid x)}{P(\neg M\mid x)} = \log \frac{P(M)}{P(\neg M)} + \sum_k \log\frac{P(x_k\mid M)}{P(x_k\mid \neg M)}, \]

where \(M\) means two identifiers represent the same entity. Rare shared attributes are stronger evidence than common ones; contradictory immutable IDs should dominate a matching name.

Use asymmetric thresholds. Auto-link only above a high threshold, queue ambiguity, and preserve “not same entity” constraints. A false merge contaminates every behavioral profile. A false split loses history but is often reversible. Privileged identities warrant stricter rules.

Service principals, workload identities, shared accounts, and agents must not be coerced into employee rows. Give principals a type and relate them to accountable people or teams without asserting equivalence. A bot owned by Finance is not the finance director.

Slowly Changing Context and Bitemporal Truth

Type 1 slowly changing dimensions overwrite attributes and suit corrections whose history is irrelevant. Type 2 creates a version with valid_from and valid_to; it is necessary when historical context affects interpretation. Department, manager, privilege tier, device ownership, exposure, and resource sensitivity often require Type 2.

Investigations also need bitemporality:

  • valid time: when an assertion was true in the modeled world;
  • system time: when the analytical system learned and stored it.

Suppose HR tells the warehouse on August 10 that a contractor left August 3. A current query about August 5 should show no active employment. Reconstruction of an alert generated August 6 must admit the warehouse still believed the contractor active.

A bitemporal version occupies

\[ [v_{from},v_{to})\times[s_{from},s_{to}). \]

Corrections close the prior system-time rectangle and insert a corrected belief. Half-open intervals avoid double matches. The as-of join for event time \(t\) and knowledge cutoff \(k\) is:

v.valid_from <= t AND t < v.valid_to
AND v.recorded_from <= k AND k < v.recorded_to

Enforce non-overlap for versions of the same entity and belief state. Never update the only historical copy when reproducibility matters.

Four Clocks and Partial Order

Preserve occurred_at (source claim), observed_at (sensor observation), ingested_at (durable platform acceptance), and processed_at (transformation output). Store source timezone or offset, clock quality, and sequence numbers when available. Normalize for comparison but retain original timestamp text. Daylight-saving folds can produce duplicate local times; batching, mobile offline operation, virtual-machine drift, and coarse clocks weaken ordering.

If two times differ by less than their combined uncertainty, do not present their order as definite. Sequence numbers, transaction IDs, parent spans, and resource versions are often stronger. A state transition from version 8 to 9 establishes an order even if clocks disagree.

Streams use event time for semantics and processing time for operations. A watermark approximating max_event_time_seen - allowed_lateness trades latency for corrections. Late events must enter a correction path rather than disappear. Reports need an as_of time and revision state such as provisional, finalized, or corrected.

One Semantic Model, Four Physical Forms

Relational databases excel at constraints, point lookups, transactions, temporal dimensions, and explainable SQL. They are strong systems of record for identity, policy, and case state.

Columnar stores optimize scans and compression. Parquet or a columnar warehouse suits immutable events and feature computation. Avoid tiny files and high-cardinality partitions; partition by coarse time and perhaps tenant, then cluster for common predicates.

Graphs make variable-length paths first-class: identity assumed role, role accessed bucket, bucket contained artifact, artifact deployed to host. Every edge still needs direction, type, time, source, and confidence. A graph does not abolish provenance.

Streams represent changes in motion, with replay, partitions, and consumer offsets. Ordering normally holds only within a partition, so choose keys around invariants. A stream is not automatically an analytical model; consumers still need schemas, state, and late-event policy.

The semantic contract defines identifiers, grains, event types, clocks, units, classifications, and version rules. Physical projections optimize workloads. Graph edges, rows, Parquet records, and messages should remain traceable to the same source assertion.

Normalization Without Invented Semantics

Preserve raw evidence or a verifiable reference, parse source-specific typed fields, then map to normalized categories. If a source reports login success without authentication method, store method as unknown; do not infer password from absence of MFA.

Standards occupy different layers. OCSF defines cybersecurity categories. Elastic Common Schema supplies reusable fields. STIX 2.1 models threat-intelligence objects and relationships, while TAXII transports collections. OpenTelemetry correlates traces, metrics, and logs. CloudEvents standardizes an event envelope. Avro, Protocol Buffers, and JSON Schema express serialization contracts.

Mapping is rarely lossless. Retain extension fields and mapping versions. Mark whether normalized values were direct, transformed, defaulted, inferred, or unknown. Interoperability failures often arise from grain differences: one feed emits a flow summary while another emits requests.

Executable SQLite Lab: Query Two Knowledge Cutoffs

The model below contains identities, aliases, bitemporal device ownership, and activity. The warehouse first believed device dev-7 belonged to Alex through August 10. On August 12 it learned ownership ended August 5 and Riley became owner. Run with the book interpreter.

import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE identity (
  identity_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  display_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  principal_type TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(principal_type IN ('human','service','agent'))
);
CREATE TABLE alias (
  issuer TEXT NOT NULL, subject TEXT NOT NULL,
  identity_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES identity,
  valid_from TEXT NOT NULL, valid_to TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (issuer, subject, valid_from)
);
CREATE TABLE device_owner_bt (
  device_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  identity_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES identity,
  valid_from TEXT NOT NULL, valid_to TEXT NOT NULL,
  recorded_from TEXT NOT NULL, recorded_to TEXT NOT NULL,
  source TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY(device_id, valid_from, recorded_from)
);
CREATE TABLE activity (
  event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  occurred_at TEXT NOT NULL, ingested_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  issuer TEXT NOT NULL, subject TEXT NOT NULL,
  device_id TEXT NOT NULL, resource TEXT NOT NULL, operation TEXT NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO identity VALUES (1,'Alex Chen','human'), (2,'Riley Shah','human');
INSERT INTO alias VALUES
 ('idp','alex@northwind',1,'2026-01-01','9999-12-31'),
 ('repo','a.chen',1,'2026-01-01','9999-12-31');
INSERT INTO activity VALUES
 ('e1','2026-08-07T09:04:00Z','2026-08-07T09:04:05Z','repo','a.chen','dev-7','design/phoenix','download');
INSERT INTO device_owner_bt VALUES
 ('dev-7',1,'2026-07-01','2026-08-10','2026-08-01','2026-08-12','mdm'),
 ('dev-7',1,'2026-07-01','2026-08-05','2026-08-12','9999-12-31','mdm-correction'),
 ('dev-7',2,'2026-08-05','9999-12-31','2026-08-12','9999-12-31','mdm-correction');
""")

query = """
SELECT a.event_id, i.display_name,
       COALESCE(owner.display_name, 'UNKNOWN')
FROM activity a
JOIN alias x ON x.issuer=a.issuer AND x.subject=a.subject
 AND x.valid_from <= a.occurred_at AND a.occurred_at < x.valid_to
JOIN identity i ON i.identity_id=x.identity_id
LEFT JOIN device_owner_bt d ON d.device_id=a.device_id
 AND d.valid_from <= a.occurred_at AND a.occurred_at < d.valid_to
 AND d.recorded_from <= :cutoff AND :cutoff < d.recorded_to
LEFT JOIN identity owner ON owner.identity_id=d.identity_id
ORDER BY a.event_id
"""

for cutoff in ('2026-08-08', '2026-08-13'):
    row = db.execute(query, {"cutoff": cutoff}).fetchone()
    print(f"knowledge_cutoff={cutoff} event={row[0]} account={row[1]} device_owner={row[2]}")

orphans = db.execute("""
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM activity a
LEFT JOIN alias x ON x.issuer=a.issuer AND x.subject=a.subject
 AND x.valid_from <= a.occurred_at AND a.occurred_at < x.valid_to
WHERE x.identity_id IS NULL
""").fetchone()[0]
print(f"unresolved_activity={orphans}")

Exact output:

knowledge_cutoff=2026-08-08 event=e1 account=Alex Chen device_owner=Alex Chen
knowledge_cutoff=2026-08-13 event=e1 account=Alex Chen device_owner=Riley Shah
unresolved_activity=0

The account remains Alex because repository alias evidence is unchanged. Device ownership changes with knowledge cutoff. An August 8 alert reconstruction shows Alex as then-believed owner; a current timeline shows Riley and exposes the correction. Their mismatch is valuable and must not be erased by overwriting either fact.

Production needs constraints or validation to reject overlapping intervals. Tests should cover boundary instants, alias reuse, null identifiers, late corrections, deleted entities, timezone folds, and accidental one-to-many as-of joins.

Review the Model by Trying to Break History

Ask whether every fact has a grain and stable source locator. Verify that identifiers include namespace and type. Label joins as exact, asserted, inferred, or convenient. Require intervals for changing relationships. Preserve unknown as distinct from false, empty, and zero. Make units explicit.

Then test a renamed user, reimaged device, recycled IP, assumed role, shared mailbox, and workload identity. Can an analyst reproduce what was known at an earlier decision time? Can late facts revise aggregates without destroying the first result? Can replay create duplicates? If any answer depends on manually remembering context, the model is incomplete.

Cardinality tests deserve special attention. A fact-to-dimension join expected to be many-to-one can become many-to-many when temporal versions overlap or an alias is reused. The resulting row multiplication inflates counts while every individual row still appears valid. Assert expected cardinality before and after each join, publish unmatched and multiply matched rates, and fail closed for high-consequence products. When ambiguity is real, represent a set of candidate links rather than selecting the first database row.

Deletion also needs semantics. Privacy erasure, source retention, and entity retirement do not mean the same thing. A tombstone can state that an identifier existed and is no longer available without retaining prohibited attributes. Referential integrity may use durable pseudonymous keys while restricted lookup material expires. Analysts must be able to distinguish “entity deleted under policy,” “source never supplied this entity,” and “resolution currently failed.” Collapsing all three to null destroys both auditability and missingness analysis.

Schema evolution should therefore be rehearsed with historical queries. Add a new principal type, split one operation into two, change a resource hierarchy, and retire an alias namespace in a test snapshot. The acceptance criterion is not only that new events load; old as-of queries, alert reconstructions, and lineage pointers must continue to mean what they meant under their recorded versions.
