  • Gao et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey,” 2023: https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.10997

The synthesis matters: AI RMF requires governed evaluation, zero trust supplies least-privilege enforcement, incident handling supplies temporal evidence discipline, and OWASP identifies instruction and agency attacks. Grounding is an integrity control; least privilege is an execution control; neither substitutes for the other.

Interview Practicum

You are interviewing for a Staff Security ML role at a global retailer. Its SOC wants an agent to investigate impossible-travel alerts. The identity team offers a broad service account; analysts want one-click session revocation; Legal prohibits retaining raw prompts containing employee data beyond seven days. A pilot looks impressive, but it missed privileged cloud activity in two red-team cases and cited a change ticket belonging to another user.

Prompt: Design the production system and the evaluation that determine whether it may move from shadow mode to analyst-facing use. Midway through your answer, assume the identity API begins returning results 18 minutes late. Near the end, assume the VP asks to enable autonomous revocation for “confidence above 95%.”

Strong clarifying questions are specific: What is the population and base rate? Which sources establish device, proxy, token, and privileged-action state? What counts as a correct disposition? Are evidence IDs immutable? Which actions are reversible? Who owns approval? How often are sources late or absent? Can normalized evidence outlive raw prompts? What adverse outcome is tolerable in the canary?

Worked Answer

I would reject the broad service account and start with case-scoped read capabilities. The alert supplies the identity, two sign-ins, and a 24-hour horizon. A deterministic planner may request only approved evidence classes for entities linked by cited relations. Normalized evidence enters a vault with immutable IDs, hashes, source time, and retrieval time. Prompts may expire after seven days; the evaluation record retains minimized structured claims, citations, policy decisions, versions, and permitted fields under the case schedule.

The output separates observations, inferences, unknowns, and proposed actions. Every material observation cites evidence. Every alert family has required questions. The two failures become regression fixtures: cross-subject citations fail validation, and privileged follow-on activity must be answered or explicitly unavailable before a close candidate.

Offline evaluation uses temporally held-out cases plus synthetic cases varying proxy use, token theft, device continuity, and privileged actions. I report weighted citation entailment, invalid citation rate, omission loss, disposition loss, abstention quality, and analyst time to correct decision. Experts adjudicate a stratified sample. Shadow mode then measures connector behavior, freshness, disagreement, and near misses without changing cases.

The 18-minute delay is evidence freshness failure, not model uncertainty. The case displays the watermark, marks dependent questions unavailable, and prevents close or containment recommendation until freshness recovers or an analyst accepts the gap. A separate alarm prevents rising abstention from being misdiagnosed as model regression.

I would refuse autonomous revocation based on 95% confidence. Calibration drifts, loss depends on account criticality, and confidence grants no authority. If automation is later desired, define a narrow reversible policy—for example, revoke only a newly issued session for a non-service identity when a deterministic replay signature and an independent signal agree. That policy gets its own replay set, canary, action budget, rollback, and incident owner.

Promotion requires zero cross-subject citations in the release suite, a lower bound on weighted citation precision, acceptable omission loss in every high-consequence stratum, no unauthorized execution, acceptable correction time, and tested behavior under missing sources. A randomized audit stream remains because visible suggestions can anchor analysts and corrupt future labels.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

How do you measure automation bias? Randomize whether the draft appears before or after an analyst records an initial disposition on a safe sample. Compare error-conditioned agreement, reversals toward the agent, and decision time.

What if required questions create friction? Determine which questions change decisions. Remove low-value items through controlled review, not silent UI shortcuts. Prefetch evidence and automate unavailable states.

Can an LLM judge its own citations? It may be one noisy signal, never the sole gate. Identity, subject, time, and field checks are deterministic; semantic entailment needs an independently versioned evaluator and human sampling.

What stops a release? Any unauthorized execution, cross-subject leakage, or material increase in high-weight omissions—even if average disposition accuracy improves.

Give the executive answer. The agent gets narrow read access, produces cited and omission-aware drafts, and cannot contain anything itself. It advances only when it preserves decision quality under missing and delayed evidence; actions stay behind an independent broker.

Key Takeaways

  • Ground every material claim in immutable, subject-correct, time-valid evidence.
  • Evaluate what the investigation omitted, not only what it asserted.
  • Represent authority as case-scoped capabilities and recheck it outside the model.
  • Make abstention name the missing evidence or failed control.
  • Promote synthesis and response authority as separate risks.
  • Optimize time to a correct, reviewable decision—not summary speed.

Chapter 38: AI for Vulnerability Discovery and Code Security

A vulnerability finding is not a model prediction. It is a falsifiable claim that a particular weakness exists in a particular revision, is reachable under stated conditions, has a defensible impact, and can be removed without introducing a regression. AI code review becomes useful only when it carries that claim through evidence collection, safe reproduction, root-cause grouping, remediation, and patch validation.

This chapter follows one example through that chain. A service parses a user-controlled archive manifest and joins each member name to an extraction directory. A scanner flags path traversal. The useful question is not whether the code resembles known vulnerable code. We must establish whether untrusted data reaches the path operation, whether canonicalization prevents escape, whether deployment configuration exposes the route, whether several alerts share one root cause, and whether the proposed patch closes all variants while preserving legitimate archives.

A Finding Is an Evidence Bundle

The unit sent to an engineer should contain:

  • repository, commit, build target, file, symbol, and line range;
  • weakness hypothesis and relevant CWE, without treating CWE as proof;
  • source-to-sink path with sanitizer and configuration evidence;
  • reachability assumptions and deployment preconditions;
  • a harmless reproducer or counterexample in an isolated harness;
  • deduplication group and root-cause explanation;
  • patch candidate, tests, and residual uncertainty;
  • identities and versions for scanner, model, rules, dependencies, and build.

A bare natural-language explanation loses exactly the information needed to dispute, reproduce, or close the issue. Conversely, a failing test without provenance may be real but impossible to map to a deployed artifact.

From Repository to Validated Repair

flowchart TB
    C[Commit and build manifest] --> S[Static facts: AST, call graph, dataflow]
    C --> D[Dependency and configuration facts]
    S --> H[Weakness hypotheses]
    D --> H
    H --> R{Reachability adjudicator}
    R -->|not connected| X[Archive as non-reachable]
    R -->|uncertain| Q[Request build or runtime evidence]
    R -->|candidate path| B[Ephemeral safe harness]
    B --> F{Behavior reproduced?}
    F -->|no| Q
    F -->|yes| G[Root-cause graph]
    G --> U[Deduplicated developer issue]
    U --> P[Patch candidate]
    P --> T[Positive, negative, metamorphic tests]
    T --> V{Original path gone and behavior preserved?}
    V -->|no| P
    V -->|yes| M[Merge evidence and post-deploy watch]

Static analysis supplies broad coverage. Dynamic reproduction supplies behavioral evidence for executable paths. Dependency analysis supplies version and advisory context. Semantic reasoning proposes connections and repairs. None is sufficient alone. The pipeline records disagreements rather than allowing the language model to smooth them away.

Reachability Has Several Meanings

Teams often say “reachable” while referring to different predicates:

  1. Syntactic reachability: a call graph contains a path from an entry point to the vulnerable function.
  2. Data reachability: attacker-influenced bytes can propagate to the dangerous argument.
  3. Control feasibility: path conditions can be simultaneously satisfied.
  4. Deployment reachability: the entry point, feature, and dependency version exist in the shipped configuration.
  5. Impact reachability: the path reaches a security-relevant effect despite sandboxing or downstream validation.

Represent a candidate as a graph \(G=(V,E)\). Each edge has confidence \(p_e\), and each required condition has support \(r_j\). A ranking score can prioritize analysis:

\[ R(\pi)=\left(\prod_{e\in\pi}p_e\right) \left(\prod_j r_j\right)I_{deploy}I_{untrusted}, \]

but it is not a probability of exploitation unless calibrated against representative outcomes. Multiplication appropriately punishes one unsupported link; it can also over-penalize correlated evidence, so production systems should retain component values.

For the archive example, the evidence chain is: HTTP upload route enabled; body saved as an archive; manifest member name attacker-controlled; member name flows to base / name; no canonical containment check; process can write outside the intended directory. A unit test calling the join helper establishes code behavior but not route deployment. A route trace establishes execution but not attacker control. The finding requires both.

Schema for a Reviewable Finding

finding_version: 2
finding_id: F-2026-00418
artifact:
  repository: inventory-importer
  commit: 7a61c9e
  build_target: importer-api
location:
  file: src/archive.py
  symbol: extract_members
  lines: [88, 104]
hypothesis:
  weakness: path traversal during archive extraction
  cwe: CWE-22
  source: upload.manifest.member_name
  sink: filesystem.write
reachability:
  entrypoint: POST /v2/import
  dataflow_edges: [df-81, df-93, df-101]
  feature_flag: bulk_import=true
  deployment_evidence: deploy-55
  unresolved: []
reproduction:
  harness: tests/security/test_archive_containment.py
  safe_effect: write_attempt_outside_temp_root
  network: disabled
dedupe:
  root_cause_key: archive.extract.missing_canonical_boundary
patch:
  commit: pending
validation: pending

The reproduction records a safe effect, not an offensive payload. The harness uses a temporary directory, fabricated files, no network, no privilege, and an assertion that detects an attempted boundary escape before any persistent harm.

Safe Reproduction as a Scientific Test

Reproduction should answer the smallest claim necessary. For path traversal, the claim is that a crafted member name resolves outside a temporary root. There is no need to overwrite a real file. For command injection, a harness can replace process execution with an instrumented fake and assert argument boundaries. For server-side request forgery, route all traffic to a local stub. For authorization flaws, use synthetic tenants.

Safety controls belong in the harness contract: disposable container or process; no external network; read-only source mount; synthetic secrets; low CPU, memory, process, and time limits; unprivileged identity; bounded output; and destruction after collection. A reproducer is reviewed before it enters a shared corpus because “test code” can still carry dangerous primitives.

Reproduction outcomes need more nuance than pass/fail: confirmed, counterexample, environment_mismatch, build_failed, inconclusive, or unsafe_to_run. A build failure is not evidence that the finding is false. Similarly, failure to reproduce under one configuration does not refute another declared deployment.

Deduplication by Root Cause, Not Text Similarity

One missing containment check can trigger alerts at the join expression, file open, overwrite, and archive entry loop. Filing four tickets wastes engineering time and corrupts precision metrics. Yet grouping every CWE-22 alert can hide independent fixes.

Build a finding graph. Nodes are candidates; edges express shared source, sink, sanitizer gap, vulnerable symbol, dependency instance, call path, or patch locus. Cluster when findings share a plausible fix boundary. Text or embedding similarity is supporting evidence only.

For findings \(i,j\), a pair score might be

\[ D_{ij}=0.30J(E_i,E_j)+0.25I(s_i=s_j)+0.20I(k_i=k_j) +0.15J(P_i,P_j)+0.10\cos(z_i,z_j), \]

where \(E\) is dataflow edges, \(s\) vulnerable symbol, \(k\) sink class, \(P\) path-condition features, and \(z\) a text embedding. This is a candidate generator. A deterministic constraint prevents grouping across repositories or deployed dependency instances unless an explicit shared root cause exists.

Evaluate grouping with pairwise precision and recall, cluster purity, over-merge rate, under-merge rate, and developer issue count. Weight over-merges heavily because one closed ticket can otherwise suppress an unfixed vulnerability.

Patch Validation Is a New Security Evaluation

The patch is not validated merely because the reproducer stops failing. A superficial fix may block ../ while missing absolute paths, alternate separators, encoded forms, symlink resolution, or time-of-check/time-of-use behavior. A broad fix may reject legitimate nested paths.

Validation uses several test families:

  • regression: the original harmless witness no longer escapes;
  • variants: equivalent path representations remain contained;
  • positive behavior: legitimate nested members still extract;
  • metamorphic: harmless transformations preserve the security decision;
  • static reanalysis: source-to-sink path is cut or a proven sanitizer dominates it;
  • dependency/build: lockfile, artifact, and deployment actually contain the patch;
  • differential: compare old and new behavior only inside the safe harness;
  • post-deploy: monitor errors and recurrence without exposing exploit detail.

Define patch assurance as a vector rather than one score: \(A=(r,v,b,d)\), where \(r\) is original regression closure, \(v\) variant closure, \(b\) benign behavior preservation, and \(d\) deployed-artifact confirmation. Release policy can require every component, preventing a high average from hiding a zero.

Safe Lab: Reachability, Grouping, and Repair Validation

This lab uses a toy call graph and pure path normalization. It does not extract archives or write files.

from collections import defaultdict, deque
from pathlib import PurePosixPath

edges = {
    "upload_route": ["parse_manifest"],
    "parse_manifest": ["extract_member", "audit_name"],
    "extract_member": ["join_path", "write_file"],
    "join_path": [], "write_file": [], "audit_name": []
}
tainted = {"upload_route", "parse_manifest", "extract_member", "join_path", "write_file"}
findings = [
    ("F1", "extract_member", "write_file", "missing_boundary"),
    ("F2", "join_path", "write_file", "missing_boundary"),
    ("F3", "audit_name", "log", "log_forging"),
]

def reachable(start, goal):
    queue, seen = deque([start]), set()
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        if node == goal:
            return True
        if node not in seen:
            seen.add(node)
            queue.extend(edges.get(node, []))
    return False

def contained(member):
    parts = PurePosixPath(member).parts
    depth = 0
    for part in parts:
        if part in ("", ".", "/"):
            continue
        if part == "..":
            depth -= 1
        else:
            depth += 1
        if depth < 0:
            return False
    return not PurePosixPath(member).is_absolute()

groups = defaultdict(list)
for fid, symbol, sink, root_cause in findings:
    if reachable("upload_route", symbol) and symbol in tainted:
        groups[(sink, root_cause)].append(fid)

tests = ["reports/q1.csv", "../escape.txt", "a/../../escape.txt", "/tmp/escape"]
print("reachable_groups=" + str(dict(groups)))
for name in tests:
    print(f"{name}: {'ALLOW' if contained(name) else 'BLOCK'}")
print("patch_valid=" + str(all(contained(x) == expected for x, expected in {
    "reports/q1.csv": True, "../escape.txt": False,
    "a/../../escape.txt": False, "/tmp/escape": False}.items())))

Expected output:

reachable_groups={('write_file', 'missing_boundary'): ['F1', 'F2']}
reports/q1.csv: ALLOW
../escape.txt: BLOCK
a/../../escape.txt: BLOCK
/tmp/escape: BLOCK
patch_valid=True

The lab deliberately separates reachability, grouping, and validation. F3 is not grouped because its symbol is not on the tainted set, even though a textual model might find both discussions of names similar.

That separation is operationally important: each stage can fail, be appealed, and be improved without relabeling every downstream outcome.

Metrics and Production Operations

Finding-level precision is inadequate. Track candidate precision, reachable precision, root-cause precision, confirmed-finding recall on seeded and historical cases, time to first reviewable evidence, developer acceptance, median duplicates per root cause, reopen rate, patch variant escape rate, and deployed remediation time. Stratify by language, framework, repository criticality, scanner version, and weakness family.

Avoid measuring recall solely with public benchmark snippets: they are susceptible to memorization, structurally simpler than production code, and often lack build or deployment context. Use temporally held-out internal fixes where permitted, synthetic transformations, seeded weaknesses reviewed by experts, and naturally occurring prospective findings. Prevent leakage by separating benchmark authorship, model-development access, and final evaluation custody; hash and access-log hidden cases.

Production services need build isolation, artifact retention, queue limits, repository access minimization, secret redaction, dependency-cache provenance, and an emergency stop for reproduction. Every finding state transition is append-only. Engineers can dispute source control, reachability, duplicate grouping, severity, or proposed repair separately; disagreement is valuable labeled evidence.

Roll out by repository cohort. Begin with read-only shadow scanning, then expose evidence bundles without auto-created tickets, then create tickets only for high-assurance families. Never auto-merge security patches solely on model judgment. Canary monitoring includes build failures, test flakiness, reviewer rejection, grouping changes, sensitive-code exposure, and any unexpected network attempt from a harness.

Sources and Further Reading

  • NIST, SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, 2022: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218
  • NIST, SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment, 2008: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-115
  • MITRE, Common Weakness Enumeration: https://cwe.mitre.org/
  • FIRST, Exploit Prediction Scoring System: https://www.first.org/epss/
  • CISA, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog: https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
  • OWASP, Code Review Guide: https://owasp.org/www-project-code-review-guide/
  • Pearce et al., “Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions,” 2022: https://doi.org/10.1109/SP46214.2022.9833571
  • Jimenez et al., “SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?”, 2024: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770

SSDF situates discovery inside a controlled development lifecycle; CWE standardizes weakness language but does not establish exploitability; EPSS and KEV add population-level exploitation evidence without replacing local reachability; secure code-generation studies show why generated repairs need independent tests. The combined lesson is to link weakness, context, behavior, repair, and deployed artifact.

Interview Practicum

A payments company’s new AI reviewer emits 1,800 findings across 300 repositories. Developers report duplicates and false positives. Leadership claims 92% accuracy from a public benchmark. You discover the model had access to benchmark solutions, many services disable the flagged routes, and the reproduction service can reach the corporate network.

Prompt: Redesign the system and decide whether any findings can continue to developers this quarter. After your initial design, the build team says only 60% of repositories build reproducibly. Then a critical library alert appears in 47 services, but only four load the vulnerable parser at runtime.

Useful questions: What is the unit behind 92%? Was the benchmark held out temporally and organizationally? Which build, call-graph, deployment, and runtime facts exist? How are duplicates counted? What is the safe effect for reproduction? Which repositories process untrusted input? Can fixes be tested and traced into deployed artifacts?

Worked Answer

I would suspend the unsafe reproduction service immediately because corporate network reach is an independent hazard. Static scanning may continue in shadow mode. I would not discard all findings: quarantine them, preserve commit and scanner provenance, and allow developers to see only evidence bundles that pass subject, revision, and reachability checks without dynamic execution.

The public benchmark result is invalid for release because solution access creates contamination and because snippet accuracy does not measure deployed reachability, duplicate burden, or repair quality. I would establish a custodied temporal suite containing internal historical fixes, expert-seeded cases, benign hard negatives, and transformed variants. Reporting is per weakness family and language, with candidate and root-cause metrics separated.

For the 40% that do not build reproducibly, the state is environment_mismatch, not false positive. We can still establish partial static evidence, but cannot claim behavioral confirmation. I would fund build manifests as security infrastructure and make evidence grade visible. High-criticality repositories with missing builds receive human review rather than model confidence inflation.

The 47 library alerts should become one campaign with 47 deployment instances, not one ticket and not 47 unrelated vulnerabilities. Dependency presence, vulnerable version, runtime load, untrusted entry point, and vulnerable function use are separate predicates. The four runtime-reachable services receive prioritized remediation with safe regression tests. The others remain inventory records with reasons—unused code path, feature disabled, or non-attacker-controlled input—and are re-evaluated when configuration changes.

I would rebuild reproduction on ephemeral isolated workers with no external network, synthetic secrets, resource limits, instrumented effects, and reviewed harness templates. Patch validation must close the original and transformed cases, preserve benign behavior, pass the repository suite, and confirm the fixed artifact reaches deployment. This quarter, only finding families with reliable builds or strong static proofs, acceptable root-cause precision, and safe reviewed harnesses advance to ticket creation.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

How do you estimate recall without exposing hidden cases? Run the evaluator in a custodied service that returns aggregate metrics and limited diagnostics. Rotate cases, log access, and reserve a final untouched slice.

Why not use EPSS as reachability? EPSS estimates exploitation probability for published CVEs in a population. It does not show that this service loads the component, invokes the vulnerable function, or exposes attacker-controlled input.

What is the most damaging dedupe error? Over-merging independent root causes, because closing one issue can suppress unfixed paths. Track and manually sample merges, especially across repositories and dependency instances.

When can an AI patch be merged? When normal ownership and review remain intact, security regression and variant tests pass, deployed artifact provenance is verified, and risk-appropriate human approval is recorded. Model confidence is not a merge authority.

Key Takeaways

  • Treat every finding as a revision-specific, falsifiable evidence bundle.
  • Distinguish syntactic, data, control, deployment, and impact reachability.
  • Reproduce the smallest harmless security effect in an isolated environment.
  • Deduplicate around the repairable root cause, not wording or CWE alone.
  • Validate variants, benign behavior, and the deployed artifact—not only the original test.
  • Keep contaminated benchmark performance out of release evidence.

Chapter 39: Cybersecurity Capability and Misuse Evaluations

Does an AI system make a person meaningfully more capable at a cyber task than the person, ordinary tools, or the model alone? That is a causal question, not a leaderboard question. A model may solve benchmark challenges yet provide no uplift to experienced practitioners; it may help novices while slowing experts; it may accelerate harmless reconnaissance but not end-to-end success; or it may teach transferable methods that persist after access ends. Release decisions require an experiment that distinguishes these effects without turning the evaluation into a training package for misuse.

This chapter designs a randomized study in a sandboxed enterprise-like range. Participants receive one of several assistance conditions, work on matched task families, and are measured on verified outcomes, time, intervention burden, and unsafe behavior. The design controls contamination among participants and between evaluation cases and model development. It also limits information hazards by separating task authorship, execution, scoring, and reporting.

Define the Estimand Before the Range

“Cyber capability” is not one scalar. Choose a population, task distribution, treatment, comparator, and outcome. One primary estimand might be the novice average treatment effect of an agentic assistant relative to conventional search and command-line tools:

\[ \tau_N=E[Y_i(\text{agent})-Y_i(\text{tools})\mid E_i=\text{novice}], \]

where \(Y\) is a preregistered score based on independently verified milestones. A separate \(\tau_E\) covers experts. Combining them can hide the release-relevant result.

Possible outcomes include validated task completion, time to first correct hypothesis, time to completion, number of substantive hints, unsafe actions attempted, solution quality, and retention on a later unassisted task. Token count or perceived helpfulness is not capability. A composite can be useful if weights are declared before results:

\[ Y=100C+20M-0.5T-15H-40U, \]

with complete success \(C\), verified partial milestones \(M\), minutes \(T\), human hints \(H\), and unsafe policy violations \(U\). Report components beside the composite so weights cannot conceal tradeoffs.

Experimental Architecture

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Task Authors
    participant V as Secure Vault
    participant R as Randomization Service
    participant P as Participant
    participant X as Isolated Range
    participant M as Model/Tool Gateway
    participant S as Blind Scorers
    participant D as Disclosure Board

    A->>V: Deposit task, solution, hazard tier, scoring tests
    V->>R: Release task ID and strata only
    R->>P: Assign condition and matched task family
    P->>X: Work through instrumented interface
    X->>M: Permit condition-specific assistance
    M-->>X: Logged, filtered response
    X->>V: Encrypted transcript and state changes
    V->>S: Redacted outcome bundle, condition hidden
    S->>V: Milestone and safety scores
    V->>D: Aggregate effects and controlled exemplars
    D-->>P: Tiered report; no reusable harmful procedure

Task authors cannot inspect participant assignments. Scorers do not see condition labels or model-branded interfaces. The model team sees neither hidden solutions nor final tasks before the evaluation freezes. The disclosure board decides which artifacts may leave the restricted environment.

Conditions and Factorial Questions

A credible baseline is not “human with no internet.” It reflects actual alternatives. For many studies, use four conditions:

  1. human with standard documentation, search, and ordinary security tools;
  2. human with a chat model but no execution tools;
  3. human with a tool-using agent under the same range permissions;
  4. model or agent alone, to separate collaboration from automation.

If resources permit, a factorial design can isolate model quality and tool access: model present/absent crossed with specialized tools present/absent. The interaction

\[ \delta=(Y_{M,T}-Y_{0,T})-(Y_{M,0}-Y_{0,0}) \]

estimates whether the model adds more value when tools are available. Avoid too many thin arms; an underpowered factorial produces attractive but unstable rankings.

Randomize within experience strata and task families. Measure prior skill with a short, non-overlapping pretest and collect role, years of experience, programming familiarity, and prior exposure to common challenge platforms. Block randomization keeps these variables balanced without using post-treatment behavior.

Freeze the experiment as a machine-readable protocol before allocation:

protocol_version: cyber-uplift/3
population:
  strata: [novice, expert]
arms: [standard_tools, chat_model, tool_agent]
unit_of_randomization: participant
primary_estimand: novice_risk_difference_agent_vs_standard
primary_outcome: verified_end_to_end_completion
secondary_outcomes:
  - restricted_mean_completion_time
  - unsafe_intervention_rate
  - seven_day_unassisted_transfer
exclusions:
  - range_failure_before_task_start
contamination_flags:
  - prior_task_exposure
  - participant_contact
  - author_model_team_access
stopping_rules:
  - range_escape
  - external_target_contact
  - credible_real_world_zero_day
analysis: intention_to_treat

Changing the primary outcome after viewing arm results creates a new protocol version and is reported as exploratory, not silently substituted.

A crossover design saves participants but creates learning and carryover. If participants see related tasks under two conditions, the first treatment teaches the second. Prefer parallel assignment for primary dangerous-capability estimates. A limited crossover may be used for usability on unrelated tasks with order randomized and washout acknowledged.

Tasks That Measure Work Rather Than Trivia

Use a ladder of safe, instrumented tasks: identify a misconfiguration in synthetic logs; trace a vulnerable dataflow in a toy service; prioritize remediation across a fabricated asset graph; write a detection for simulated behavior; or recover a benign token from a deliberately vulnerable range. No task should target public infrastructure, use real credentials, or require persistence, destructive effects, stealth, or uncontrolled propagation.

Realism comes from dependency, ambiguity, and partial evidence—not from live victims. Tasks should require several linked milestones, such as discover service, form hypothesis, validate harmless effect, and explain remediation. Scoring tests inspect range state rather than trusting self-reported success.

Difficulty must be calibrated before the main study. If nearly everyone succeeds, uplift is censored by a ceiling; if nobody succeeds, a floor masks differences. Pilot with participants outside the analysis set. Maintain anchor tasks across releases, but rotate most cases to reduce memorization.

Randomization, Attrition, and Analysis

Create assignments before sessions using a reproducible seed held by an independent statistician. Allocation is concealed until the session begins. Analyze intention-to-treat: participants remain in assigned arms even if the assistant fails or they barely use it. A per-protocol analysis can be secondary, but selection into “used the model effectively” is itself an outcome.

For binary completion, estimate risk difference and risk ratio with cluster-robust uncertainty when each participant attempts multiple tasks. For time, incomplete tasks are right-censored; survival analysis is preferable to replacing failures with the time limit. A proportional-hazards model may be inappropriate when assistance helps early discovery but hurts late debugging, so show Kaplan–Meier curves and restricted mean completion time.

With participant \(i\) and task \(j\), a hierarchical model separates variation:

\[ Y_{ij}=\alpha+\tau Z_i+\beta E_i+u_i+v_j+\tau_EZ_iE_i+\epsilon_{ij}, \]

where \(u_i\) is participant ability, \(v_j\) task difficulty, and \(\tau_E\) treatment heterogeneity by experience. Preregister exclusions, transformations, multiplicity correction, missing-data handling, and the minimum effect that changes a release decision.

Attrition is security-relevant. If agent sessions crash or safety filters frustrate users, excluding them inflates capability. Report assignment-to-outcome flow, infrastructure failures by arm, and bounds under plausible missing outcomes.

Contamination Controls

There are at least four contamination channels:

  • training contamination: hidden tasks or solutions appeared in model training or fine-tuning;
  • developer contamination: model or scaffold engineers saw final cases and tuned to them;
  • participant spillover: participants share task details or strategies;
  • measurement contamination: scorers infer the condition from style and score differently.

Controls include post-cutoff task creation, private synthetic environments, similarity searches against known corpora, canary strings, frozen model hashes, access logs, separate author and model teams, session scheduling that limits contact, nondisclosure rules proportionate to risk, and blind scoring from normalized artifacts. No single check proves absence of training data. The result should state residual contamination risk.

Rotate surface details while preserving latent skills. If performance collapses when hostnames, file layouts, or irrelevant wording change, the system may be recalling a procedure rather than transferring capability. Use isomorphic task pairs and calculate a transfer gap between original and transformed forms.

Information-Hazard Controls

Evaluation evidence can itself increase misuse capability. Classify artifacts before collection:

TierExampleHandling
0aggregate completion ratepublic or normal internal report
1general failure categorystandard restricted project access
2detailed transcript for synthetic tasknamed evaluators; encrypted; limited retention
3reusable exploit chain or novel techniqueisolated vault; two-person access; no broad export
4credible real-world zero-day evidencestop task; disclosure counsel and affected vendor process

The range gateway blocks external targets, unapproved binaries, secret-like outputs, and destructive primitives. It logs policy interventions as outcomes. Filters must not silently alter one condition more than another; otherwise the treatment includes an unmeasured handicap. Record interventions and report them.

Public reporting should communicate the task family, population, assistance conditions, effect estimates, uncertainty, limitations, and release rationale. It need not publish hidden solutions, exact high-hazard prompts, vulnerable images, or procedural transcripts. Reproducibility can be served through controlled researcher access and lower-hazard analogues.

Safe Lab: Stratified Randomization and Uplift

This simulation creates balanced assignments and computes novice/expert uplift on harmless synthetic scores.

import random
from collections import defaultdict

participants = [
    ("p01", "novice"), ("p02", "novice"), ("p03", "novice"),
    ("p04", "novice"), ("p05", "expert"), ("p06", "expert"),
    ("p07", "expert"), ("p08", "expert")
]
conditions = ["tools", "agent"]
rng = random.Random(3901)

assignment = {}
for level in ("novice", "expert"):
    ids = [pid for pid, skill in participants if skill == level]
    rng.shuffle(ids)
    for index, pid in enumerate(ids):
        assignment[pid] = conditions[index % 2]

# Preregistered, fabricated outcome: verified milestones out of 10.
scores = {"p01": 4, "p02": 7, "p03": 8, "p04": 3,
          "p05": 8, "p06": 7, "p07": 9, "p08": 8}
cells = defaultdict(list)
skill_by_id = dict(participants)
for pid, condition in assignment.items():
    cells[(skill_by_id[pid], condition)].append(scores[pid])

print("assignment=" + ",".join(f"{p}:{assignment[p]}" for p in sorted(assignment)))
for level in ("novice", "expert"):
    means = {c: sum(cells[(level, c)]) / len(cells[(level, c)]) for c in conditions}
    print(f"{level}_tools={means['tools']:.1f}")
    print(f"{level}_agent={means['agent']:.1f}")
    print(f"{level}_uplift={means['agent'] - means['tools']:.1f}")

Expected output:

assignment=p01:tools,p02:agent,p03:agent,p04:tools,p05:agent,p06:agent,p07:tools,p08:tools
novice_tools=3.5
novice_agent=7.5
novice_uplift=4.0
expert_tools=8.5
expert_agent=7.5
expert_uplift=-1.0

The fabricated result demonstrates why pooling is dangerous: strong novice uplift coexists with expert harm. A real study needs far more participants and uncertainty intervals; the lab demonstrates allocation and estimand calculation, not adequate power.

Release Thresholds and Operations

A dangerous-capability threshold must be written before results. Example: hold release if the upper and lower evidence jointly show at least a 15 percentage-point increase in verified completion for low-skill participants on a high-consequence task family, without a compensating control that survives adaptive testing. The precise value is a governance choice, not a statistical constant.

Use a decision table including capability uplift, uncertainty, unsafe action rate, control bypass, task realism, contamination confidence, affected population, availability of comparable systems, and mitigation effectiveness. A null result is not proof of safety when the study is underpowered or tasks have poor external validity.

Production evaluation operations resemble a high-integrity lab: freeze artifacts, hash range images, verify clocks, monitor scorer drift, document deviations, rotate credentials, review data export, and rehearse discovery of a real vulnerability. Stop conditions include escape from the range, unexpected external contact, participant distress, a plausible undisclosed real-world flaw, loss of assignment integrity, or exposure of hidden solutions.

Repeat evaluations when model weights, system prompts, tools, autonomy, context limits, or safety policies materially change. Capability can emerge from scaffolding even with unchanged weights. Maintain version-specific results; do not attach a permanent “safe” label to a model family.

Benchmark frameworks contribute task patterns, but controlled release evidence additionally needs human baselines, randomization, contamination handling, and outcome verification. AI RMF supplies the risk-governance frame; agent governance emphasizes system-level capabilities; research-integrity guidance supports preregistration, custody, and transparent deviations.

Interview Practicum

A frontier-model company plans a release in six weeks. Twenty-four internal participants completed cyber-range tasks: novices using the agent outperformed novices using search, experts showed little difference, and agent users triggered more safety interventions. Product argues the tasks are “just CTFs.” The evaluation lead admits three participants discussed tasks at lunch and two task authors recently joined the post-training team.

Prompt: Decide what can be concluded, design the confirmatory study, and state a release rule. Halfway through, learn that only 30 qualified experts are available. Then learn that one hidden task resembles a newly disclosed real vulnerability.

Clarifying questions should cover assignment, baseline tools, prior skill, task families, verified outcomes, censoring, intervention definitions, task/model custody, timing of author transfers, participant contact, effect sizes and intervals, real-world mapping, and existing mitigations.

Worked Answer

The pilot suggests heterogeneous uplift but cannot support a release decision. With 24 people, uncertain spillover, and possible developer contamination, I would present it as hypothesis-generating. I would preserve all records, flag contaminated participants and tasks without simply deleting unfavorable observations, and preregister a confirmatory analysis.

The primary study would use parallel assignment within novice and expert strata to standard tools, chat-only, and agent assistance. Because experts are scarce, allocate expert participants between the most decision-relevant contrast—agent versus standard tools—and use repeated independent task families with a hierarchical model. Keep the larger novice three-arm study. Pretest skill, conceal allocation, blind scorers, verify milestones from range state, analyze intention-to-treat, and treat incomplete sessions as censored rather than failures at an invented time.

New tasks are authored after the model freeze by a team barred from model development. Isomorphic variants test transfer. Access logs, canary strings, semantic similarity review, and participant scheduling reduce contamination. The two transferred authors cannot contribute cases or see results until unblinding. Lunch-discussion participants remain in a sensitivity analysis; the confirmatory study uses clearer isolation and records contact.

The newly disclosed real vulnerability changes hazard classification. I would remove that task from ordinary execution, ask a restricted review group whether it contains nonpublic actionable detail, and follow coordinated disclosure if needed. It cannot be published as reproducibility material. Replace it in the primary analysis according to a preregistered contingency, while reporting the deviation.

My release rule would use a confidence interval around novice completion uplift on high-consequence families, unsafe intervention rate, and mitigation robustness. If meaningful novice uplift crosses the predefined dangerous threshold and controls fail adaptive evaluation, hold or restrict the agentic configuration. If evidence is inconclusive because power or validity is weak, do not translate that into safety; narrow deployment and collect better evidence. Expert null effects do not cancel novice uplift.

The report publishes aggregate design and uncertainty but withholds solutions, exact high-hazard prompts, and range images. A restricted assurance record retains enough detail for independent review. We repeat the study when tools, autonomy, or policies change because the evaluated object is the complete system.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Why randomize people rather than prompts? The causal unit is assisted human performance. Prompt-only tests omit learning, tool selection, frustration, and unsafe action.

How do you handle participants who ignore the agent? Keep them in intention-to-treat. Assistant use can be analyzed as a secondary mediator, but conditioning the primary estimate on use breaks randomization.

Can you publish enough for credibility without publishing dangerous details? Yes: publish estimands, populations, task taxonomy, baselines, scoring method, effect estimates, uncertainty, contamination assessment, and deviations. Provide controlled access to sensitive artifacts.

What would immediately stop the study? Range escape, external targeting, uncontrolled disclosure of a plausible real vulnerability, loss of solution custody, or a serious participant-safety event.

Key Takeaways

  • Measure causal uplift over realistic human-and-tool baselines, not model score alone.
  • Randomize within skill and task strata and preserve intention-to-treat analysis.
  • Treat contamination as several distinct threats with documented residual risk.
  • Build realism from linked reasoning and verified outcomes, not live targets.
  • Separate reproducibility from unrestricted release of hazardous artifacts.
  • Make release thresholds depend on effect, uncertainty, controls, and consequence.

Chapter 40: Production Monitoring for AI Security Systems

An AI security release is not one model file. It is a behavior-producing assembly: model, prompt, retrieval index, policy, tool adapters, feature code, evaluator, runtime, and the data available at a moment in time. If any component changes, yesterday’s assurance claim may no longer apply. Production safety therefore begins with a versioned event record, continues through deterministic replay and segmented canaries, and ends with an assurance case whose claims are supported—or explicitly weakened—by current evidence.

This chapter implements that release discipline for an agent that triages suspicious identity activity. The methods also apply to AI code review, fraud investigation, abuse detection, and response copilots. The central objective is not to prove the system safe. It is to make the release decision reviewable, bound its exposure, detect invalidated assumptions quickly, and preserve enough evidence to learn after failure.

The Release Unit and Behavior Manifest

A semantic version for the model alone is insufficient. Create an immutable behavior manifest:

behavior_release: soc-agent/2026.08.3
model:
  provider: internal
  id: sec-model-12b
  weights_digest: sha256:4a82...
prompt_bundle: prompt/37@sha256:ca19...
retrieval:
  encoder: embed-v7
  index_snapshot: evidence-index/2026-08-18T0200Z
policy: response-policy/14@sha256:06f1...
tools:
  idp_connector: 3.2.1
  case_writer: 2.8.0
feature_code: git:91dd2a7
runtime_image: registry/soc-agent@sha256:7bd0...
evaluator_bundle: assurance-eval/22
schema_versions: [trace-v4, evidence-v2, decision-v3]
approved_scope: [shadow, analyst_draft]

The manifest is signed and referenced by every trace. Mutable aliases such as latest are prohibited in assurance evidence. Configuration flags are included because they can change authority without changing code. External service versions that cannot be pinned require observed response metadata and a declared dependency risk.

Versioned Replay Without Pretending to Recreate History

Replay runs a candidate release against recorded inputs and compares it with the incumbent. It can reveal regression, but only if the record preserves what the system actually observed. Re-querying today’s identity graph for a case from last month leaks future facts and masks historical outages. Store minimized evidence snapshots or content-addressed references subject to retention rules.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Frozen: sign behavior manifest
    Frozen --> Replay: run gold, incident, drift, adversarial suites
    Replay --> Blocked: invariant or severity gate fails
    Replay --> Shadow: gates pass
    Shadow --> Blocked: live divergence or telemetry gap
    Shadow --> CanaryA: owner approval
    CanaryA --> Rollback: guardrail breach
    CanaryA --> CanaryB: segment evidence sufficient
    CanaryB --> Rollback: guardrail breach
    CanaryB --> General: assurance case accepted
    General --> Rollback: incident or invalidated assumption
    Rollback --> Replay: corrected release
    Blocked --> Replay: new candidate

A replay envelope needs event time, ingestion time, evidence snapshot, randomness controls, and all versions:

{
  "$id": "ai-security-replay-v1",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["trace_id", "event_time", "behavior_release", "input_ref", "seed", "outcome"],
  "properties": {
    "trace_id": {"type": "string"},
    "event_time": {"type": "string", "format": "date-time"},
    "ingested_at": {"type": "string", "format": "date-time"},
    "behavior_release": {"type": "string"},
    "input_ref": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^sha256:"},
    "evidence_snapshot": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^snapshot/"},
    "seed": {"type": "integer"},
    "sampling": {"type": "object"},
    "tool_fixtures": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
    "outcome": {"enum": ["correct", "incorrect", "abstain", "error", "policy_block"]},
    "segment": {"type": "object"}
  },
  "additionalProperties": false
}

Nondeterminism is managed, not wished away. Fix seeds and tool fixtures where possible, then run multiple samples for stochastic components. Report the probability of a violation and distribution of quality, not only one canonical output. Some provider-hosted models cannot guarantee bitwise replay; the record should say “behavioral replay under version claim” rather than “exact reproduction.”

Building the Replay Corpus

No single test set represents production. Maintain named suites with different custody and refresh rules:

  • gold: carefully adjudicated ordinary and difficult cases;
  • incident: sanitized cases from real failures and near misses;
  • invariant: synthetic cases for hard properties such as no cross-tenant citation;
  • adversarial: prompt injection, tool manipulation, ambiguity, and malformed inputs;
  • drift: recent sampled traffic with delayed labels or expert review;
  • contract: connector, schema, timeout, and policy compatibility tests.

Prevent incident-suite overfitting by retaining hidden variants and testing the underlying property. A fix for one exact injected string is not evidence of injection resistance. Corpus membership is versioned; deleted cases remain documented so improvements cannot be manufactured by quietly removing failures.

Compare candidate \(c\) and incumbent \(b\) at trace level. For loss \(L\), paired difference \(\Delta_i=L(c,i)-L(b,i)\) removes much case difficulty. Bootstrap cases, clustering by incident or customer when correlated, to obtain an interval around mean or tail regression. Average loss is insufficient for severe invariants. A single unauthorized action may be a deterministic block even if mean quality rises.

Define release gates as a vector:

\[ G=(\Delta\bar L,\ \Delta L_{p95},\ V_{auth},\ V_{privacy},\ A_{critical},\ E_{runtime}), \]

where the components are mean loss change, tail loss change, authority violations, privacy violations, critical-segment abstention, and runtime error. Each has its own threshold. Do not collapse privacy leakage and latency into a weighted score that allows one to compensate for the other.

Shadowing and Online Comparability

Shadow mode sends a copy of live inputs to the candidate but suppresses side effects. It catches current schemas, traffic mix, connector behavior, cost, and latency. It does not test analyst interaction or action consequences. Candidate and incumbent must see equivalent evidence; if shadow traffic uses stale fixtures while production uses live connectors, disagreement is uninterpretable.

Log coverage is itself a gate. If only 70% of candidate traces contain policy decisions, a zero observed violation rate is meaningless. Track trace completeness, dropped events, join success, label delay, and clock skew. Monitoring must distinguish system behavior change from observability failure.

Use disagreement sampling rather than reviewing random outputs alone. Review candidate/incumbent disposition flips, new actions, new abstentions, citation changes, and large confidence movements. Retain a random sample too; disagreement sampling misses shared failures.

Segmented Canary Design

A one-percent global canary sounds cautious but can expose the wrong one percent. Security risk is concentrated by account privilege, tenant, language, connector, alert family, and action type. Define segments before rollout and route by stable hashing so the same case or tenant does not bounce between releases.

Start with low-consequence, high-observability segments: internal synthetic tenants, analyst drafts, common alert families, no response action. Exclude service accounts, privileged identities, regulated tenants, and rare action paths until their targeted evidence is adequate. Later stages deliberately include each critical segment under smaller absolute budgets; otherwise “general availability” rests only on easy traffic.

For segment \(s\), exposure budget can be expressed as

\[ B_s=N_s\,p_s\,T_s\,h_s, \]

where \(N_s\) is eligible volume, \(p_s\) routed fraction, \(T_s\) duration, and \(h_s\) consequence weight. Use both count and consequence budgets. A canary automatically pauses when either is consumed without enough reviewed evidence.

Guardrails include unauthorized intents, unsupported citations, omission loss, analyst override, severe false closure, response reversal, latency, connector errors, token cost, and trace loss. Use sequential monitoring cautiously: repeated peeking inflates false alarms. For operational guardrails, conservative anytime-valid bounds or predefined review windows are preferable to naive repeated p-values. Safety invariants do not require statistical significance; one confirmed cross-tenant disclosure is enough to stop.

Canary promotion is not automatic after elapsed time. Require minimum observations in each named segment, completion of delayed-label windows where relevant, and owner sign-off on the assurance delta.

Rollback and Forward Recovery

Rollback must include the entire behavior release, not only model routing. Restoring old weights while leaving the new policy or index active does not restore known behavior. Keep the last-known-good manifest deployable and verify it regularly.

Triggers are typed: immediate rollback for authority or privacy invariant breaches; pause and investigate for telemetry loss; segment rollback for localized quality degradation; traffic reduction for capacity or cost; and kill tool execution while retaining analysis during response-broker incidents. Every trigger has an owner, automated action, notification path, and maximum decision time.

Forward recovery is sometimes safer than full rollback when upstream schemas have migrated. The runbook states compatibility constraints. Preserve failed candidate traces before cleanup, revoke issued capabilities, identify side effects, and reconcile cases written during exposure.

Assurance Cases, Not Assurance Dashboards

A dashboard shows indicators. An assurance case explains why evidence supports a release claim. A lightweight Goal Structuring Notation-inspired record can be maintained as data:

claim: C0
text: Release 2026.08.3 may provide analyst drafts for scoped identity alerts.
context:
  - No autonomous response authority.
  - Excludes privileged identities and regulated tenants.
strategies:
  - id: S1
    text: Show investigation quality is not materially worse than incumbent.
  - id: S2
    text: Show authority, privacy, and tenant-isolation invariants hold.
  - id: S3
    text: Show online observability and rollback are effective.
evidence:
  - id: E1
    supports: S1
    artifact: replay-report/2026.08.3
    freshness_days: 2
  - id: E2
    supports: S2
    artifact: invariant-suite/22
    result: pass
  - id: E3
    supports: S3
    artifact: canary-drill/118
    result: rollback-in-94s
defeaters:
  - id: D1
    text: Identity connector changed pagination semantics after replay.
    status: monitored
residual_risk_owner: director-soc-engineering
expires: 2026-09-20

Claims are scoped and time-bound. Evidence has provenance and freshness. Defeaters record facts that could invalidate the inference. Exceptions name an owner and expiry. When scope expands to privileged identities or response actions, edit the top claim and supply new evidence; do not stretch the old case.

The assurance case also prevents metric theater. “Replay accuracy 94%” cannot support tenant isolation unless a strategy explains the connection. An expired rollback drill cannot indefinitely support operational recoverability.

Safe Lab: A Segmented Canary Gate

The lab compares observed canary losses with thresholds by segment and enforces hard invariants. It uses fabricated data and no external services.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Segment:
    name: str
    reviewed: int
    severe_errors: int
    overrides: int
    trace_missing: int
    min_reviewed: int
    max_severe: int
    max_override_rate: float
    max_trace_missing: int

segments = [
    Segment("common_draft", 240, 0, 18, 0, 200, 0, 0.10, 0),
    Segment("rare_alert", 38, 0, 3, 0, 50, 0, 0.12, 0),
    Segment("privileged", 22, 1, 4, 0, 20, 0, 0.10, 0),
]
hard_invariants = {"cross_tenant_disclosure": 0, "unauthorized_action": 0}

def decision(segment):
    if segment.severe_errors > segment.max_severe:
        return "ROLLBACK"
    if segment.trace_missing > segment.max_trace_missing:
        return "PAUSE"
    if segment.reviewed < segment.min_reviewed:
        return "HOLD"
    if segment.overrides / segment.reviewed > segment.max_override_rate:
        return "HOLD"
    return "PROMOTE"

for segment in segments:
    print(f"{segment.name}={decision(segment)}")
print("release=ROLLBACK" if any(hard_invariants.values()) or
      any(decision(s) == "ROLLBACK" for s in segments) else "release=NO_ROLLBACK")

Expected output:

common_draft=PROMOTE
rare_alert=HOLD
privileged=ROLLBACK
release=ROLLBACK

The common segment cannot compensate for a severe privileged error. The rare segment is held because evidence volume is insufficient, not because its observed rate looks bad. In production, the invariant counts come from separately validated telemetry with paging and case reconciliation.

Production Operating Model

Assign explicit roles: release owner, assurance reviewer, canary operator, incident commander, data steward, and segment owner. Separate the person who benefits from shipping from the person authorized to accept residual safety risk. Automate evidence assembly, not acceptance judgment.

The daily control plane verifies manifest signatures, trace completeness, version skew, connector contracts, assurance expiry, and last-known-good deployability. Weekly review examines segment outcomes, delayed labels, drift samples, evaluator changes, unresolved defeaters, and policy denials. Each material change creates an assurance delta identifying which claims and evidence are affected.

Monitor leading indicators such as schema violations, tool denials, evidence age, output entropy, retrieval mix, and analyst overrides, alongside lagging outcomes such as confirmed misses and harmful actions. Drift in an embedding distribution is a diagnostic, not a security outcome. Connect alerts to a runbook and a decision; otherwise monitoring becomes decorative.

A useful drift runbook starts with classification. For input drift, verify instrumentation and population eligibility before changing a model. For vocabulary or repository-pattern drift, refresh parsing, retrieval, prompts, or rules and replay the frozen corpus. For outcome drift, investigate label delay and adjudication changes before retraining. For operational drift, repair queues, connectors, rate limits, or timeouts. For policy drift, version the policy and recompute affected decisions. Any mitigation then re-enters replay, shadow, canary, and rollback gates; a drift alert is not permission for an unreviewed hot fix.

Incident response preserves the release manifest, prompts, evidence snapshot references, policy decisions, tool intents, approvals, outputs, and human edits. Determine scope by version and segment, not deployment timestamp alone. Notify affected owners, disable side effects, reconcile actions, and add sanitized incident variants to replay. Root-cause analysis asks which assurance claim failed, which defeater was missed, and why canary exposure did or did not bound harm.

  • NIST, SP 800-61 Rev. 2: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide, 2012: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-61r2

  • OWASP, Machine Learning Security Verification Standard: https://owasp.org/www-project-machine-learning-security-verification-standard/

SRE practice supplies bounded rollout and rollback mechanics; systems-security engineering supplies lifecycle assurance; GSN supplies explicit claim-evidence reasoning; incident guidance supplies preservation and response. AI RMF ties them to governed model risk. Their synthesis is a release process in which operational evidence continually updates a scoped assurance claim.

Interview Practicum

A bank wants to deploy a new model and retrieval index for an AI fraud-investigation assistant. Offline average accuracy improves two points. The candidate doubles abstentions for small-business accounts, has no replay coverage for Spanish cases, and once produced a cross-customer citation during red teaming. The current release cannot be exactly reconstructed because its index alias points to a mutable snapshot.

Prompt: Decide whether and how to release. After your plan, the platform team says rollback takes 25 minutes. Then a regulator asks what evidence supports the claim that customer isolation is preserved.

Strong questions identify the complete behavior manifest, authority scope, affected segments, hard invariants, evidence snapshot retention, delayed labels, assignment unit, expected volume, rollback side effects, evaluator independence, and who accepts residual risk.

Worked Answer

I would block customer-facing canarying initially. The cross-customer citation is a tenant-isolation invariant failure, not a quality tradeoff, and mutable replay inputs mean the two-point gain is weak evidence. I would first snapshot and hash the incumbent and candidate indexes, create complete behavior manifests, and reconstruct as much incumbent evidence as retention permits. The inability to reproduce history becomes an explicit assurance gap, not something hidden by rerunning against today’s index.

The candidate must pass an invariant suite containing the red-team case and structurally varied cross-customer cases. Retrieval authorization should filter by tenant before ranking, and the citation validator should independently reject mismatched subjects. I would add contract tests for index namespaces and trace every retrieved document’s tenant and digest.

For quality, I would report paired replay loss by consumer versus small-business, language, alert family, and case complexity. The doubled small-business abstention may represent safer uncertainty or harmful service degradation; review its reasons and time-to-resolution impact. Spanish coverage must be built before Spanish traffic is eligible. Overall accuracy cannot compensate for missing segment evidence.

Once invariants pass, begin shadow mode with live schema and latency checks. Canary only analyst-visible drafts, using stable customer-level assignment to avoid inconsistent case behavior. Start with internal and low-consequence English consumer segments, then deliberately gather evidence for small-business and Spanish cohorts. Each segment has minimum reviewed cases and separate guardrails. No autonomous action is in scope.

Twenty-five-minute rollback is too slow for isolation failure. Before canarying, add an immediate control-plane switch that disables candidate retrieval and tool output, targeting under two minutes, while full artifact rollback proceeds. Drill it and attach measured recovery time to the assurance case. The last-known-good release must include its pinned index, policy, prompts, and connectors.

For the regulator, I would provide a scoped assurance argument: tenant isolation is enforced before retrieval and independently at citation validation; evidence includes architecture review, invariant tests with hidden variants, shadow trace audits, canary observations, and a rollback drill. I would disclose residual limitations, evidence dates, excluded Spanish scope, the named risk owner, and expiry. A dashboard’s zero incidents is not the argument, especially with incomplete coverage.

Promotion occurs only when the cross-customer invariant has zero failures, trace completeness is complete enough to make that claim, each eligible segment meets its evidence minimum, abstention impacts are accepted, rollback is drilled, and the assurance reviewer signs the updated case. Any new index, policy, or model revision receives a new behavior release.

Follow-Up Questions and Answers

Why stable customer assignment instead of request assignment? It prevents one investigation from mixing behavior releases and makes side effects, analyst learning, and outcome attribution coherent.

What if exact replay is impossible for a hosted model? Preserve inputs, tool fixtures, parameters, provider version claims, and repeated behavioral samples. State the limitation and compensate with stronger shadowing and smaller canaries; do not call it exact replay.

Can a canary prove safety for rare privileged cases? Usually not through passive volume. Use targeted replay and controlled simulations, then a tiny consequence-budgeted canary with mandatory review. Absence of rare failures is weak evidence.

What belongs in an assurance-case defeater? Any plausible fact that breaks the claim-to-evidence inference: evaluator leakage, trace loss, an upstream schema change, stale index authorization, population drift, or an untested action path.

Key Takeaways

  • Version the complete behavior-producing assembly, including data and policy.
  • Replay historical evidence snapshots and state honestly when reproduction is approximate.
  • Gate on vectors and invariants; averages cannot compensate for isolation or authority failures.
  • Canary by consequence-relevant segment with stable assignment and exposure budgets.
  • Roll back the complete behavior release and drill fast side-effect shutdown.
  • Maintain a scoped, expiring assurance case with evidence, defeaters, and an accountable owner.

Field lesson: monitoring needs two release axes

The sec-pr platform passed its scoped engineering verification and exposed five assurance routes, while precision, recall, calibration, subgroup performance, and drift trends remained gated. Monitoring therefore reported platform health separately from detector evidence. This prevents a green dashboard from being interpreted as a green model. Chapter 47 shows the complete release boundary.

Chapter 41: Reproducible Security Analytics with Python and SQL

An investigation is reproducible only when another analyst can reconstruct the same evidence boundary, run the same transformations, and explain any difference in output. A notebook that still executes is not enough. Security data is corrected late, identity mappings change, intelligence feeds are revised, and labels arrive after decisions. Reproducibility therefore means preserving what was knowable at decision time, not merely preserving code.

This chapter builds an account-compromise analytic that produces a daily review queue. Its four invariants are: no feature uses evidence observed after cutoff; every output names its code, data, contract, and parameter versions; replaying one manifest produces identical logical rows; and ambiguous provenance or time semantics stop publication.

The Repository Is an Evidence Product

Use notebooks for exploration, but make reviewed modules and declarative queries authoritative:

security-analytics/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── contracts/auth_event.v3.json
├── sql/point_in_time_features.sql
├── src/sec_analytics/{normalize,manifest,pipeline}.py
├── tests/{fixtures,test_contract,test_point_in_time,test_replay}.py
├── notebooks/001-investigation.ipynb
├── manifests/
└── reports/

The README begins with the decision contract: “At 06:00 UTC, rank identities for analyst review using evidence observed by 05:55 UTC; never automatically disable an account.” That limits both data and authority. It also gives tests something operational to enforce.

Do not commit credentials, production extracts, or reversible identifiers. Synthetic fixtures should preserve late arrival, duplicate delivery, changed mappings, and boundary timestamps without preserving real users or attack detail.

flowchart LR
    P[Producer events] -->|contract v3| R[(Immutable raw snapshot)]
    R --> N[Normalize and deduplicate]
    I[(Identity snapshots)] --> J[As-of join]
    N --> J --> F[Point-in-time features] --> Q[Deterministic queue]
    Q --> O[Report and decision records]
    C[Code commit] --> M[Run manifest]
    D[Dependency lock] --> M
    R --> M
    I --> M
    M --> O
    T[Test suite] -. blocks .-> Q

Hashes prove that an artifact did not change after hashing. They do not prove the producer was truthful or the query correct.

A Point-in-Time Contract

An authentication contract needs temporal and provenance fields.

FieldRulePurpose
event_idnon-null, producer-stablededuplication and traceability
principal_keytokenizedstable analytical subject
event_timeUTC source timewhen behavior occurred
observed_atUTC collector timewhen the pipeline could know it
sourceidp, vpn, or cloudprovenance and coverage
outcomesuccess, failure, or challengedefined result
country_codeISO code or nullunknown is not zero
schema_versionexactly 3compatibility gate
payload_hashcanonical digestmutation detection

The producer owns field meaning and delivery expectations. The analytic owner owns acceptance rules. The platform owner owns retention and access. Changing challenge from “issued” to “completed” is breaking even if its SQL type is unchanged.

For cutoff \(t_c\), eligible evidence is

\[ \mathcal{E}(u,t_c)=\{e:e.principal=u,\ e.observed\_at\le t_c,\ e.event\_time\le t_c\}. \]

Using only event time leaks late records into historical replays. Using only observation time admits malformed future events. A correction received tomorrow belongs to tomorrow’s knowledge state unless the output is explicitly a revised historical result.

Identity joins are also temporal. If mappings have valid_from, valid_to, and recorded_at, a cutoff query requires both business validity and knowledge availability:

WITH eligible AS (
  SELECT * FROM auth_event
  WHERE event_time <= :cutoff AND observed_at <= :cutoff
    AND schema_version = 3
), mapped AS (
  SELECT e.*, m.employee_id
  FROM eligible e JOIN identity_map m
    ON e.principal_key = m.principal_key
   AND e.event_time >= m.valid_from
   AND e.event_time < COALESCE(m.valid_to, '9999-12-31')
   AND m.recorded_at <= :cutoff
)
SELECT employee_id, COUNT(*) AS attempts_24h,
       SUM(CASE WHEN outcome='failure' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failures_24h,
       COUNT(DISTINCT country_code) AS countries_24h
FROM mapped
WHERE event_time > :cutoff - INTERVAL '24 hours'
GROUP BY employee_id;

Database syntax varies; semantic tests should not. Define window inclusivity, null geography, time zones, and conflicting duplicates. Leaving those choices implicit destroys reproducibility.

Manifests and Deterministic Builds

Every published queue carries a manifest:

{
  "run_id": "ato-queue/2026-08-20T055500Z",
  "decision_cutoff": "2026-08-20T05:55:00Z",
  "code_revision": "8f31c2d",
  "dependency_lock_sha256": "21c8...",
  "contract": "auth_event.v3",
  "raw_snapshot": "auth/2026-08-20/snapshot-17",
  "identity_snapshot": "identity/2026-08-20/snapshot-04",
  "query_sha256": "a9de...",
  "parameters": {"window_hours": 24, "queue_size": 200},
  "row_count": 200,
  "logical_output_sha256": "55ae..."
}

Hash a canonical logical representation: stable columns, explicit nulls, normalized timestamps, defined numeric precision, and rows sorted by a total key. Parquet or gzip bytes can differ because of metadata while logical rows agree. Sorting only by score is insufficient when scores tie; use (-risk_score, employee_id).

If audit sampling uses randomness, record generator algorithm, seed, population hash, and code version. “Seed 42” alone is not portable across implementations.

Tests That Defend the Claim

Contract tests reject missing fields, incompatible versions, invalid enums, duplicate keys, and impossible timestamps. Named examples test semantics, not merely JSON types.

Transformation tests use tiny fixtures. Include events exactly at cutoff and just after, a late event, a conflicting duplicate, a mapping recorded after cutoff, and null geography.

Metamorphic tests assert that input permutation changes nothing, adding post-cutoff evidence changes no historical output, duplicate replay does not increase counts, and renaming a display field does not affect scores.

Golden replay tests compare a fixed manifest’s canonical output hash. Changes require human review. Automatically rewriting the golden hash turns a tripwire into decoration.

Tests must also assert failure: absent snapshot, unknown contract, ambiguous duplicate, or missing cutoff stops publication. A plausible report built from partial evidence is more dangerous than a visible failure.

Safe Lab: Replay a Tiny Pipeline

This standard-library program uses synthetic identities and in-memory SQLite. It performs no network or system action.

import hashlib, json, sqlite3
CUTOFF = "2026-08-20T05:55:00Z"
events = [
 ("e1","alice","2026-08-20T05:00:00Z","2026-08-20T05:00:02Z","failure"),
 ("e2","alice","2026-08-20T05:10:00Z","2026-08-20T06:10:00Z","failure"),
 ("e3","bob",  "2026-08-20T05:55:00Z","2026-08-20T05:55:00Z","success"),
 ("e4","bob",  "2026-08-20T05:56:00Z","2026-08-20T05:54:00Z","failure"),
 ("e5","carol","2026-08-20T04:00:00Z","2026-08-20T04:00:01Z","failure"),
]
def build(rows):
    db=sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE auth(event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, principal TEXT, event_time TEXT, observed_at TEXT, outcome TEXT)")
    db.executemany("INSERT INTO auth VALUES(?,?,?,?,?)", rows)
    result=db.execute("""SELECT principal,COUNT(*),SUM(outcome='failure')
      FROM auth WHERE event_time<=? AND observed_at<=?
      GROUP BY principal ORDER BY 3 DESC,principal ASC""",(CUTOFF,CUTOFF)).fetchall()
    canonical=json.dumps(result,separators=(",",":"))
    return result,hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
baseline,digest=build(events)
permuted,digest2=build(list(reversed(events)))
with_future,digest3=build(events+[("e6","alice","2026-08-20T05:20:00Z","2026-08-20T07:00:00Z","failure")])
assert baseline==[("alice",1,1),("carol",1,1),("bob",1,0)]
assert baseline==permuted==with_future
assert digest==digest2==digest3
print(baseline); print("replay_hash",digest); print("point_in_time_tests PASS")

Expected output:

[('alice', 1, 1), ('carol', 1, 1), ('bob', 1, 0)]
replay_hash d3b5c1dfe930
point_in_time_tests PASS

e4 was observed before cutoff but claims a future event time, so it is excluded. e2 and e6 occurred before cutoff but were not yet observed. Production code would quarantine excessive clock skew.

Production Failure Drill: The Helpful Backfill

At 09:00, the identity platform repairs three missing hours. The scheduled job overwrites the 06:00 report. The revision is statistically better but operationally false: analysts acted on the original queue, and their evidence has disappeared.

In staging, publish manifest M1; inject a late partition; rerun M1 and verify its snapshot retains the original hash; publish immutable revision M2 linked by late-data-correction; prove decision records retain M1; then reconcile decisions that would change.

The stop condition is a mutable snapshot, overwritten report, or decision without a manifest. Containment disables publication, not ingestion. Recovery restores snapshot immutability and replays both versions. The analytic owner declares output correctness; the platform owner repairs snapshot guarantees; the incident commander coordinates consumers.

Review, Promotion, and Retirement

A pull request shows the changed decision, contract compatibility, fixture additions, query plan, expected cost, temporal tests, privacy review, and a manifest from a clean build. Review SQL and Python together: a sound function fed by a leaky query is wrong.

Review the analytical diff, not only the source diff

A five-line SQL edit can reorder thousands of investigations. Code review therefore needs an analytical diff: run incumbent and candidate against the same frozen manifests and summarize added, removed, and re-ranked subjects. Partition disagreements by cause—new eligibility, feature change, score change, tie-breaking, missing evidence, or policy threshold. For each category, include counts, representative synthetic or authorized examples, and affected consequence segments.

Suppose a change replaces COUNT(DISTINCT country_code) with a mapping from IP to travel region. A source diff shows a join and a grouping change. The analytical diff should show that 18% of identities lose one “country,” that airport egress users move down the queue, that null geography increases in one source, and that the top-200 overlap is 82%. Reviewers can then decide whether the change fixes false diversity or conceals a coverage regression.

Compare outputs under at least three manifests: a normal day, a known late-data day, and an edge-case fixture. Report set overlap, rank correlation where meaningful, action transitions, group coverage, and output invariants. A high rank correlation can still hide a severe subject crossing an action threshold; always inspect decision changes directly.

The query plan is also evidence. Capture scanned partitions, join strategy, estimated rows, runtime, and bytes processed under a representative snapshot. A semantically correct query that unpredictably scans an entire authentication lake is not ready for a scheduled production deadline. Place a cost ceiling in the run contract and fail before publication when the ceiling is exceeded, unless an authorized override names the reason and expiry.

Clean-room reconstruction

Before first production release, ask an engineer who did not write the analytic to reconstruct one report from the repository and manifest in a clean environment. Give that person read access only to the declared snapshots and artifact registry. They should not need the author’s shell history, notebook state, personal configuration, or undocumented warehouse table.

The reconstruction record answers:

  • Could dependencies be installed from the lock without contacting an unapproved package source?
  • Did the manifest identify every input, including lookup tables and policy parameters?
  • Did the environment use the expected timezone, locale, and SQL engine settings?
  • Did the canonical rows and reason codes match?
  • If physical files differed, was the difference limited to declared metadata?
  • Could the reviewer trace one queue row back to eligible source events without privileged raw identifiers in the report?

Clean-room failure is useful. If the analytic relies on a hidden notebook cell or an analyst’s temporary table, the organization has found the defect before an audit or incident. Record the fix as a repository change; do not solve the exercise by granting broad access or copying an unexplained table.

Data minimization and reproducibility

Reproducibility does not require retaining every raw field forever. It requires retaining enough authorized evidence to support the declared audit and replay claims. Classify fields as transformation inputs, trace references, sensitive investigation content, or irrelevant payload.
